entries.q: How do I hand-pollinate squash for pure seed?
entries.a: Tape a female blossom shut in the evening, hand-pollinate with a chosen male flower at dawn, then re-tape. Mark the fruit for seed. This isolates pollen when multiple squash varieties are flowering.

entries.q: What are biennial seed crops?
entries.a: Carrots, beets, cabbage, and onions flower in their second year, so roots or plants must survive winter—in ground under mulch or stored and replanted—before yielding seed. Plan ahead or keep purchased seed of biennials as backup. Do not expect seed from first-year roots.

entries.q: How do I save dry seeds like beans and lettuce?
entries.a: Let seed mature on the plant until pods rattle or heads brown, finish drying indoors on screens, then thresh and winnow chaff away in a light breeze. Store only snap-dry seed. Label variety and year immediately.

entries.q: How do I save tomato seed?
entries.a: Scoop seeds from fully ripe fruit and ferment with pulp and a splash of water 2–3 days until a film forms, then rinse clean and dry on a plate or coffee filter. Fermentation removes germination-inhibiting gel and reduces some diseases. Dry until seeds snap, not bend.

entries.q: How do I save cucumber or squash seed?
entries.a: Take seed from fully ripe fruit, rinse clean, and dry until snap-dry on a non-stick surface. For purity, control pollination because cucurbits cross readily. Do not save from immature eating-stage fruit.

entries.q: How should I store vegetable seeds?
entries.a: Enemies are moisture, heat, and light. Store bone-dry seed in paper envelopes inside an airtight jar in a cool dark place, with silica gel or a cloth-wrapped spoon of dry rice or powdered milk. Label variety and year; refrigerator storage extends life.

entries.q: Can I freeze garden seeds?
entries.a: Yes—truly dry seed stores for many extra years in the freezer. Let jars reach room temperature before opening to avoid condensation on cold seed. Freezing damp seed ruins it.

entries.q: How long do vegetable seeds stay viable?
entries.a: Typical well-stored viability: onions/parsnips 1–2 years; corn, peppers, carrots 2–3; beans, peas, brassicas, squash, tomatoes 3–5+ (tomatoes often longer); lettuce 5–6. Refrigeration roughly doubles these spans. Test doubtful lots each spring.

entries.q: How do I test seed germination?
entries.a: Roll 10 seeds in a damp paper towel inside a loosely closed bag somewhere warm; check after the packet’s germination window. 8–10 sprouts means sow normally; 5–7 sow thickly; under 5 replace or sow very thickly. Test before the season, not during panic.

entries.q: How do I build a household seed bank?
entries.a: Keep three tiers: this year’s working seed, a reserve of last year’s proven varieties, and a deep frozen reserve of core calorie crops enough to replant everything twice. Refresh deep reserves by growing them out every few years. Prioritize OP potatoes (tubers), dry beans, winter squash, kale, cabbage, carrots, onions, and tomatoes.

entries.q: Should I save hybrid seed?
entries.a: You can grow F1 hybrid seed for experiments, but plants will not stay true to the parent. For reliability and trading, save open-pollinated varieties only. Buy hybrids knowingly when you want that specific season’s performance.

entries.q: Why must seed be snap-dry before storage?
entries.a: A seed that bends still holds moisture and will mold or die in jars. Dry until seeds snap cleanly, then package with a humidity guard. Moisture is the first enemy of stored seed.

entries.q: How do I label saved seed?
entries.a: Write variety name and year on every envelope before you forget—memory fails by February. Add notes on plant performance if useful. Unlabeled jars become mysteries you will not trust in a crisis.

entries.q: Can I trade seed locally?
entries.a: Yes—locally saved open-pollinated seed is often pre-adapted to your conditions, and swaps build useful community networks. Share only well-dried, honestly labeled seed. Avoid spreading diseased plant material with seed gifts.

entries.q: How do I save potato “seed”?
entries.a: Save small healthy tubers for replanting, knowing disease can accumulate over years—refresh with certified seed potatoes when possible. Store like eating potatoes cool and dark, not in the freezer. Potatoes are a top calorie crop worth keeping in the household seed/tuber bank.

entries.q: How do I winnow seeds?
entries.a: After threshing, pour seed between bowls in a light breeze so chaff blows away while heavier seed falls. Repeat until clean. Work over a sheet so you can recover seed if wind gusts.

entries.q: Do peppers cross-pollinate?
entries.a: Peppers are mostly self-pollinating but can cross with help from insects. For pure seed, separate varieties or bag flower clusters. Hot and sweet types can cross, surprising next year’s fruit heat.

entries.q: Why ferment tomato seeds before drying?
entries.a: A short ferment dissolves the gel that inhibits germination and helps kill some seed-borne diseases. Two to three days until a film forms is enough, then rinse and dry. Skipping ferment still can work but is less ideal for storage seed.

entries.q: Where should I keep working seed during the season?
entries.a: Keep this year’s working seed cool, dark, and dry in labeled envelopes—kitchen heat and humidity shorten life. A jar in a cupboard beats a shed that bakes. Move long-term reserves to the fridge or freezer.

entries.q: What core crops belong in a deep seed reserve?
entries.a: Prioritize open-pollinated dry beans, winter squash, kale, cabbage, carrots, onions, tomatoes, and potato tubers, plus a grain if you have space. Keep enough to replant twice and grow out to refresh. Calorie and storage crops come before novelty varieties.

entries.q: Can I dry seeds on a paper towel?
entries.a: Avoid paper towels for wet-processed seed—they glue themselves down. Use a plate or coffee filter instead, then package only when snap-dry. Good drying prevents storage mold.

entries.q: When should I harvest vegetables?
entries.a: Pick in the cool of morning and handle gently—bruises rot first. Learn crop cues: beans and zucchini small and often; tomatoes at full color; potatoes after tops die back; onions/garlic when tops fall; winter squash when rinds resist a thumbnail. Frequent harvest keeps many plants producing.

entries.q: How do I harvest leafy greens?
entries.a: Use cut-and-come-again: take outer leaves and let the plant keep producing from the center. Morning harvest keeps leaves crisp. Avoid stripping the whole plant unless you want a final cut.

entries.q: How do I know potatoes are ready?
entries.a: Harvest after tops die back for storage potatoes, then cure 1–2 weeks in a dark, airy place so skins set. New potatoes can be stolen earlier carefully from the edges. Damaged tubers eat first; store only sound ones.

entries.q: How do I harvest and cure onions and garlic?
entries.a: Harvest when tops fall, then cure until necks are papery in a dry, airy place. Store cold and dry in mesh bags or braids. Soft or thick-necked bulbs keep poorly—use them first.

entries.q: How do I harvest winter squash for storage?
entries.a: Pick when rinds resist a thumbnail, leave stems on, and cure warm for about two weeks. Store cool and dry around 10–15 °C. Cuts and missing stems invite rot in storage.

entries.q: Should I pick beans and zucchini young?
entries.a: Yes—pick small and often so plants keep producing instead of shifting to seed. Oversized zucchini and tough beans signal you waited too long. Check plants every day or two in peak season.

entries.q: Can I ripen green tomatoes indoors?
entries.a: Yes—before hard frost, pick sound green tomatoes and ripen indoors in a single layer out of direct harsh sun. Compost damaged fruit. This salvages late fruit that would otherwise freeze on the vine.

entries.q: How should I handle produce after harvest?
entries.a: Handle like eggs—bruises become rot in storage. Keep dirt off cuts, cool produce quickly when possible, and sort out damaged pieces before storing. Clean, gentle handling extends every preservation method.

entries.q: When do I harvest dry beans?
entries.a: Leave pods on the plant until they dry and rattle, then finish drying indoors before shelling. Store bone-dry beans in airtight containers. Damp beans mold in storage.

entries.q: How do I harvest cabbage for storage?
entries.a: Cut firm heads and keep outer leaves on for cold, humid storage. Avoid bruised heads in the long-term pile. Use split or damaged heads first through fermentation or cooking.

entries.q: How do I store vegetables without a root cellar?
entries.a: Match crop needs: potatoes and most roots want cold humid 4–8 °C (basement corner, insulated garage box, buried barrel, or in-ground clamp); onions and garlic cold dry in mesh; winter squash cool dry 10–15 °C; cabbage cold humid. Check every couple of weeks and remove anything softening. Carrots and beets keep well in barely damp sand.

entries.q: How do I store carrots and beets?
entries.a: Layer carrots and beets in boxes of barely damp sand in a cold place around 4–8 °C. Trim tops, keep roots undamaged, and check periodically for soft spots. This mimics root-cellar humidity without a dedicated cellar.

entries.q: What conditions do potatoes need in storage?
entries.a: Store cured potatoes cold and humid, about 4–8 °C, dark and ventilated. One rotten potato spoils neighbors—inspect often. Avoid storing with apples if sprouting becomes a problem in your setup.

entries.q: How do I make sauerkraut?
entries.a: Shred cabbage, add 2% salt by weight (20 g per kg), massage until brine flows, pack below brine with a weight, and ferment loosely covered at cool room temperature 1–4 weeks, then cold-store. Cloudy brine and a sour smell are normal; skim white kahm yeast; discard fuzzy or foul growth. The same salt-and-brine method works for many vegetables.

entries.q: What is lacto-fermentation for vegetables?
entries.a: Lacto-fermentation preserves vegetables with only salt and time—no electricity—while adding vitamins and probiotics. Keep veggies submerged under brine; cool room temperature for days to weeks, then cold storage. Master cabbage, then apply the method to carrots, beets, turnips, beans, and cucumbers.

entries.q: Is white film on ferment bad?
entries.a: A white surface film is often kahm yeast—skim it off if the ferment otherwise smells pleasantly sour. Fuzzy mold or a foul smell means discard. Keep vegetables under brine with a weight to reduce surface issues.

entries.q: How do I dry herbs and vegetables?
entries.a: Hang herbs in bunches; dry fruit, tomatoes, mushrooms, and thin slices in a dehydrator, low oven with door cracked, or sun in dry climates until leathery to brittle. Blanch most vegetables briefly before drying. Store airtight and dark.

entries.q: Which foods can I water-bath can?
entries.a: High-acid foods—jams, fruit, vinegar pickles, and tomatoes with added lemon juice or citric acid—are suitable for boiling-water bath canning. Follow tested recipes exactly. Low-acid plain vegetables and meat need a pressure canner, not a water bath.

entries.q: When do I need a pressure canner?
entries.a: Use a pressure canner for low-acid foods such as plain vegetables, meat, and broth, following tested recipes exactly. Water-bath canning is unsafe for these. When in doubt, freeze, dry, or ferment instead.

entries.q: Is freezing a good long-term survival strategy?
entries.a: Freezing preserves quality well but depends on electricity. Treat the freezer as short-tier storage and keep deep stores in dried, canned, fermented, and cellared forms. A full freezer stays safer longer unopened—about 48 hours vs roughly 24 if half full.

entries.q: How long does a freezer stay cold in an outage?
entries.a: A full freezer holds safe temperatures roughly 48 hours if unopened; about 24 hours if half full. Frozen bottles of water inside buy more thermal mass. If thawing meat warms above 4 °C for more than a couple of hours, pressure-can, dry, brine, cook, or share it promptly.

entries.q: How do I make an in-ground clamp for roots?
entries.a: Pile cured roots or potatoes, cover with straw and soil for insulation, and mark the spot for winter access. This buried cache keeps produce cold and humid without a basement. Check for water intrusion and rodents.

entries.q: How do I store onions and garlic long term?
entries.a: Cure until necks are papery, then hang in mesh in a cold, dry place. Humidity softens and spoils alliums—keep them away from damp root stores. Use thick-necked bulbs first.

entries.q: What temperature for winter squash storage?
entries.a: After warm curing, store winter squash cool and dry around 10–15 °C—warmer and drier than potato storage. Keep stems on and wipe only dirty spots; do not wash before storage. Check for soft spots regularly.

entries.q: Can I ferment vegetables other than cabbage?
entries.a: Yes—use the same ~2% salt-by-weight method for carrots, beets, turnips, green beans, and cucumbers; add a grape or oak leaf for cucumber crunch if available. Keep food under brine and watch for true mold. Fermentation needs no special starter culture for these vegetables.

entries.q: Should I blanch vegetables before drying?
entries.a: Blanch most vegetables briefly before drying to help preserve color and vitamins. Herbs are typically dried without blanching. Cool quickly, then dry until leathery to brittle and store airtight in the dark.

entries.q: What is a safe fallback if I am unsure about canning?
entries.a: If you are unsure whether a food is safe to can with your equipment, freeze, dry, or ferment instead. Botulism risk makes improvising low-acid canning dangerous. Use tested recipes only for canning.

entries.q: How often should I check stored crops?
entries.a: Inspect cellared or boxed stores every couple of weeks and remove anything softening immediately—one rotten potato can spoil the box. Good airflow and correct temperature reduce losses. Eat the borderline produce first.

entries.q: How do I dry tomatoes?
entries.a: Slice ripe tomatoes and dry in a dehydrator, low oven with door cracked, or hot dry sun until leathery. Store airtight and dark. Dried tomatoes concentrate flavor and keep without freezer space.

entries.q: Where can I store cabbage without a cellar?
entries.a: Keep cabbage cold and humid with outer leaves on—a cool basement corner or insulated box can work. Avoid freezing solid and thawing repeatedly. Ferment surplus as sauerkraut for long keeping.

entries.q: How do I grow tomatoes successfully?
entries.a: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost, give strong light, harden off, and plant in full sun with support and steady deep watering. Use open-pollinated varieties if you want to save seed. Blossom problems often trace to cold nights, heat spikes, or uneven water.

entries.q: How do I grow lettuce without bolting too fast?
entries.a: Sow succession plantings every 2–3 weeks, give partial shade in heat, and harvest outer leaves often. Hot, dry stress triggers bolting. Choose heat-tolerant varieties for summer and grow prime crops in spring and autumn.

entries.q: How do I grow beans for food storage?
entries.a: Direct sow after frost danger, give them space or a trellis, and let drying types mature until pods rattle. Shell only when snap-dry and store airtight. Dry beans are a core calorie and seed-bank crop.

entries.q: How do I grow cabbage in a home garden?
entries.a: Start transplants 4–6 weeks before last frost or buy sturdy starts, plant with firm soil contact, and use row cover against moths. Rotate brassicas yearly and harvest firm heads for storage or sauerkraut. Consistent water prevents split heads.

entries.q: Why did my squash plants flower but make no fruit?
entries.a: Squash needs pollination—bees move pollen from male to female flowers; poor weather or row cover left on during bloom blocks fruit set. Hand-pollinate if needed and remove cover once flowers open. Excess nitrogen can also favor vines over fruit.

entries.q: Why are my carrot seedlings sparse?
entries.a: Carrot seed is small, short-lived (often 2–3 years), and needs evenly moist fine soil without crusting. Sow shallow, keep the surface damp until germination, and thin for proper spacing. Fresh seed and a board or row cover to hold moisture help.

entries.q: What basic tools do I need for a vegetable garden?
entries.a: A sturdy spade or border fork, hand trowel, hoe, watering can or hose with a gentle nozzle, pruners, and a soil knife or weeding tool cover most tasks. Add a wheelbarrow and rake as beds grow. Sharp, clean tools beat a shed full of gadgets.

entries.q: What tools help with seed starting?
entries.a: Useful gear includes drainage trays, clean 5–8 cm cells, sterile mix, a humidity dome, a simple LED grow light on a timer, and optionally a heat mat for peppers and tomatoes. A small fan strengthens stems. You do not need a greenhouse to start well.

entries.q: Why do my peppers stay small and few?
entries.a: Peppers need warmth, full sun, and a long enough season—start 6–8 weeks indoors and harden off carefully. Cold soil stunts them; uneven water causes blossom drop. Choose earlier varieties in short summers.

entries.q: What causes blossom end rot on tomatoes?
entries.a: Blossom end rot is usually uneven watering and calcium uptake stress, not simply “not enough calcium in soil.” Keep moisture steady with mulch and deep watering, and avoid wild wet-dry swings. Damaged fruit should be removed; new fruit can form normally once water is steady.

entries.q: Why do my beans get powdery leaves or spots?
entries.a: Leaf diseases increase with wet foliage, crowding, and reused bean ground. Water soil not leaves, space for airflow, rotate legumes, and bin badly infected debris. Healthy soil and morning watering reduce pressure.

entries.q: How do I use a hoe effectively?
entries.a: Hoe shallowly while weeds are small, preferably on a dry day, without chopping into crop roots. Permanent paths and mulch cut how often you need the hoe. A sharp blade makes light scuffling enough.

entries.q: What failure kills new gardeners’ seedlings most often?
entries.a: The classic killers are damping-off from dirty wet conditions and leggy collapse from weak light. Use sterile mix, bottom water, airflow, and lights 5–10 cm above plants. Hardening off poorly is the next outdoor killer.

entries.q: How do I grow kale as a reliable food crop?
entries.a: Transplant or sow in time for cool weather, give moderate fertility and steady water, and harvest outer leaves ongoing. Kale survives hard frost and remains a winter vitamin crop under light protection. Save open-pollinated seed from strong plants in year two if biennial flowering is allowed.

entries.q: What should I do when a whole bed fails?
entries.a: Diagnose before replanting: water extremes, poor sun, pests, wrong season, or exhausted soil each need different fixes. Re-compost, rotate families, and try a forgiving succession crop like beans or greens. Write what failed so next year’s calendar changes.

entries.q: How do I grow mint?
entries.a: Mint is vigorous: plant in a pot or contained bed so it does not take over. Moist soil, part sun to shade, and regular harvesting keep it productive. Root divisions in spring expand your stock. This is the culinary herb — not Qortal minting.

entries.q: What is composting?
entries.a: Composting is controlled rotting of plant and kitchen scraps into humus-rich soil amendment. Mix browns (dry carbon: leaves, cardboard) with greens (nitrogen: food scraps, fresh cuttings), keep lightly moist and aerated, and avoid meat/dairy/oils in simple home piles. Finished compost feeds soil life and reduces landfill waste. Trench composting buries scraps directly in beds; hot piles heat when large and turned.

entries.q: What tools belong in a basic home kit?
entries.a: A kit that handles most jobs: claw hammer, multi-bit screwdriver (PH/PZ/flat/Torx), adjustable wrench, locking and needle-nose pliers, utility knife with spare blades, tape measure, spirit level, handsaw, cordless drill with bits, hex keys, duct and electrical tape, super glue and epoxy, wood glue, penetrating oil plus lubricating oil, screws/nails/wall plugs, zip ties, wire, sandpaper, work gloves, safety glasses, and a headlamp. Add a stud/cable finder before drilling walls and a voltage tester before any electrical work.

entries.q: What is the difference between penetrating oil and lubricating oil?
entries.a: Penetrating oil (like WD-40-type sprays) creeps into rusted threads and frees stuck parts. Lubricating oil stays put and keeps moving parts moving. They are not the same job — free first with penetrant, then protect with real oil so the problem does not return.

entries.q: Why should I own a voltage tester pen?
entries.a: A non-contact voltage tester lets you confirm a circuit is dead before you touch wires or fittings. Always test the tester on a known live outlet first, then on the work, then re-check the known live outlet. Never assume a breaker is off until you have verified it at the point of work.

entries.q: When do I need a stud finder?
entries.a: Use a stud/cable finder before drilling into walls so you hit framing when you need strength and avoid cables and pipes when you do not. Mark both edges of the stud, drill a small pilot hole, and stop if you feel unexpected resistance or see dust that looks like plastic insulation.

entries.q: What safety gear belongs with every tool kit?
entries.a: Keep work gloves, safety glasses, and a headlamp with the tools — not in another room. Eyes and hands are the usual casualties of rushed jobs. A headlamp frees both hands and lights the work instead of casting shadows from a handheld torch.

entries.q: How should I store hand tools so they last?
entries.a: Wipe tools clean after use, dry them, and wipe metal with a light film of oil. Hang or rack them so edges are protected and moisture does not sit in a closed damp box. Wooden handles get a yearly coat of linseed oil so they do not crack and splinter.

entries.q: What fastener assortment should I keep at home?
entries.a: Keep a mixed tin of wood screws, machine screws, nails, and wall plugs in common sizes, plus a few spare nuts and washers. Matching the plug to the wall (plasterboard, brick, concrete) matters more than owning every screw length. Zip ties and a coil of soft wire cover countless temporary fixes.

entries.q: Why keep both duct tape and electrical tape?
entries.a: Duct tape is for temporary mechanical holds and sealing drafts — not for live electrical joints. Electrical tape is for insulating and bundling wires where heat and flex matter. Using the wrong tape can fail under load or create a fire risk; keep both and use each for its job.

entries.q: What should I know before buying a cordless drill?
entries.a: A mid-range cordless drill with a charger, spare battery if you can, and a mixed bit set covers hanging shelves, assembling furniture, and driving screws. Learn clutch settings so you do not strip soft wood, and keep a masonry bit for brick and a wood bit set for timber. Torque control prevents more damage than raw power fixes.

entries.q: How do hex keys (Allen keys) help around the house?
entries.a: Hex keys tighten the recessed bolts on flat-pack furniture, bike components, and many appliances. Keep a full metric set; most modern hardware is millimetre-sized. The correct size seats fully — a rounded hex usually means the wrong size or a worn tool.

entries.q: Why keep spare utility knife blades?
entries.a: A sharp blade cuts where you aim with less force; a dull one slips. Swap blades when cutting cardboard or tape starts to tear instead of slice, and dispose of used blades in a sealed tin. Never leave an open knife in a toolbox where hands reach blindly.

entries.q: What is a spirit level used for in home repairs?
entries.a: A spirit level shows when a surface is horizontal or vertical so shelves, pictures, and appliance legs sit true. Check both directions on long runs, and mark a light pencil line before drilling. A few millimetres of tilt becomes obvious once something heavy sits on a shelf.

entries.q: Which household shutoffs should everyone know?
entries.a: Locate and physically test four controls: main water shutoff (label it), water heater valve, gas shutoff (know which tool it needs and keep that tool nearby), and the main electrical breaker. Everyone in the household should know all four. Practising once in calm weather beats learning during a flood or gas leak.

entries.q: What do I do if a pipe bursts?
entries.a: Shut the main water off first. If water is near wiring or outlets, shut the electricity at the main breaker next. Open taps downhill of the leak to drain remaining pressure, then contain the water with towels and a bucket. Call for help once the house is safer — water off beats mopping while it still sprays.

entries.q: What should I do if I smell gas?
entries.a: Do not flip switches, light flames, or use phones inside. Get everyone out, turn the gas valve off only if you can reach it safely on the way, then call the emergency gas line from outside. Ventilate from outdoors if instructed. Treat any strong gas smell as urgent, not something to investigate with a lighter.

entries.q: How do I label home shutoffs clearly?
entries.a: Use waterproof tags or paint-marker labels at each valve and breaker: Main Water, Water Heater, Gas, Main Power. Add a simple arrow for open/closed if the handle is confusing. A torch and a laminated card by the door listing locations helps guests and children act without searching.

entries.q: Where is the main water shutoff usually found?
entries.a: Often near where the supply enters the building — basement, utility cupboard, under the kitchen sink, or in a meter box outside. Turn it only as far as it will go without forcing; if it is stiff, work it gently a few times a year so it does not seize. Know whether yours is a lever (90°) or a multi-turn valve.

entries.q: Why keep the gas shutoff tool next to the valve?
entries.a: Some gas valves need a specific key or wrench. If that tool lives in a drawer upstairs, you will not find it in the dark during an emergency. Keep the correct tool tied or hung at the valve, and show every adult where it is during your shutoff drill.

entries.q: What is the difference between a room breaker and the main breaker?
entries.a: Individual breakers cut power to one circuit (lights, kitchen, etc.). The main breaker kills everything from the panel. For floods near wiring or major electrical smells, use the main. For a single faulty appliance circuit, switching that one breaker is enough and keeps the rest of the house usable.

entries.q: How often should I test shutoff valves?
entries.a: Turn each critical valve fully off and back on once or twice a year so seals do not stick. Do this when you can tolerate a short water or heating interruption. If a valve will not move, do not muscle it until it snaps — plan a replacement before you need it in a crisis.

entries.q: What should children know about household emergencies?
entries.a: Age-appropriately: where to meet outside, how to leave without hunting for shoes, and who to tell. Older children can learn which adult turns water or gas and that they must not touch electrical panels alone. Calm rehearsal builds competence; fear lectures do not.

entries.q: Why shut electricity if water is near wiring?
entries.a: Water and energised circuits are a shock and fire risk. If a leak, flood, or spray is approaching outlets, switches, or appliances, cut power at the main before wading in. Never stand in water to unplug something that may still be live.

entries.q: How do I unclog a drain without harsh chemicals?
entries.a: Start with a cup plunger: enough water to cover the cup, firm seals, and steady thrusts. If that fails, place a bucket under the U-bend (trap), loosen the slip nuts, empty the trap, and clear debris. Skip caustic drain openers — they rarely finish the job and make later hand work dangerous.

entries.q: How do I stop a running toilet?
entries.a: Lift the lid and watch: a worn flapper that does not seal, or a float set too high so water never stops, causes most continuous runs. Adjust the float so the water stops 2–3 cm below the overflow tube, or replace the flapper. A running toilet can waste hundreds of litres a day.

entries.q: How do I replace a tap washer or cartridge?
entries.a: Shut the water to that tap or the main, open the tap to drain pressure, then dismantle in order — photograph each layer with your phone or paper sketch. Replace the washer or cartridge with the matching size, reassemble hand-tight plus a snug finish, and restore water slowly while watching for leaks.

entries.q: How do I patch a small drywall or plasterboard hole?
entries.a: For small holes, seat a self-adhesive mesh patch or backer, spread thin layers of joint compound, let each dry, then sand flush and paint. Deep holes need a scrap backing screwed or glued behind the opening first. Thin coats beat one thick blob that cracks and shrinks.

entries.q: How do I fix a door that sticks?
entries.a: Tighten hinge screws first — a longer screw into the frame often pulls the door back into alignment. Check for swollen wood after damp weather and plane or sand the rub point lightly if needed. Confirm the latch meets the strike plate before you cut anything permanently.

entries.q: How do I bleed a radiator?
entries.a: With the heating on, hold a rag under the bleed valve and open it slowly with a radiator key until the hiss of air becomes a steady water trickle, then close. Top up system pressure if your boiler gauge drops below the marked range. Cold tops with hot bottoms usually mean trapped air.

entries.q: What plug and fuse skills are worth learning?
entries.a: Where local rules allow DIY: learn correct wiring colours for your region, firm cord grip, and the right fuse rating for the appliance. If you are unsure, stop and use a qualified person — electricity mistakes are not practice projects. A voltage tester and power off are non-negotiable before opening anything.

entries.q: What car basics should every driver practise?
entries.a: Practise changing a wheel at home: jack points, loosen nuts before lifting, and lower fully before final tightening in a star pattern. Learn correct jump-start cable order, check oil and coolant when the engine is cool, and replace wipers and bulbs before they fail in rain. Confidence on the driveway beats learning on a dark roadside.

entries.q: How do I use a plunger correctly?
entries.a: Choose a flange plunger for toilets and a cup plunger for sinks. Seal the overflow on sinks with a wet cloth, keep water over the cup, and push-pull with steady force rather than splashing. Ten controlled strokes often beat random slamming.

entries.q: Why avoid chemical drain cleaners?
entries.a: Caustic and acid cleaners can burn skin, damage pipes, and leave a hazardous soup if you later open the trap by hand. Mechanical clearing — plunger, auger, trap removal — solves the clog and stays safer for the next person who works on the pipe.

entries.q: How do I tighten a loose chair or table joint?
entries.a: Clean old glue from the joint if it is open, apply wood glue, clamp square overnight, and wipe squeeze-out. For screws that spin in stripped wood, use a longer screw, a matchstick-and-glue plug, or a wall plug sized to the hole. Stability comes from glue surface and clamp pressure, not more screws alone.

entries.q: How do I hang a heavy shelf safely?
entries.a: Find studs and drive screws into timber framing whenever the load is real books or tools. Use rated anchors only when studs are impossible, and match anchor type to wall material. A spirit level and two-person lift prevent the “almost level” shelf that creeps over months.

entries.q: How do I silence a squeaky hinge?
entries.a: A drop of light lubricating oil or graphite at the hinge pin usually works. Lift or tap the pin slightly to let oil travel, wipe excess so it does not stain floors, and open-close the door to work it in. Penetrant can free a seized pin; follow with real lubricant.

entries.q: How do I reset a tripped breaker safely?
entries.a: Move the breaker fully to Off, then back to On. If it trips again immediately, leave it off and unplug devices on that circuit before retrying once. Repeated trips mean overload or a fault — find the cause rather than holding the breaker on.

entries.q: How do I stop a minor leak under a sink temporarily?
entries.a: Shut water, dry the area, and use a rubber patch with a hose clamp or proper repair tape rated for plumbing as a short-term hold. Buckets and a phone call for parts beat ignoring drips that ruin cabinets. Temporary fixes are for hours or days, not permanent plumbing.

entries.q: What is a simple way to free a stuck jar lid or bolt?
entries.a: For lids: rubber grip, tap around the rim, or warm the metal lid under hot water so it expands. For bolts: penetrant, time, and alternating gentle tighten-loosen; heat only when you understand fire risk around the part. Force that rounds the head makes the job harder.

entries.q: How do I replace a broken light bulb safely?
entries.a: Power off at the switch (or breaker for stubborn fixtures), let the bulb cool, and use a dry cloth or glove for grip. For glass that breaks in the socket, power must stay off — press a raw potato or folded cardboard into the base to unscrew, or use a proper bulb extractor. Match wattage and fitting type.

entries.q: How do I fix a running or dripping outdoor tap in frost season?
entries.a: Drain outdoor taps before hard frost, isolate indoor valves feeding them, and leave the outdoor valve open after draining so residual water can expand without cracking. Insulate exposed pipes where you can. A cracked outdoor tap in spring is usually winter water that had nowhere to go.

entries.q: How do I sharpen a kitchen knife with a whetstone?
entries.a: Use a two-sided stone: coarse (~400–1000 grit) to set the edge, fine (~3000+) to polish. Hold a consistent ~20° angle, edge trailing, until a burr forms along the other side; flip, repeat, then strip the burr and finish on a strop or cardboard. Wet the stone as its type requires, and go slow — angle consistency beats speed.

entries.q: Why is a sharp knife safer than a dull one?
entries.a: A sharp edge bites where you aim with less force. A dull edge skids off skins and boards into fingers. Keep knives sharp, cut with fingers curled, and store blades sheathed or on a magnetic strip — not loose in a drawer.

entries.q: How do I sharpen an axe or garden spade?
entries.a: Secure the tool, then push a file along the existing bevel in one direction to restore a clean edge — axes and spades usually want a slightly blunter angle than kitchen knives. Deburr lightly, then oil the metal. Digging tools cut roots and soil cleaner when edged, which also means less strain on your body.

entries.q: How do I care for wooden tool handles?
entries.a: Sand raised grain lightly, wipe on boiled linseed oil, let it soak, then wipe dry. Yearly oiling keeps handles from drying, cracking, and blistering your hands. Replace any handle with a deep split before it fails mid-swing.

entries.q: How do I stop rust on hand tools?
entries.a: Dry tools after damp work, store with airflow, and wipe a light oil film on bare steel. Light rust yields to fine abrasive and oil; heavy scale may need a wire brush then re-oil. Silica gel in a closed toolbox helps in humid climates.

entries.q: How do I sharpen scissors at home?
entries.a: For quality scissors, a fine stone or dedicated scissor sharpener along the factory bevel works; cheap scissors are often not worth hours. Clean sticky residue first — gummed blades feel dull. Test on scrap fabric, not on your skin.

entries.q: What angle should I use when sharpening chisels?
entries.a: Most bench chisels work well around 25–30° primary bevel with a small honing microbevel. Keep the back flat and polished — a chisel cuts as a partnership between bevel and back. Same burr-and-strip logic as knives, then strop.

entries.q: How do I maintain cast-iron cookware?
entries.a: Wash with hot water and a brush (minimal soap if well seasoned), dry thoroughly on low heat, then wipe a very thin oil coat while warm. Never soak or leave wet. Thin polymerised layers of oil are seasoning — sticky thick oil is not.

entries.q: What belongs in a basic sewing kit?
entries.a: Needles in a few sizes, strong polyester thread (black, white, and a colour you wear), patches, safety pins, spare buttons, fabric scissors, and a thimble. Add fabric glue, seam sealer, and repair tape for waterproof gear. That small kit covers most clothing and bag failures.

entries.q: How do I sew a button back on?
entries.a: Anchor the thread with a few stitches through the fabric, sew through each button hole 4–6 times leaving a slight thread shank for thick coats, then wind thread under the button and knot behind. Match thread colour and double the thread for strength. A missing button is a ten-minute fix, not a reason to discard the garment.

entries.q: How do I whip-stitch a seam that has opened?
entries.a: Turn the garment inside out, align the seam edges, and sew over-and-over stitches that bite both edges evenly. Knot firmly at each end. Whip stitch is quick insurance until you can do a neater seam; for load-bearing splits, backstitch or machine sew when you can.

entries.q: How do I patch clothing so the repair holds?
entries.a: For anything that takes stress — knees, backpacks, work trousers — back an iron-on patch with stitches around the edge. Clean fabric, round the patch corners so they peel less, and stitch with a small running or whip stitch. Iron-on alone is temporary under real load.

entries.q: How do I darn a sock?
entries.a: Stretch the sock over a jar lid or darning egg, stitch a grid of threads across the hole, then weave across that grid until the hole is filled. Keep tension even so the darn is flat. Wool socks especially reward repair and can last years.

entries.q: How do I repair a delaminating shoe sole?
entries.a: Clean both surfaces, roughen lightly, apply contact cement per instructions, let it tack, then press firmly and clamp or weight overnight. Replace laces with paracord if needed for field strength. Good boots repaired beat cheap boots replaced.

entries.q: Why buy quality clothes and repair them?
entries.a: Quality fibres — especially wool — mend cleanly and last decades when cared for. Fast fashion fails at seams and pills into landfill. Learning four mending skills (button, seam, patch, darn) turns clothing into a renewable resource instead of a recurring bill.

entries.q: How do I mend a tear in a waterproof jacket?
entries.a: Clean and dry the area, apply repair tape on the outside for a temporary seal, then seam-seal stitch holes from the inside if you sew. Fabric-specific patches designed for shells hold better than random duct tape. Test waterproofing with a sprinkle of water before trusting a storm.

entries.q: What thread should I use for strong repairs?
entries.a: Polyester all-purpose thread handles most clothing; heavy polyester or nylon thread for jeans, packs, and outdoor gear. Cotton thread is fine for light cotton garments but weakens faster when wet. Match thickness to fabric — thick thread on silk punches ugly holes.

entries.q: How do I replace a zipper pull or free a stuck zip?
entries.a: Graphite from a soft pencil or a drop of soap can free teeth; never yank sideways. A missing pull can be replaced with a small zip-tie or keyring through the slider hole. If teeth are missing, a zipper replacement or sewing the opening shut as a pocket may be the honest fix.

entries.q: How do I hem trousers by hand?
entries.a: Fold to length, press or finger-crease, pin, then use a blind hem stitch or neat running stitch catching only a thread or two of the outside fabric. Try on shoes first so length is right. A clean hem restores dignity to clothes that otherwise drag and fray.

entries.q: What is a thimble for, and do I need one?
entries.a: A thimble protects your finger when pushing needles through thick denim, leather, or multiple layers. Metal or leather both work if they fit. For occasional button sewing you can skip it; for real mending sessions your fingertip will thank you.

entries.q: What basic cleaners replace a cupboard of products?
entries.a: White vinegar (descaling, glass, fabric softener, weed spray), baking soda (scouring, odors, drain refresh with vinegar), citric acid (kettles, bathroom scale), soap flakes or Castile soap (nearly everything), washing soda (laundry booster, degreasing), and isopropyl alcohol (disinfecting, sticker residue). Cheap, long-storing staples beat branded bottles for most jobs.

entries.q: What cleaners should I never mix?
entries.a: Never mix bleach with vinegar, other acids, or ammonia — the fumes can seriously harm lungs and eyes. Use one product, rinse, then another if needed. Simple soap and water remain the default for ordinary dirt.

entries.q: How do I clean glass without streaks using vinegar?
entries.a: Mix roughly 1 part white vinegar to 3–4 parts water in a spray bottle, wipe with a lint-free cloth or newspaper, and finish dry. Avoid cleaning hot glass in direct sun (it flashes dry and streaks). A little goes further than soaking the pane.

entries.q: How do I descale a kettle with citric acid or vinegar?
entries.a: Fill with water plus a spoon or two of citric acid (or a good splash of vinegar), bring to near boil or soak warm, then rinse thoroughly and boil plain water once to clear taste. Regular light descaling beats chipping thick scale. Citric acid is gentle on most kettles when rinsed well.

entries.q: How do I freshen a drain with baking soda and vinegar?
entries.a: Pour ~100 ml baking soda down the drain, follow with ~200 ml vinegar, let foam work 10–15 minutes, then flush with hot water. This refreshes odours and light gunk; it is not a miracle for solid blockages — use a plunger or trap for those.

entries.q: How do I scour a sink or oven racks with baking soda?
entries.a: Make a paste of baking soda and a little water, rub with a cloth or non-scratch pad, then rinse. For greasy racks, loosen with washing soda solution first. Mild abrasive action cleans without scratching most enamels when you stay gentle.

entries.q: How do I remove sticker residue simply?
entries.a: Warm the residue slightly, peel what you can, then rub isopropyl alcohol or a drop of cooking oil, wait, and wipe. Finish with soap and water. Patience dissolves glue better than aggressive scraping that scars the surface.

entries.q: How do I use washing soda for laundry and degreasing?
entries.a: Add a small amount of washing soda to the wash to boost detergent in hard water and help cut grease on work clothes. For greasy tools or pans (not aluminium), dissolve in hot water and soak. Store dry and labelled — it is stronger than baking soda and can irritate skin.

entries.q: How do I clean with Castile or soap flakes?
entries.a: A teaspoon of Castile or grated soap flakes in a spray bottle of water makes an all-purpose wipe-down cleaner. Use sparingly on floors so residue does not build. Soap lifts dirt; rinse matters as much as the soap itself.

entries.q: How do I mop floors without specialised floor products?
entries.a: Sweep or vacuum first, then mop with warm water and a drop of soap — or a splash of vinegar for mineral haze on hard floors (not on unsealed stone that vinegar can etch). Wring the mop well; soaking wood floors causes more damage than dirt. Change water when it is visibly dirty.

entries.q: How do I clean a bathroom without specialty sprays?
entries.a: Citric acid solution softens mineral scale on taps and tiles; baking soda paste scrubs basins; vinegar helps glass screens. Ventilate, give acids time to work, then scrub and rinse. Keep a dedicated brush — bathrooms need mechanical action more than fragrance.

entries.q: How do I neutralise household odours without aerosols?
entries.a: Open windows when weather allows, wash the source, and leave an open bowl of baking soda in fridges or closed spaces. Charcoal or dry coffee grounds can sit in a jar nearby for smells. Masking scent over a dirty source only hides the problem briefly.

entries.q: How do I bake simple bread with only flour, water, and salt?
entries.a: Mix flour, water, salt, and a little yeast or sourdough starter into a shaggy dough; let time develop gluten (no-knead styles rest many hours). Bake in a hot pot or on a stone until the crust is deep brown and the loaf sounds hollow. Practise now so you can bake when shops are closed.

entries.q: How do I keep a sourdough starter without buying yeast?
entries.a: A starter is flour plus water plus patience — feed it regularly with equal parts (by weight if you can) and keep a portion going. Once active, it leavens bread indefinitely without commercial yeast. If you refrigerate between bakes, feed it and let it warm and bubble before mixing dough.

entries.q: How do I cook without a fridge for a few days?
entries.a: Favour shelf-stable staples: rice, pasta, dried beans, oats, flour, oil, salt, hard cheeses if cool, whole winter squash, onions, garlic, potatoes in a dark ventilated place, and tinned goods. Cook what spoils first, use cool night air and shade, and trust your nose and eyes — when in doubt, heat thoroughly or discard.

entries.q: How do I stretch meals from pantry staples?
entries.a: Beans-and-rice, soups, and stews turn small amounts of flavouring vegetables, spices, and fat into filling meals. Soak beans when you can, cook thoroughly, and salt near the end. One pot feeding many is the classic resilience pattern — practise favourite spice combinations before you need them.

entries.q: How do I make stock from scraps?
entries.a: Simmer clean bones, onion skins, carrot ends, and herb stems in water for hours; strain and use as soup base or cook grains in it. Cool quickly and reheat to a boil before reuse if held without reliable cold storage. Stock turns leftovers into the next meal’s depth.

entries.q: How do I save cooking fat safely?
entries.a: Strain warm fat through cloth into a clean jar, keep cool and covered, and use within a sensible window for frying and flavour. Label animal fats by type. In no-fridge conditions, use sooner and keep jars as cool and dark as you can.

entries.q: Why cook every stored recipe before you need it?
entries.a: Unfamiliar grains, yeast habits, and cooker quirks show up only when you practise. Cooking from your storage pantry now teaches timing, water ratios, and what your household will actually eat. Crisis is a poor first kitchen lesson.

entries.q: How do I store potatoes, onions, and garlic without a fridge?
entries.a: Cool, dark, dry, and ventilated — not in plastic sealed bags. Keep potatoes away from onions (they shorten each other’s life), and remove any that sprout badly or rot so one bad tuber does not spoil the crate. A cardboard box or basket beats a sweaty cupboard.

entries.q: How do I cook dried beans so they are digestible and done?
entries.a: Sort stones, soak overnight in plenty of water, drain, then simmer in fresh water until soft — often 1–2 hours depending on age and type. Skim foam, salt late, and never eat undercooked kidney beans. A pressure cooker shortens time if you have one and know its safe use.

entries.q: What one-pot meals work when power or time is short?
entries.a: Sauté onion in oil if you can, add grains or soaked beans, water or stock, salt, and whatever vegetables keep. Simmer covered until soft. Rotating spices (cumin, chilli, herbs, curry powders you already own) keeps the same pattern from tasting like punishment.

entries.q: How do I keep food cooler without a working fridge?
entries.a: Use the coolest room, night air, a shaded porch, or a zeolite/evaporative cool box where climate allows. Insulated bags with frozen bottles help while ice lasts. Prioritise eating or preserving dairy, meat, and cooked leftovers first.

entries.q: How do I measure without proper kitchen scales?
entries.a: Learn your mug and spoon volumes once with water and a scale if available, then write them inside a cupboard door. Many traditional recipes use handfuls and cups successfully. Consistency matters more than laboratory precision for daily staple cooking.

entries.q: How do I wash dishes with minimal water?
entries.a: Scrape first, wash greasiest last, use a small basin of soapy water and a rinse basin rather than a running tap. Wipe pans while warm. Greywater rules vary — at minimum, keep fats out of drains that clog easily.

entries.q: How do I prove dough in a cold kitchen?
entries.a: Use a longer rise, place dough near (not on) a gentle heat source, or insulate the bowl with towels. Cold slow fermentation still works — it just takes more hours. Rushing with harsh heat can kill yeast; patience is part of the method.

entries.q: What spices matter most for plain staple foods?
entries.a: Salt first, then a short shelf you will actually use: chilli or pepper, a curry blend or cumin, garlic/onion powder if fresh runs out, dried herbs, and something acidic like vinegar or lemon powder. Flavour is morale. Buy what your household likes, not a huge unused rack.

entries.q: How do I know if stored flour or grains are still good?
entries.a: Smell for rancid or musty odours, look for insects or clumping from moisture, and sift if needed. Store cool, dry, and sealed; bay leaves are folk help but dryness and sealed containers matter more. When unsure for long-stored soft wheat flour, bake a small test before committing a large dough.

entries.q: How do I wash clothes by hand?
entries.a: Sort lights and darks, dissolve soap in a basin of water, soak, then agitate and rub soiled areas against themselves. Rinse until water runs clearer, wring or press out water, and hang in air and sun when possible. Hot water helps grease; cold is fine for many daily clothes and saves fuel.

entries.q: How do I make a simple hand-laundry soap solution?
entries.a: Grate soap flakes or use a mild laundry soap dissolved fully in warm water before clothes go in — undissolved lumps spot fabric. A little washing soda helps in hard water. More soap is not cleaner; it just needs more rinsing.

entries.q: How do I rinse and wring laundry without a spinner?
entries.a: Change rinse water until it is only lightly soapy. Press water out against the basin rather than twisting delicate knits to death; roll in a clean towel and step on the roll to extract more. Hang immediately so creases do not set.

entries.q: How do I dry clothes when the weather is damp?
entries.a: Use the warmest ventilated room, space items so air flows, and rotate positions. A dehumidifier or brief heating helps if you have power; open windows on opposite sides when outdoor air is less humid than indoor. Damp cloth left in a pile breeds smell and mildew.

entries.q: How do I wash wool by hand without felting it?
entries.a: Use cool water and wool-safe soap, soak gently without agitation or wringing twists, rinse in same-temperature water, then press water out in a towel and dry flat. Heat plus friction felts wool. Reshape while damp.

entries.q: Can vinegar help in hand laundry?
entries.a: A splash of white vinegar in the rinse can act like a fabric softener and help rinse soap from towels. Smell fades as clothes dry. Do not mix vinegar with bleach products.

entries.q: How do I treat common stains before washing?
entries.a: Blot, do not rub, fresh stains. Scrape mud when dry; work soap into grease; cold water first on protein stains like blood (warm can set them). Wash after pre-treatment. Sunlight helps bleach some natural fibre stains after washing — test on hidden seams.

entries.q: How do I wash bedding by hand in small batches?
entries.a: Wash one sheet or duvet cover at a time in the bathtub with soap, tread carefully with clean feet or agitate with a clean plunger dedicated to laundry, rinse twice, wring with a partner, and hang over multiple lines. Sheets are bulky — batching keeps it humanly possible.

entries.q: How do I keep hand-washed work clothes wearable?
entries.a: Pre-treat collars and cuffs with soap paste, add washing soda to the soak for grease, and rinse thoroughly. Dry fully before storing so mildew does not claim the fabric. Rotating two work sets beats destroying one set with endless wear between rare washes.

entries.q: What is a practical clothes-washing rhythm off-grid?
entries.a: Wash small loads more often rather than waiting for a mountain. Soak while you do other chores, wash in daylight, and dry whenever weather allows. A simple rhythm — soak, wash, rinse, hang — keeps the household in clean clothes without a machine.

entries.q: What basic knots should everyone know?
entries.a: Learn square (reef) knot for joining similar cords under light load, bowline for a fixed loop that does not slip, clove hitch for tying to a post, taut-line hitch for adjustable guy lines, and a simple stopper knot so rope ends do not run. Practise until you can tie them in poor light. A few reliable knots beat a dozen half-remembered ones.

entries.q: How do I tie a bowline?
entries.a: Make a small loop in the standing part (“the rabbit hole”), bring the working end up through the hole, around the standing part, and back down the hole; snug carefully. A bowline makes a secure loop at the end of a rope for rescue, hanging, or tying around an object. Practise the rhyme until muscle memory holds.

entries.q: How do I tie a square (reef) knot?
entries.a: Left over right and under, then right over left and under — the knot should lie flat and symmetrical. Use for parcels and non-critical joins of similar-thickness rope, not for climbing or life-safety loads. If it looks crooked, it is probably a weaker granny knot — untie and redo.

entries.q: How do I tie a clove hitch?
entries.a: Wrap the rope around the post, cross over itself, wrap again, and tuck the working end under the last crossing; snug both ends. Good for starting lashings or hanging something to a rail. On smooth poles under changing load, back it up — clove hitches can roll.

entries.q: How do I tie a taut-line hitch for guy lines?
entries.a: Around the stake or peg loop, wrap the working end around the standing part twice inside the loop and once outside, then snug. The hitch should slide to tension and grip under load — ideal for tent guys. Re-tension after fabric stretches.

entries.q: What is a stopper knot used for?
entries.a: A stopper knot (overhand or figure-eight) thickens a rope end so it cannot pull through a block, cleat, or zipper pull. Figure-eight is bulkier and easier to untie after loading. Put stoppers on any line you cannot afford to lose through a hole.

entries.q: How should I care for rope and cordage?
entries.a: Coil dry rope loosely, avoid sharp kinks and chemical contamination, and retire rope with glazed, fuzzy, or cut cores. Sunlight ages synthetics — store out of UV when possible. Know the difference between decorative string and load-rated rope before you trust weight to it.

entries.q: How do I join two ropes of different thickness?
entries.a: Use a sheet bend: form a bight in the thicker rope, bring the thinner up through, around both parts of the bight, and under itself. Dress and snug. Square knots slip on mismatched diameters — sheet bends are the practical join.

entries.q: What knot is useful for a temporary clothesline?
entries.a: Anchor with clove hitches or round-turns and two half-hitches to solid points, keep the line high enough that laundry clears the ground, and use a taut-line or trucker’s hitch style tension if the span sags. Protect bark if tying to living trees.

entries.q: Why practise knots with eyes closed or gloves on?
entries.a: Real conditions include cold, dark, rain, and numb fingers. If you can only tie a bowline at a desk with coffee, you do not know it yet. Short daily practice builds the automatic skill you need when stressed.

entries.q: How do I read a topographic map basics?
entries.a: Contour lines connect equal elevation — tightly packed lines mean steep ground; wide spacing means gentle slopes. Read the scale bar in metres/kilometres, note the north arrow, and match symbols to the legend. Orient the map to the land before you navigate.

entries.q: How do I orient a map with a compass?
entries.a: Place the compass on the map, rotate the map until map north matches magnetic north (adjust for local declination if you know it), and keep both aligned as you plan. Thumb and terrain features confirm you are reading the right ridge. A map that is upside-down to the land causes classic wrong turns.

entries.q: What is a map scale and why does it matter?
entries.a: Scale tells you how ground distance relates to map distance — for example 1:25,000 means 1 cm on the map is 250 m on the ground. Always use the printed scale bar, which survives photocopy resizing better than assumptions. Underestimating scale is how short walks become epics.

entries.q: How do I estimate distance and time on foot from a map?
entries.a: Measure route distance with the scale (string along the path works), then allow roughly 4–5 km/h on easy paths and much less for climbs, poor trails, or heavy packs — plus rest. Contours tell you when “only 3 km” includes a hard ascent. Always leave daylight margin.

entries.q: How do I use handrails and landmarks when navigating?
entries.a: Handrails are linear features you can follow — rivers, ridges, roads, fence lines. Aim off deliberately toward a catching feature so you know which way to turn when you hit it. Collecting landmarks as you go beats staring only at the compass needle.

entries.q: What if I do not have a compass?
entries.a: Orient by terrain association: match visible hills, rivers, and settlements to the map. Sun rises roughly east and sets roughly west (seasonal variation exists), and at night known star patterns help if you have learned them beforehand. Still carry a compass when you can — improvisation is backup, not a plan.

entries.q: How do I fold and protect a paper map in the field?
entries.a: Fold so the active area faces out, keep it in a clear waterproof sleeve, and mark your position with a grease pencil rather than destroying detail. Write magnetic declination and emergency notes on the margin. Paper maps work without batteries — treat them as critical kit.

entries.q: What do common map symbols mean at a glance?
entries.a: Always check that map’s legend — colours and icons vary by publisher. Typically blue is water, green is vegetation, black/grey built features, and red/orange roads. Contours and spot heights show relief. Guessing symbols is how people walk into marshes.

entries.q: How do I take a simple compass bearing?
entries.a: Point the travel arrow at your target, rotate the bezel until north marks align with the needle (with declination set if your compass allows), then follow the arrow while keeping the needle boxed. Pick interim aiming points so you are not staring at the dial every step. Recheck after obstacles.

entries.q: How do I avoid getting lost in poor visibility?
entries.a: Slow down, use short legs between features, count paces if you have measured your pace length, and consider stopping if navigation becomes guesswork. Group members should know the plan. Turning back early is a navigation skill, not a failure.

entries.q: How should I think about a household financial buffer?
entries.a: Build layers: small-denomination cash at home for outages and local trade, a modest emergency fund for bills when income hiccups, and lower recurring costs so less income still covers life. Frugality is resilience, not punishment — every fixed bill you remove is weight off your back in hard months.

entries.q: Why keep cash at home in small notes?
entries.a: Card networks and ATMs fail in outages; large notes are hard to change when shops are stressed. Keep a discreet, modest cash reserve in small denominations for food, fuel, and transport. Tell only trusted household members where it is.

entries.q: What is a simple offline household budget method?
entries.a: List monthly must-pays (housing, water, food staples, medicine, debt minimums), then needs, then wants. Use envelopes or labelled jars for cash categories if that helps your brain. Review weekly with pencil and paper — awareness beats fancy apps you cannot open without power.

entries.q: How do I cut recurring costs without hurting morale?
entries.a: Cancel unused subscriptions first, cook more staples, repair before replacing, and share tools with neighbours. Keep a few cheap joys so thrift does not feel like despair. Sustainable frugality outlasts crash austerity.

entries.q: What is a healthy barter mindset?
entries.a: Trade surplus for surplus — skills, labour, eggs, repairs, childcare hours — with clear agreements and goodwill. Fairness and reputation matter more than squeezing the last unit of value. Barter thrives on trust; cheating once can close many doors.

entries.q: How do I price my skills in informal trade?
entries.a: Anchor on time, materials cost, and local going rates when you know them. Be explicit: “two hours of plumbing for a week of eggs” beats vague promises. Write it down. Relationships last when both sides leave feeling respected.

entries.q: What records should I keep for cash and barter?
entries.a: A simple paper notebook: date, what moved, with whom, and any remaining obligation. You do not need accounting software. Clear notes prevent the friendship-damaging phrase “I thought you said…”

entries.q: How do I prioritise spending in a tight month?
entries.a: Secure shelter, water, basic food, essential medicine, and heat/light before discretionary spending. Talk with the household so everyone understands the temporary rules. Panic purchases and shame spending both blow holes in thin budgets.

entries.q: How can communities support each other economically offline?
entries.a: Tool libraries, bulk food buys, skill shares, childcare swaps, and repair cafés keep wealth circulating locally. Knowing who grows, who fixes, and who teaches turns a street into a network. Start small and reliable rather than launching a grand scheme that fades.

entries.q: Why minimise debt as a resilience strategy?
entries.a: Fixed debt payments continue when income does not. Less compulsory outflow means more options — time, relocation, helping family — when systems wobble. Pay high-interest consumer debt aggressively when you can; avoid new debt for wants.

entries.q: How do I shop for staples economically?
entries.a: Compare unit prices (price per kg or litre), favour versatile staples your household eats, and buy larger packs only if you can store them dry and use them before spoilage. Waste is not a bargain. Make a list and eat before you shop to reduce impulse buys.

entries.q: What is “enough” cash to keep at home?
entries.a: Enough for several days of food, local transport, and a modest contingency — not life savings under a mattress. Balance convenience against theft risk with discreet storage and only necessary household knowledge. Exact amounts depend on your local prices and risk.

entries.q: How do I teach children about money offline?
entries.a: Use real coins for small choices, let them save toward a goal, and involve them in simple shopping maths. Model calm trade-offs aloud. Shame and secrecy around money teach fear; clear age-appropriate practice teaches competence.

entries.q: How do I prepare financially for a short income gap?
entries.a: Know your minimum monthly number, trim optional costs early, pause non-critical projects, and communicate with anyone you owe before silence makes things worse. A written plan on paper reduces 3 a.m. spirals. Community and skills are part of the plan, not only cash.

entries.q: Why are neighbours part of emergency preparedness?
entries.a: In real emergencies, nearby people are the actual first responders — sharing tools, information, care, and muscle. Know names, skills, and needs on your street before crisis. Isolation is fragility; trust built in peacetime is infrastructure.

entries.q: How do I start knowing my neighbours’ skills?
entries.a: Casual conversations and small favours reveal who gardens, who wires, who minds kids, who speaks extra languages. Share your own skills first so it feels like exchange, not interrogation. A simple paper list at home helps when phones are down.

entries.q: What is a repair café mindset at home?
entries.a: Before binning an object, ask whether cleaning, a screw, glue, or a stitch would restore it — alone or with a neighbour who knows. Repair culture saves money and builds competence. Celebrate fixed things; they are quiet victories.

entries.q: How do I borrow and lend tools without losing friends?
entries.a: Return cleaner and sooner than promised, replace consumables you used (blades, bits), and confess damage immediately with a repair or replace plan. Label your tools. Clear expectations keep generosity alive.

entries.q: How do I organise a simple skill-share?
entries.a: Pick a date, one skill each session (bread, bike puncture, sewing), keep groups small, and bring materials list on paper. Tea helps. Consistency beats ambitious curricula that never meet.

entries.q: What local groups strengthen community resilience?
entries.a: Repair cafés, garden groups, radio clubs, seed swaps, and mutual-aid circles all practise cooperation before it is urgent. Join or start one modest gathering. Shared hobbies become emergency networks almost without trying.

entries.q: How do I offer help without creating awkward debt?
entries.a: Offer specific help (“I can watch the kids Tuesday”) rather than vague “let me know.” Accept help when you need it so the street’s economy of care flows both ways. Gratitude and reciprocity matter more than perfect scorekeeping.

entries.q: How should a street communicate if phones fail?
entries.a: Agree a meeting point, a paper contact list, and who checks on whom — especially elders and anyone with medical needs (non-medical check-ins). A whistle, knock code, or scheduled porch check can be enough. Practise once so it is not theoretical.

entries.q: How do I host a calm household meeting about preparedness?
entries.a: Keep it short, practical, and kind: shutoffs, meet point, who carries which bag, and one skill to practise this month. Listen to fears without mockery. End with one concrete action — not a lecture that leaves everyone anxious.

entries.q: What makes someone a good community teammate in hard times?
entries.a: Show up when you said you would, tell the truth about capacity, share fair portions, and stay steady rather than spreading panic. Competence plus kindness beats heroic talk. Reputation is built in small errands long before a disaster.

entries.q: How do I handle conflict with a neighbour constructively?
entries.a: Speak early, privately, and specifically about the behaviour and its effect; propose a practical fix; listen. Written agreements help for recurring issues. Escalation is sometimes needed, but starting loud usually hardens sides.

entries.q: Why share surplus instead of hoarding everything?
entries.a: Hoarding past your household’s real need strains trust and leaves unused goods spoiling while others go without. Sensible reserves plus sharing surplus builds the goodwill you may need later. Resilience is social as well as material.

entries.q: What documents belong in a household binder?
entries.a: ID copies, insurance policies, property documents, medical summaries and prescriptions, and key contacts — with a waterproof copy in the go-bag and an encrypted digital copy on offline USB (Faraday storage if you use that setup) plus one off-site copy. One binder beats a scavenger hunt during eviction, fire, or travel.

entries.q: How should I back up irreplaceable digital files?
entries.a: Follow 3-2-1: three copies, on two different media types, with one copy off-site. Include photos, documents, and recovery codes. Test that you can open a backup once a year. Cloud-only is not a plan when networks fail.

entries.q: How do I store password recovery codes offline?
entries.a: Use a password manager for daily use, then print recovery codes and store them with your document binder — not on a sticky note on the monitor. Anyone with physical access to codes can become you; protect them like cash and ID.

entries.q: What medical information should be on paper at home?
entries.a: A one-page summary: conditions, medications with doses, allergies, blood type if known, and clinician contacts. Keep a copy in the binder and go-bag. This is documentation for continuity — not a substitute for professional care.

entries.q: How do I waterproof important paper copies?
entries.a: Sealed plastic sleeves inside a zip bag, or a small waterproof document pouch, kept above likely flood level. Avoid constant damp sheds. After any water event, air-dry papers carefully; freeze wet papers if you must pause drying of irreplaceable items.

entries.q: Why keep an off-site document copy?
entries.a: Fire, flood, or theft can take the home binder. A trusted relative, safe deposit, or sealed cache elsewhere means identity and ownership proofs survive. Update off-site copies when major documents change.

entries.q: What contact list should every household keep on paper?
entries.a: Family, neighbours, landlord, utilities, insurance, doctors, school/work, and out-of-area contact who can relay messages. Include addresses, not only phone numbers. Phones die; paper still reads by candlelight.

entries.q: How do I organise receipts and warranties usefully?
entries.a: One envelope or section per year for major purchases, with date, shop, and serial numbers noted. Photograph nameplates on appliances into your offline backup. When something fails, proof beats memory.

entries.q: Should I keep original IDs in the go-bag?
entries.a: Prefer high-quality copies in the grab bag and originals in the most secure accessible place — unless you are actively evacuating, in which case originals come with you in waterproof protection. Never leave the only copy of anything in a car that can be stolen.

entries.q: How do self-hosted and local files help resilience?
entries.a: Files on your own drives and local services keep working when accounts lock or platforms change. Export critical data regularly. Decentralised and self-hosted tools are part of digital resilience, not only a hobby.

entries.q: What property papers should I be able to find in minutes?
entries.a: Proof of ownership or tenancy, mortgage or lease contacts, and insurance policy numbers. Know where the originals live and that copies are in the binder. Minutes matter when you must prove the right to re-enter or claim.

entries.q: How often should I review the document binder?
entries.a: At least twice a year and after any birth, death, move, new policy, or new diagnosis/medication change. Remove obsolete copies so the binder stays thin enough to grab. A dated checklist on the inside cover helps.

entries.q: Why is bicycle repair a life skill?
entries.a: A working bicycle is quiet, repairable transport when fuel and transit fail. Learning punctures, brakes, and chain care keeps you mobile with hand tools. Practise before you depend on it.

entries.q: How do I fix a bicycle puncture?
entries.a: Remove the wheel, lever the tyre carefully, find the hole by air and ears or dunking the tube, roughen, apply patch kit glue as directed, press patch, replace tyre without pinching the tube, and inflate firmly. Check the tyre casing for the thorn or glass that caused it before you celebrate.

entries.q: How do I adjust bicycle brakes?
entries.a: Centre the callipers or pads so they hit the rim (or disc) squarely without rubbing when released; tighten cable anchor bolts after pulling slack. Replace pads worn to the indicator. Test at walking speed before riding downhill. Strong brakes are non-negotiable safety kit.

entries.q: How do I care for a bicycle chain?
entries.a: Wipe grit off, apply a suitable chain lubricant to each link while turning pedals backwards, then wipe excess so it does not attract dirt. A dry, squeaking chain wears faster; a dripping oily chain paints your trousers and grime. Recheck after wet rides.

entries.q: What tools belong in a small bike repair kit?
entries.a: Tyre levers, patch kit or spare tube, mini pump or CO₂ you know how to use, multi-tool with hex keys and screwdrivers, and a rag. Add a spare chain quick-link if you ride far. Know how to use each tool at home before the roadside lesson.

entries.q: How do I put a bicycle chain back on?
entries.a: Shift to the smallest rear sprocket and middle or smallest front ring if you have gears, feed the chain onto the teeth, and turn the pedals gently by hand to seat it. Dirty hands beat a walk home. If it falls off constantly, the limit screws or hanger may need adjustment.

entries.q: How do I check bicycle tyre pressure without a fancy gauge?
entries.a: Tyres should feel very firm when squeezed hard with your thumb — soft sidewalls pinch-flat easily. Use a gauge when you can; learn what correct pressure feels like for your tyres. Inspect for cuts and embedded glass while you are there.

entries.q: How do I keep a bike secure and ready?
entries.a: Lock with a quality lock through frame and a fixed object when leaving it, store dry, and spin the wheels monthly if unused so parts do not seize. A pre-ride ABC check — air, brakes, chain — catches problems early.

entries.q: How do I true a slightly wobbly wheel at a basic level?
entries.a: Spin the wheel in the frame, watch the rim against a fixed reference, and gently tighten spokes on the opposite side of a sideways wobble in small quarter-turns. Go slow — over-tightening makes new warps. Serious damage needs a wheelbuilder; minor truing is learnable.

entries.q: What riding habits reduce bike breakdowns?
entries.a: Avoid harsh pothole impacts, keep pressure up, do not twist the chain through extreme gear crosses, and dry and lube after heavy rain. Listen for new noises — they are cheap warnings. Smooth inputs save parts.

entries.q: How do I choose a practical utility bicycle?
entries.a: Comfortable upright fit, reliable brakes, mounts for racks and mudguards, and tyres wide enough for your roads matter more than racing weight. Steel frames are forgiving to repair in many places. Test the riding position with a load before you commit.

entries.q: How do I carry loads safely on a bicycle?
entries.a: Use a rack and panniers low and balanced rather than a heavy backpack that raises your centre of gravity. Secure loose straps, keep brake and steering clear, and practise in an empty area. Weight changes stopping distance.

entries.q: How do I keep a calmer household during stressful times?
entries.a: Protect sleep and meals as anchors, keep daily routines simple and visible, reduce news noise indoors, and give everyone one useful job so anxiety has somewhere to go. Speak lower and shorter when tension rises. Calm is contagious — so is panic.

entries.q: How do I set household rules kids can follow offline?
entries.a: Few rules, clearly worded, consistently kept: where we meet if separated, shoes by the door, ask before touching tools/fire, kindness in words. Post them on paper at child eye level. Consistency from adults matters more than a long list.

entries.q: How do I help children with big feelings without screens?
entries.a: Name the feeling, stay nearby, offer water/snack/rest, and a simple physical outlet (walk, cushions, drawing). Connection before correction. You are not diagnosing — you are being a steady presence while the storm passes.

entries.q: How do I run a fair chore system without apps?
entries.a: A wall chart with pictures for pre-readers, rotating jobs, and chores finished before optional fun. Match tasks to age and teach the skill first. Praise specific effort (“you hung the towels straight”) more than generic “good job.”

entries.q: How do I hold a family meeting that children respect?
entries.a: Same time weekly, short agenda, everyone speaks once without interruption, decisions written down. Include appreciation rounds so it is not only complaints. End on a concrete plan for the week. Predictability builds buy-in.

entries.q: How do I reduce sibling conflict day to day?
entries.a: Separate needs from shared scarce resources, teach turn-taking with timers, avoid comparing children, and intervene when safety or dignity is at risk — not in every squabble. Boredom and hunger fuel many fights; check those first.

entries.q: How do I create bedtime calm without electronics?
entries.a: Dim lights, same sequence each night (wash, story, lights out), cooler room if possible, and no thrilling play at the end. Stories and low voices downshift brains. Consistency beats perfection after hard days.

entries.q: How do I talk to children about hard world events calmly?
entries.a: Tell the truth briefly at their level, emphasise what adults are doing to keep them safe, and invite questions. Limit graphic repeated exposure. Reassurance is honesty plus a plan, not pretend nothing happened.

entries.q: How can shared meals strengthen a household?
entries.a: Even simple pot meals eaten together without devices build connection and let adults notice how everyone is coping. Assign small serving jobs to children. Conversation at the table is daily community practice.

entries.q: How do I manage adult stress so it spills less onto children?
entries.a: Take short resets: water, breath outdoors, swap duties with another adult when possible, and sleep as a priority. Apologise when you snap — repair teaches children that relationships can mend. Your nervous system sets the household weather.

entries.q: How do I keep learning playful for children offline?
entries.a: Stories, measuring in the kitchen, nature walks, cards, building with scrap materials, and letting them help with real skills (washing, planting, tool names). Curiosity grows when adults answer some questions and explore others together.

entries.q: What household jobs are appropriate for children?
entries.a: Toddlers can put toys in a bin; older children can set tables, fold cloths, wash produce, feed animals, and eventually cook simple food with supervision. Teach, then step back. Useful work builds belonging — token busywork does not.

entries.q: What is the meta-skill of practical learning?
entries.a: Fix or learn one new practical thing each month with a manual or careful practice before calling a professional when safety allows. Competence compounds — each skill makes the next easier. Keep paper references: repair manuals, first aid, regional plant guides, and this kind of handbook.

entries.q: How do I learn a hands-on skill from a paper manual?
entries.a: Read the whole procedure once, gather tools, then do each step slowly while checking the diagram. Write your own notes in the margin about what differed in your house. Teaching the skill to someone else the next week locks it in.

entries.q: Why keep paper reference books at home?
entries.a: When power and networks fail, paper still works. A repair manual, first-aid guide, regional plant guide, and cookbook earn their shelf space. Annotate them with local phone numbers and your own discoveries.

entries.q: How do I practise skills so they stick under stress?
entries.a: Rehearse in realistic conditions: dim light, gloves, time limits, and with the actual tools from your kit. Spaced practice beats one long cram. If you only ever watched someone else do it, you do not know it yet.

entries.q: How do I choose which skill to learn next?
