entries.a: Pre-download or photocopy local hazard maps, plant guides, and first-aid references. Know skilled neighbors. Information blackouts reward what you already stored and who you already trust. Contested global narratives matter less than local know-how when the wide-area network is gone.

entries.q: What is a sane weekly prep habit if earth changes worry me?
entries.a: Each week: rotate a few pantry items, check water dates, charge power banks, test a torch/radio, walk to your rally point once a month, talk to one neighbor, and add one skill micro-lesson. Small cadence beats rare panic. Stop when basics are solid; do not escalate into endless fear shopping.

entries.q: How should faith or meaning practices interact with earth-change fear?
entries.a: Meaning practices can stabilize people — prayer, meditation, nature time, service — when used to cultivate courage and kindness, not to declare secret timelines as certainty. If a spiritual claim dates a micronova absolute, treat it with the same falsifiability care as secular prophecy. Serve neighbors; that is resilient spirituality.

entries.q: How do extinction-event popular claims differ from mainstream Younger Dryas research?
entries.a: Mainstream research on the Younger Dryas includes climate and ice-sheet dynamics debates; some catastrophist impact hypotheses remain contested. Davidson-style uses of Younger Dryas as proof of his solar micronova cycle go beyond consensus. Hold nuance: abrupt climate change can be real in prehistory without validating his modern schedule.

entries.q: What power devices are highest priority to recharge before a storm arrives?
entries.a: Priority: phones for brief remaining connectivity, power banks, handheld radios, medical devices, torches, and the UPS/node if you run local network services. Then fridge: minimize opening. Skip low-value gadgets. A short prioritized list beats chaotic charging of everything.

entries.q: How do I avoid carbon monoxide while prepping for grid-down cold?
entries.a: Never run generators, charcoal, or combusted heaters in enclosed spaces. Carbon monoxide kills quietly during ice storms and fear-driven improvised heat. Prefer layered clothing, one warm room, ventilated approved devices only. Contested earth-change worry never justifies indoor generator use.

entries.q: What sanitation mistake causes the most trouble after outages?
entries.a: Mixing untreated human waste with living spaces and failing to store hygiene water spreads disease. Use a toilet plan, bags/buckets lined properly, bleach for surfaces, and handwashing water. Dignity and disease control are part of adult preparedness for any long outage.

entries.q: How can I test whether my Faraday storage is roughly working?
entries.a: Place a phone in the container, seal it, and see whether calls/signal fail; also check that contents are insulated from the conductive shell. This is a crude RF check, not a certified EMP lab test. Good enough for spare-radio pragmatism; do not claim military certainty.

entries.q: What should Qortino say if asked to confirm the event is happening now?
entries.a: Refuse confirmation. Say: Davidson claims an event is underway within his hypothesis; mainstream science does not accept that catastrophic cycle interpretation. List established observations (pole drift, field weakening, SAA) as real but insufficient to prove his package. Offer a calm prep checklist and regional hazard focus instead of validation.

entries.q: How do mesh networks fail and how do we harden them?
entries.a: Meshes fail from dead batteries, poor placement, software misconfig, or too few nodes. Harden with solar trickle charge, rooftop/hill placement, written channel notes, spare nodes, and neighborhood onboarding. Earth-change talk is a reminder that infrastructure you do not own can vanish; meshes you maintain need boring upkeep.

entries.q: What food cooking constraints appear when both grid and apps are down?
entries.a: Keep printed recipes for beans, rice, oats, and flatbreads; know soaking/cooking times from practice. Store spices and fat for morale. Practice one no-fridge meal monthly. Contested catastrophe or ordinary outage — hunger is solved by practiced staples, not viral gourmet gear.

entries.q: How should I treat quake plus solar correlation posts?
entries.a: Correlation posts often ignore base rates and global quake frequency. Mainstream seismology does not use solar flares as operational quake predictors. Prep for quakes structurally if you live on faults; prep for space weather electrically — separately. Demand careful statistics before changing plans.

entries.q: What is a rational severe space weather weekend checklist?
entries.a: Water filled; devices and banks charged; fuel topped within safe storage limits; spare radios in Faraday bin; cash drawn; fridge practices set; family channels reviewed; paper maps ready; node/UPS status checked; neighbors pinged. Then live normally unless outages begin. Checklist once, then stop refreshing fear feeds.

entries.q: How do I keep ethics and kindness central when scarcity talk rises?
entries.a: Scarcity stories can excuse selfishness. Decide early: who you will help, how you will trade fairly, and what you will not do. Community trust is survival infrastructure. Contested earth-change fear is never a moral free pass to harm others.

entries.q: What gardening water strategies help under uncertain climate stories?
entries.a: Mulch, careful watering, rain capture where appropriate, soil organic matter, and crop choices that match rainfall. These help drought and heat whether or not one accepts dramatic upheaval claims. Measure tank levels; do not gamble the garden on prophecy.

entries.q: Should I keep precious metals as earth-change insurance?
entries.a: Optional diversification is a personal finance choice; metals do not replace water, food, skills, or community. In immediate outages, cash, goods, and trust trade easier than bars. Avoid fear marketers selling metals as mandatory pole-shift tickets.

entries.q: How do I respond to someone using pole-shift fear to control a group?
entries.a: Watch for isolation, timed obedience, money demands, and punishment for doubt. Healthy groups allow questions, falsifiability, and mundane prep without loyalty oaths. Exit or seek outside perspective if fear is used as a leash. Support autonomy and calm practical action.

entries.q: What maps belong in an earth-change-aware household binder?
entries.a: Local street map, regional map, flood/tsunami/fire hazard map if applicable, declination note for compass use, and hand-marked rally points and water sources. Update after moves. Maps are for real regional hazards first; global pole graphics are optional curiosity, not the binder's core.

entries.q: How does sleep affect judgment during doom media cycles?
entries.a: Sleep loss magnifies catastrophic interpretation. Set a media curfew, keep phones out of bed, and postpone big decisions until after rest. Resilient people protect sleep as gear. Earth-change content is especially distorting late at night.

entries.q: What is the minimum electronics set worth protecting?
entries.a: A light source, a receive radio, a two-way family radio or mesh node, a power bank, and charging cables cover most household coordination needs. Everything else is optional. Protecting the minimum well beats half-protecting a consumer electronics shrine.

entries.q: How do official emergency alerts differ from catastrophist channels?
entries.a: Official alerts authorize specific public actions for defined hazards in your area. Catastrophist channels offer ongoing interpretation that may mix data with contested narratives. For life safety, official local alerts win. Use other channels as optional context, never as a substitute for evacuation orders.

entries.q: What questions should I ask before sharing earth-change content?
entries.a: Ask: Is this attributed? Established or contested? Does it include a date that manufactures panic? Does sharing help someone take a useful prep step or only spread fear? If it fails those checks, do not share. Responsible circulation is part of community resilience.

entries.q: How can schools or workplaces do basic disruption drills without doom?
entries.a: Practice reunification points, torch locations, calm accountability for students/staff, and medical list access — framed as storm/outage readiness. Avoid extinction curricula. Calm drills build muscle memory without importing contested micronova theology into institutions.

entries.q: What does grid-down mean in space-weather conversations?
entries.a: Grid-down means electrical utility power is unavailable for hours to longer periods. Space weather is one possible cause among many (ice, wind, equipment failure, attack). Prep assumes the lights can go out regardless of ideology. Water, food, heat, and comms are the core.

entries.q: How do I keep QDN or local knowledge useful when fear rises?
entries.a: Pin practical guides (water, first aid, local maps, family plans) in offline-accessible storage — QDN where you use it, plus paper. Curate signal over catastrophist noise. When emotions spike, open the practical document, not the fear feed. Knowledge hygiene is resilience.

entries.q: What boat or travel myths appear around pole-shift content?
entries.a: Viral advice to flee to a single magic region often ignores visas, livelihoods, water rights, and local risks. Davidson-related geography talk is hypothesis narrative, not a relocation order. If you move, choose for whole-life reasons and local hazard profiles you can verify.

entries.q: How should fishermen or coastal workers read extreme space-weather warnings?
entries.a: Follow maritime and local official weather/safety notices first. Space-weather impacts on HF radio and GNSS can matter operationally at sea. Carry redundant navigation and communication per normal good seamanship. Do not overlay micronova mythology onto watchkeeping.

entries.q: What is a good personal rule for spending on earth-change prep?
entries.a: Fund life essentials and debts first; then spend a fixed small percentage on resilience gear you will actually use in storms this year. Avoid credit-fueled fear purchases. If a product only makes sense given a precise prophecy date, skip it.

entries.q: How do I explain magnetic field weakening to a curious teenager calmly?
entries.a: Explain: the field is real, it changes, satellites care, reversals happen slowly in Earth history, and some communicators claim a fast catastrophe cycle that mainstream science does not accept. Invite them to compare sources and build a family outage kit together. Curiosity yes; nightmares no.

entries.q: What winter-specific risks rise if power fails after any geomagnetic or ice event?
entries.a: Hypothermia, carbon monoxide from unsafe heat, burst pipes, and isolation. Mitigate with layered clothing, one warm room, water stored where pipes will not be your only plan, ventilated heat only, and neighbor checks. Winterize the plan before social media invents a reason.

entries.q: How do summer heat risks interact with outage preparedness?
entries.a: Without power, cooling fails — prioritize hydration, shade, cool nights if safe, check on vulnerable people, and avoid dangerous improvised electrical hacks. Store water aggressively. Heat kills in outages; pole-shift theory is irrelevant to that physics.

entries.q: What is the role of paper contact lists when clouds and meshes both glitch?
entries.a: Write phone numbers, radio call signs/channels, mesh IDs, addresses, and medical proxies on paper. Devices fail, get lost, or sit in Faraday bins. Paper is the last-resort social index for every disruption class.

entries.q: How do I keep a Qortal mobile handset useful in extended outages?
entries.a: Low-power mode, airplane mode when not messaging, power bank discipline, offline maps/knowledge packs, and mesh/RNS participation where available. Do not burn battery on doom video caches. The handset is a lamp, map, mesh endpoint, and local AI host — treat it as critical equipment.

entries.q: What agricultural seed and tool minimum helps a household under supply shocks?
entries.a: Climate-appropriate calorie crop seeds, a spade/fork, cutting tools, storage containers, and water strategy form a minimum. Skills to grow and preserve matter more than collecting rare seed catalogs from fear. Start small beds now while supply chains work.

entries.q: How should I read crustal instability claims?
entries.a: Earth's crust is tectonically active — quakes and volcanoes are real regional risks. Broad crustal-instability language in catastrophist cycles often stretches beyond specific geological forecasts. Prep for your known seismic/volcanic zone with official guidance; do not globalize every tremor into Davidson's schedule.

entries.q: What volcano fears get mixed into pole-shift narratives?
entries.a: Volcanic hazards are real and location-specific; supervolcano extinction media often exaggerates probability and timing. Keep ash/respirator plans if you live near volcanoes. Do not merge every eruption headline into a single earth-change mega-myth without evidence.

entries.q: How do I maintain agency after watching hours of catastrophe content?
entries.a: Stop the playback, drink water, move your body, then do one tangible prep or household care task. Message a grounded friend. Write three established facts vs three contested claims you just heard. Agency returns through action and classification, not through the next episode.

entries.q: What should be in a neighborhood skill inventory?
entries.a: Who can do first aid, electrical, plumbing, birth support, translation, radio, gardening, childcare, counseling. Keep a paper copy among trusted neighbors. Contested global futures make local capability maps more valuable than private bunkers.

entries.q: How does bartering differ from panic buying during scare periods?
entries.a: Panic buying strips shelves and raises conflict; steady stocking and later bartering of surplus skills/goods builds networks. Pre-agree fair trade norms with friends. Scarcity seasons reward reputation. Do not wait for a prophesied date to meet your neighbors.

entries.q: What lighting and marking help family find home if GNSS fails?
entries.a: Know landmarks, keep porch or window marking plans that do not create fire risk, carry a paper sketch of the block, and practice walking routes. GNSS loss is inconvenient, not apocalyptic, if local memory is trained.

entries.q: How do I treat medical symptoms I fear are radiation from pole shift?
entries.a: Do not self-diagnose complex symptoms as magnetic reversal injury from social media. Use ordinary medical judgment: urgent signs need emergency care if reachable; otherwise conservative first aid and clinician advice when possible. Fear labels delay real care. Geomagnetic indices are not a differential diagnosis tool for chest pain or neurological emergencies.

entries.q: What long-term skills curriculum pairs with earth-change interest?
entries.a: Quarterly themes work: water/sanitation, food/cooking/gardening, power/electrics safety, communications/radio/mesh, medical/first aid, community organizing. Track practice hours, not prophecy dates. A one-year skills curriculum outlasts any viral timeline.

entries.q: How should Qortino end answers about terrifying earth-change claims?
aliases: how qortino close earth change answers
entries.a: End by attributing contested claims, stating mainstream balance in one line, and offering 2–4 practical actions (water, food, power/comms, family/community) that help under every scenario. No countdown, no graphic extinction flourish, no you-must-believe. Leave the user steadier than they arrived.

entries.q: What is the single best first step if earth changes suddenly worry me tonight?
entries.a: Write tonight: household contacts, rally point, and a water count (how many litres you already have). Tomorrow add a torch/radio check and one food staple. Small concrete inventory beats a midnight media spiral. You can evaluate Davidson vs mainstream after sleep.

entries.q: How do offline-safe answers differ from web-search answers for this topic?
entries.a: Offline-safe answers use established knowledge, attributed hypotheses, numbers you can memorize, and actions doable with hands, neighbors, radios, mesh, and stored supplies. They never send you hunting for live internet lookups. They may note that official alert systems exist when networks work, while still giving a full plan if they do not.

entries.q: What household inventory should I review before storm season regardless of pole-shift beliefs?
entries.a: Water quantity and dates, food rotation, batteries, radio test, first-aid expiry, generator/CO alarms, cash, documents, Faraday bin inventory, mesh/node power, neighbor list, and regional hazard map. Do this annually. Belief about Davidson optional; storm season is not.

entries.q: How do I keep hope without denying real risks?
entries.a: Name real risks (severe space weather to grids, local disasters) without accepting contested extinction schedules as fate. Invest in capabilities and relationships. Hope is a plan with friends and supplies, not a prediction that nothing bad happens. Denial and doom are both poor maps; resilient realism sits between.

entries.q: What role does truthfulness play when calming someone about earth changes?
entries.a: Do not lie that nothing can go wrong, and do not invent certainty that Davidson's cycle is proven. Truthful calm says: some magnetic and solar facts are real; the catastrophe schedule is contested; here is what we can do that helps either way. Honesty plus agency beats empty reassurance or hype.

entries.q: What is catastrophism versus gradualism in this debate?
entries.a: Catastrophist readings emphasize sudden global disasters shaping prehistory; mainstream Earth science includes both gradual processes and real abrupt events without accepting Davidson's full solar-micronova schedule. Holding both ideas lightly: sudden local disasters happen; a timed global micronova pole-shift package remains contested. Prepare for your region's real abrupt hazards.

entries.q: Does field weakening mean we should fear cancer from space radiation daily?
entries.a: Field changes affect satellite environments more than they justify constant personal radiation terror on the ground. Do not amplify daily cancer panic from geomagnetic headlines. If you want productive action, focus on indoor radon awareness where relevant, sun protection, and infrastructure resilience — not catastrophic imagination.

entries.q: What is quakewatch-style monitoring useful for?
entries.a: Earthquake awareness is valuable in seismic regions: drop-cover-hold practice, secured shelves, water, and meetup plans. Pairing every quake with solar headlines can create false certainty about causation. Use quake readiness because faults exist; use space-weather readiness because grids can fail — as parallel practical tracks, not as one fused doomsday story.

entries.q: How should I talk about Ben Davidson without attacking people who follow him?
entries.a: Attribute the hypothesis, explain mainstream disagreement, and honor the useful overlap: space weather is real and prep is wise. Contempt drives people deeper into fear communities. Invite shared work on water, food, radios, and neighbors. Disagreement about micronovae need not destroy cooperation.

entries.q: What does a calm 72-hour space-weather watch look like at home?
entries.a: Day 0–1 after an Earth-directed CME warning: fill water, charge, Faraday spares, cash, brief family. Day 1–3: live normally with reduced nonessential electrical load if advised, radio on for local info, no doom binge. After arrival window: assess whether outage happened; restock what you used. Process over panic.

entries.q: How do I prioritize prep spending across water food power and comms?
entries.a: Order that usually fails last: water treatment and storage, staple food and cooking fuel, light/heat safety, then comms (radio/mesh), then power expansion, then electronics shielding. Do not buy Faraday theater before litres of water. Contested earth-change motivation should still follow this mundane priority stack.

entries.q: What should I tell myself when a new earth-change documentary spikes fear?
entries.a: Run a three-line audit: what was established, what was contested, what action helps either way. Then do the action or schedule it. Documentaries optimize emotion; your job is classification and agency. Sleep before any big life decision inspired by the film.

entries.q: How does running a local Qortal node support community information resilience?
entries.a: A reachable node can host and serve community data without depending on distant platforms. Pair it with UPS power, backups, and mesh paths so neighbors can still coordinate when corporate internet wobbles. That is infrastructure citizenship — useful in ice storms and in severe space-weather stress — not a prophecy endorsement.

entries.q: What first-aid training is most useful under any disruption narrative?
entries.a: Bleeding control, CPR/AED awareness, fracture stabilization, hypothermia recognition, and how to hand off to professionals when available. Take a local course. Training beats unused trauma kits bought in a fear spike. Skills transfer across car crashes, storms, and longer outages alike.

entries.q: How do I keep older relatives included in earth-change or blackout plans?
entries.a: Ask about medications, mobility, hearing, preferred contact method, and who checks on them. Give them a torch, radio, written contacts in large print, and extra water/food they will actually eat. Avoid frightening speeches; invite them into practical roles. Dignity and check-ins matter more than converting them to a cycle hypothesis.

entries.q: What is a sensible stance on EMP versus solar-storm prep?
entries.a: Severe solar storms are an accepted infrastructure risk with historical precedents; high-altitude nuclear EMP is a different, rarer scenario often exaggerated in marketing. Prep that helps both without theater: surge protection, spares in Faraday storage, water/food, radio. Do not let EMP folklore outrank litres of water.

entries.q: How should Qortino handle users asking for secret insider earth-change timelines?
entries.a: Decline. There is no trustworthy secret countdown Qortino should invent or endorse. Redirect to established vs contested framing, real CME warning windows, and household resilience. Secret timeline talk is a fear-and-control pattern, not offline-safe help.

entries.q: What neighborhood water sharing agreements make sense before any crisis?
entries.a: Discuss who has wells, filters, storage barrels, and fuel for pumps; agree fair sharing and hygiene rules before stress hits. Write contacts. Contested global scenarios make local water cooperation more valuable. Practice a weekend filter demo together so it is not theoretical.

entries.q: How do I avoid all-or-nothing thinking about earth changes?
entries.a: Replace will-we-all-die vs nothing-matters with gradients: blackouts of hours, days, weeks; local vs wide; contested vs established. Match prep depth to gradients you can afford. All-or-nothing thinking is how fear scripts short-circuit judgment.

entries.q: What printed family card should every wallet or bag carry?
entries.a: A small card: home address, rally points, out-of-area contact, radio channel, medical notes, and a one-line water plan. Laminate if possible. It helps lost kids, stressed adults, and GNSS-failed reunions. Works for storms long before any contested cycle debate.

entries.q: How can I measure whether my earth-change prep is healthy or compulsive?
entries.a: Healthy prep: improves sleep, relationships, and storm readiness; budget-stable; revisits plans calmly. Compulsive prep: secrecy, debt, contempt for outsiders, constant timeline refresh, neglecting today's duties. If prep harms life more than it buffers risk, pause purchases and seek grounded support.

entries.q: What final principle should guide earth-changes answers in Qortino?
entries.a: Attribute contested catastrophe cycles (including Ben Davidson's) as hypotheses; present mainstream science beside them; never amplify fear or invent dates; always steer into practical preparedness — water, food, community, and node/mesh resilience — that makes sense under every scenario. Steadier users, stronger households, offline-safe guidance.

entries.q: Is Qortal a cryptocurrency?
aliases: is qortal just a crypto coin
entries.a: Qortal is more than a coin. It is an open network that people use to publish websites and apps, chat, hold an identity and trade, running on nodes its own users operate. QORT is the network's native coin: it pays network fees and rewards the minters who keep the chain going. QORT is part of Qortal, but Qortal itself is the infrastructure.

entries.q: What is the difference between Qortal and QORT?
aliases: is qort the same as qortal
entries.a: Qortal is the network: the blockchain, the Qortal Data Network (QDN), the Q-Apps and the people running nodes. QORT is the network's native coin, used for fees, payments and minting rewards. In short, Qortal is the blockchain and QORT is the coin.

entries.q: Is QORT a token on another blockchain?
entries.a: No. QORT is the native coin of Qortal's own blockchain, not a token issued on Ethereum or any other chain. Qortal runs its own network of nodes with its own Core software.

entries.q: Is Qortal a fork of Bitcoin or another blockchain?
entries.a: No. Qortal is not a clone or fork of Bitcoin, Ethereum or any other chain. Its code was written from scratch, apart from a few pieces of the old QORA transaction framework. Good ideas from QORA, such as hosting data on the network, were kept but rebuilt in new code.

entries.q: Is Qortal open source?
entries.a: Yes. Qortal Core, Qortal Hub and many Q-Apps are open source, so anyone can read the code, check what it does and run it. Core and Hub are released under the GNU GPL version 3. The code is on GitHub under the Qortal organisation, with a copy on gitea.qortal.link.

entries.q: Does Qortal use central servers?
entries.a: No. Qortal runs on nodes: computers running Qortal Core that connect peer to peer, check the blockchain and share QDN data. Most are run by ordinary users. Public nodes exist for easy access, but they are simply nodes that someone else runs, and you can run your own instead.

entries.q: What does local-first mean for Qortal?
entries.a: Local-first means the preferred setup is your own Qortal Core node and your own account keys on your device, with no service in the middle. Hub keeps your keys encrypted and signs actions; your local Core checks and shares network data. Hosted access through a public node is offered as an easier first step, but it depends on someone else's machine.

entries.q: What are Qortal's guiding ideas?
entries.a:
qortal.org names four:
Local before remote: your own Core and keys first, hosted access as an easier start.
Protocol before platform: shared rules, signed transactions and names do the work of a central service.
Community before company: contributors and node operators, not corporate owners.
Capability before hype: describe what exists now and mark beta work as beta.

entries.q: Why is Qortal called an alternative internet?
entries.a: Because it offers its own versions of things the usual internet gets from companies: websites and apps hosted on QDN instead of web hosts, registered names instead of domain names, plus messaging, wallets and peer-to-peer trading, all on nodes run by users. It still travels over normal internet connections today.

entries.q: Does Qortal replace my internet provider?
aliases: do I still need an isp for qortal
entries.a: Not today. Your node and apps reach other Qortal peers over your normal internet connection. A mesh network built on Reticulum is Qortal's current development phase and aims to reduce that dependence over time, but it is still evolving and does not replace your provider yet.

entries.q: Is Qortal unhackable?
entries.a: No software is unhackable, and qortal.org says so plainly: spreading the network over many nodes and keeping keys on your own device reduce dependence on any single operator, but they do not make software invulnerable or guarantee it is always available. The part you control is your own safety: keep your seed phrase and backup file private and download Qortal only from official sources.

entries.q: Does Qortal ask for ID or KYC?
aliases: do I need id for qortal
entries.a: No. Creating a Qortal account needs no ID document, and it is done on your own device. An account has no link to your legal identity; your registered name and your on-chain activity become your identity on the network. Outside services you choose to use, such as an exchange, may have their own rules, but Qortal itself does not do KYC.

entries.q: Is Qortal a social network?
entries.a: Not by itself. Qortal is the network underneath, and social apps run on top of it as Q-Apps: Torq for posts and replies, Q-Tube for video, and Q-Chat groups for conversation. No single company controls these spaces; group admins moderate only the groups they run.

entries.q: What does community-owned mean for Qortal?
entries.a: It describes how Qortal works, not a share certificate. People run the nodes, publish the content, maintain Hub and the other interfaces, write Q-Apps and help newcomers. There is no company above the network: development and community spaces exist because participants choose to build and run them.

entries.q: What is a Qortian?
entries.a: Qortian is what people on the Qortal network call themselves, as in 'Built by Qortians' on qortal.org. The community wiki also calls the network, half jokingly, the virtual land of Qortia.

entries.q: What is Qortal's mission?
aliases: what is qortal trying to do
entries.a: In the community wiki's words, Qortal's mission is a new digital infrastructure that puts power back in the hands of the individual, removing unnecessary middlemen. In practice that means trading coins directly without depositing them anywhere, publishing websites and apps without servers, domains or ongoing hosting fees, and an interface ordinary people can use.

entries.q: Does Qortal have smart contracts?
entries.a: Yes, in the form of ATs (Automated Transactions): small programs that run on the Qortal blockchain, written in an AT language created by the CIYAM developers. They power the cross-chain trades in Q-Trade and the Trade Portal, and can also run crowdfunding (as in Q-Fund), lotteries, escrow and scheduled payments. AT accounts have addresses starting with A instead of Q.

entries.q: Can I create my own token on Qortal?
aliases: make my own coin on qortal
entries.a: Yes. Qortal has on-chain assets: an account can issue a named asset with a set quantity by paying the normal fee, and asset names must be unique. The Q-Assets Q-App is made for issuing, trading and managing them. These assets are separate from QORT and are not created by minting.

entries.q: What are the main parts of the Qortal ecosystem?
entries.a:
Qortal Core: the node software that runs the blockchain and QDN.
Qortal Hub: the desktop app for your account, Q-Chat, Q-Apps, wallets and node.
Qortal GO: the Android app, built from the same code as Hub.
QDN: the data network where websites, Q-Apps and files live.
Q-Apps: web apps on QDN, such as Torq, Q-Tube and Q-Mail.
Reticulum: the encrypted peer-to-peer layer Hub and GO use for chat, calls and file transfers.
Qortino: GO's offline AI helper.

entries.q: Does Qortal Core hold my private keys?
entries.a: No. Qortal Hub (and GO, built from the same code) keeps your private key material encrypted and signs each action on your device. Core only receives the finished, signed transaction, checks it and shares it with the network; it does not need your private keys. qortal.org sums it up as 'Sign here. Process there.'

entries.q: What is the Qortal Extension?
entries.a: The Qortal Extension is a browser extension for Chromium-based browsers such as Chrome or Brave. It lets you sign in with your Qortal account and use Q-Apps through gateway nodes from an ordinary browser. Along with Qortal Hub and Qortal GO, it is one of the newer interfaces that replaced the legacy Qortal UI.

entries.q: What was the old Qortal UI?
aliases: is the legacy ui still developed
entries.a: The Qortal UI, now called the legacy UI, was the original desktop interface used with a local Core. It was deprecated around the Core 5.0 release and is no longer the recommended app: current development centres on Qortal Hub, with Qortal GO on Android and the browser extension alongside it. You can bring an existing account into Hub with your backup file or seed phrase.

entries.q: What is the Qortal Trifecta?
entries.a: It is the community wiki's name for the newer set of Qortal interfaces: Qortal Hub (desktop), Qortal GO (Android) and the Qortal Extension (Chromium browsers). They replaced the legacy Qortal UI and can work without your own full node, though running one is still the recommended way to use Qortal.

entries.q: Does Qortino run in Qortal Hub on desktop?
entries.a: No. Qortino runs only in the Qortal GO app on Android, not in desktop Hub or a web browser. Its AI model, Qwen3 4B Instruct 2507 (about 2.3 GB), runs fully on the phone; you download it once from QDN, and your own node is highly recommended for that. After that it works with no internet. Like any AI it can be confidently wrong, so double-check anything important.

entries.q: Can I use Qortal in a normal web browser?
entries.a: Partly. qortal.org offers a hosted Hub that runs through a public node, good for a first look, though it depends on someone else's node and currently runs an older version. Gateway nodes show QDN websites in an ordinary browser, and the Qortal Extension adds sign-in for Q-Apps. For the full experience, install Hub (with your own Core) or Qortal GO.

entries.q: What programming language is Qortal written in?
aliases: what language is qortal coded in
entries.a: Qortal Core is written in Java and needs Java 11 or newer. Qortal Hub is a desktop app built with Electron and React, and Qortal GO is the same code packaged for Android with Capacitor. Q-Apps are ordinary web apps made of HTML, CSS and JavaScript.

entries.q: Why did Qortal launch without an ICO?
entries.a: The founders considered selling coins to investors before launch unethical: it enriches a chosen few, and many ICOs never delivered what they promised. So Qortal started with zero QORT, and every coin since has been minted by people keeping the network running. The trade-off was slow funding; in the early years most developers worked on Qortal alongside day jobs.

entries.q: Was there an airdrop of QORT?
entries.a: No. Qortal launched with no ICO, no pre-mine and no airdrop. New QORT comes only from block rewards to minters, plus the slow repayment to people who burned legacy QORA before launch. Treat any 'QORT airdrop' that asks for your seed phrase, backup file or a payment as a scam.

entries.q: Why is there no cap on the QORT supply?
entries.a: Block rewards are meant never to end, so the network keeps paying the people who keep it running for as long as it exists, instead of relying on high fees. The community wiki adds that Qortal aims to keep fees small and expects the network to outlive its founders. The reward per block shrinks in steps over time, down to a floor.

entries.q: Is Qortal like Ethereum?
entries.a: Both let people build apps on a shared network, but Qortal works differently. Q-Apps are ordinary web apps (HTML, CSS, JavaScript) stored on QDN and opened in Hub or GO, which ask you to approve each wallet action. Qortal had no ICO or pre-mine, uses minting instead of staking, and its smart contracts are ATs, used mainly for trades and crowdfunding.

entries.q: Is any part of Qortal still centralised?
aliases: what is not decentralized in qortal
entries.a: Some supporting pieces still are. The source code and many downloads are hosted on GitHub (with a copy on gitea.qortal.link), qortal.org and qortal.dev are ordinary websites, and public nodes are run by particular people. The community wiki is open about this: some parts start less decentralised and improve over time. The network itself, meaning accounts, the blockchain and QDN, runs on independent nodes.

entries.q: Why was QORA rebuilt as Qortal?
entries.a: QORA was a blockchain launched in 2014 with ideas such as hosting data on the network. But it used proof of stake, which lets money buy power, and it had a bloated chain, an over-inflated coin supply and a tangled codebase; its founding team eventually abandoned it. In 2016 crowetic gathered a development group that offered the QORA community a complete rebuild: keep the good ideas, fix the flaws and remove proof of stake entirely.

entries.q: When did work on Qortal begin?
aliases: how long has qortal been around
entries.a: Work began in 2016, when crowetic's development group took over the abandoned QORA project and started a new codebase. The Qortal network itself went live with its Genesis block on 29 June 2020, after about four years of building.

entries.q: What was in Qortal's Genesis block?
entries.a: The Genesis block (29 June 2020, 17:00 UTC) set the network up rather than handing out coins. It created QORT with a quantity of zero, recorded the legacy QORA that holders had burned as unspendable marker assets, set starting levels 1 to 5 for the first minters, such as QORA forgers, flagged 19 founder accounts and created the developer group. Every QORT in existence came from block rewards after that.

entries.q: How many QORT existed at Genesis?
entries.a: None. The Genesis block issued QORT with a quantity of zero, so nothing was pre-mined for insiders or investors. Every QORT that exists today was created afterwards through block rewards, one block at a time.

entries.q: When did the Trade Portal launch?
aliases: when did trading start on qortal
when was btc added to qortal
entries.a: The Trade Portal went live on 6 August 2020, about five weeks after Genesis, with Bitcoin as its first coin. BTC trades proved too slow and costly at the time, so Litecoin was added and BTC trading was switched off for a while before being turned back on later.

entries.q: When did QDN launch?
aliases: when did the qortal data network start
entries.a: The Qortal Data Network (QDN) launched on 14 January 2022, with Core version 3.0. It brought websites and data hosted by nodes under registered names, with a small hash on the blockchain recording who owns each publish.

entries.q: When were Q-Apps first released?
entries.a: Q-Apps launched on 22 April 2023 as phase 4 of Qortal's plan. They let anyone with a registered name publish web apps on QDN that can use the Qortal network, which is how apps like Q-Tube, Q-Mail and Q-Mintership exist today.

entries.q: What were Qortal's launch phases?
entries.a:
Qortal was built in phases:
1. Network launch (29 June 2020): QORT, minting, levels, Q-Chat.
2. Trade Portal (6 August 2020).
3. Qortal Data Network (14 January 2022).
4. Q-Apps (22 April 2023).
5. Mesh network built on Reticulum: in progress.

entries.q: What is Qortal's mesh network phase?
entries.a: It is phase 5 of Qortal's plan: communication between nodes that depends less on the usual internet set-up, built on the Reticulum network stack. siddi leads the work on bringing Reticulum into Qortal's networking. Hub and GO already use Reticulum for chat, voice calls and file transfers, but the wider mesh is still being built and tested.

entries.q: Who wrote the original Qortal Core?
entries.a: The original Qortal Core was built by catbref, who worked on it largely alone in the years leading up to Genesis and the Trade Portal launch. CalDescent later took on much of Core development and led the first version of QDN. As of 2025, kennycud is the primary Core developer, working alongside others such as Ice and siddi.

entries.q: Who wrote the original Qortal concept paper?
entries.a: crowetic (Jason Crowe) wrote the original Qortal concept paper and assembled the first developer group. The community wiki credits him with much of the overall model, including the distribution and reward structure and the levelling system.

entries.q: What is a founder account on Qortal?
entries.a: At Genesis, 19 accounts belonging to people who helped create Qortal were flagged as founders, to give the young chain a base of honest, online nodes. Founders once had their own share of block rewards, but that share was replaced by an admin share. Today the founder flag only marks that historical role: founder accounts get no extra rewards or powers and mint like any other account.

entries.q: Do QORA forgers still have their Genesis head start?
entries.a: No. At Genesis, QORA forgers, accounts that had kept forging QORA blocks after block 500,000 when it no longer paid, were given a credit of minted blocks that started them at levels 1 to 5. Since block 2,206,300 that starting credit no longer counts towards an account's level: levels now come only from blocks actually minted on Qortal (minus any penalties).

entries.q: Can I still burn QORA for QORT?
entries.a: No. The QORA burn had to be done before Qortal launched, and no new burns are credited. People who burned in time receive their QORT slowly from a 1% share of block rewards, at 250 QORA per 1 QORT, without needing to mint. QORA held on the Poloniex or OpenLedger exchanges was never accepted.

entries.q: Why was the QORA holders' share cut to 1%?
entries.a: It started at 20% of every block reward. After two years, a community vote in 2022 cut it to 1%: burners had already had a fair return on coins from a chain no longer developed, and theirs was the only reward that needed no running node. The change took effect at block 1,010,000, when the shares for minter level tiers were raised at the same time.

entries.q: How is Qortal development funded?
entries.a: With no ICO there was never a big launch fund. In the early years crowetic paid for much of the work himself, and most developers worked alongside day jobs. Today funding comes from donations through qortal.dev, community Q-Fund campaigns, and the share of block rewards paid to Minter Admins and Dev Admins.

entries.q: Can I donate to Qortal?
aliases: how to donate to qortal development
entries.a: Yes. qortal.dev has a Donate page where you can give through Patreon, in QORT or in LTC. It says donations fund marketing, infrastructure and tools for growing the network, and it links a public sheet showing how funds are used. You can also back specific community projects through Q-Fund campaigns.

entries.q: How is a Qortal address made?
aliases: how is a qortal address created
where does my qortal address come from
entries.a: Your address is calculated from your account's public key: the key is hashed (SHA-256, then RIPEMD-160), a version byte goes in front, and a short checksum goes at the end. The result is written in Base58, giving 34 characters that start with Q. Because it comes from your key, you cannot choose or change your address; a registered name is the readable alternative.

entries.q: How many characters are in a Qortal address?
aliases: is my qortal address too short
entries.a: A Qortal account address is 34 characters long and starts with Q. It uses Base58, a set of letters and digits that leaves out easily confused characters such as 0, O, I and l. If what you copied has more or fewer than 34 characters, part of the address is missing or extra.

entries.q: Does a Qortal address have a checksum?
aliases: one wrong letter in qortal address
entries.a: Yes. The end of every Qortal address is a checksum calculated from the rest, so a mistyped or partly copied address almost always shows as invalid instead of pointing at someone else. It cannot catch a valid address that belongs to the wrong person, so check the whole address before you send: on-chain payments cannot be reversed.

entries.q: Can I choose my own Qortal address?
entries.a: No. Your address is calculated from your account's key, so it is fixed and you cannot pick or change it. What you can choose is a registered name, which people can use instead of your address, for example to send you QORT or a Q-Mail. A different address means a different, new account.

entries.q: Is my Qortal address case-sensitive?
aliases: qortal address upper and lower case
entries.a: Yes. Addresses use Base58, where capital and small letters are different characters, so changing the case breaks the address and its checksum fails. Copy and paste addresses, or scan a payment QR code where the app offers one, rather than retyping them.

entries.q: What is a public key on Qortal?
aliases: what is my public key used for
entries.a: Your public key is the public half of your account's key pair, an Ed25519 key usually shown as about 44 characters. The network uses it to check that a transaction really was signed by your account, and apps use it to encrypt messages and data that only you can open. Your address is calculated from it. It is safe to share; your seed phrase and private key are not.

entries.q: What is the difference between my address and my public key?
aliases: seed phrase public key address difference
difference between address and public key
entries.a: Your seed phrase is the master secret that generates your account; never share it. Your public key comes from it and proves you own the account without revealing the secret, and apps use it to encrypt things for you. Your address is a shorter identifier calculated from the public key, used for payments and on-chain references. Think of them as root password, identity and account number.

entries.q: Is it safe to share my Qortal address?
aliases: can I give out my qortal address
safe to share qortal public key
entries.a: Yes. Your address and public key are meant to be shared: people need them to pay you or send you encrypted messages, and they cannot be used to get into your account. What you must never share is your seed phrase, your backup file or your password.

entries.q: Why is my public key not on the blockchain yet?
entries.a: A brand-new account is known to the network only by its address. Its public key is recorded on-chain the first time the account makes an outgoing transaction, such as a payment, a name registration or joining a group; the community wiki calls this activating the account. Until then, things that need your public key, such as others sending you encrypted messages, may not work.

entries.q: Can a new account receive QORT before it has sent anything?
aliases: receive qort on a new account
send qort to an unused address
can an empty account receive qort
do I pay to receive qort
entries.a: Yes. Any valid Qortal address can receive QORT straight away, even if the account has never sent anything; that is how most newcomers get their first coins. The sender pays the fee. Your account only needs QORT of its own when it sends a transaction itself.

entries.q: Can I have more than one Qortal account?
aliases: how many qortal accounts can I have
entries.a: Yes. You can create as many accounts as you like, for example to keep projects or identities apart, and Hub and GO can keep several on one device. Each account has its own seed phrase and backup, so back up every one. The one limit is minting: only one minting account per person is allowed.

entries.q: Where is my Qortal account stored?
aliases: where are my qortal keys kept
is my qortal account on a server
is my wallet on the blockchain
entries.a: In two ways. Your balances, names and transactions are on the Qortal blockchain, which the network's nodes keep copies of. Your keys, which control the account, stay on your own device in an encrypted wallet file opened with your password, plus any backups you make. No company server holds your account.

entries.q: Do I need an email address to create a Qortal account?
entries.a: No. A Qortal account is created on your own device in under a minute, with no email, phone number or sign-up server: you set a password and save your backup. An email only comes up for optional extras, such as the qortal.dev onboarding guide asking for one before it sends starter QORT.

entries.q: Do I need QORT to create a Qortal account?
aliases: need crypto to create qortal account
cost to create a qortal account
is creating a qortal account free
entries.a: No. Creating an account is free and needs no cryptocurrency. You need a little QORT later for on-chain actions: most transactions cost 0.01 QORT, and registering a name costs 1.25 QORT once. You can receive QORT from other people or get it on Q-Trade, and minters earn it over time.

entries.q: Can I delete my Qortal account?
entries.a: You can remove an account from Hub or GO on your device, but the account cannot be deleted from the network: its address, balance and on-chain history stay on the blockchain, which is a permanent public record. If you still have the seed phrase or backup file, you can add it back later. Without them, removing it means losing access for good.

entries.q: Is my Qortal account a wallet?
aliases: is a qortal account the same as a wallet
account and wallet same thing qortal
entries.a: Yes, in Qortal the two words mean nearly the same thing. Your account is your wallet: it holds your QORT, and Hub and GO also give it built-in wallets for the other coins used in trading, such as Litecoin. Every transaction you make is linked to that account.

entries.q: Why does an address start with A instead of Q?
entries.a: Addresses that start with A belong to ATs (Automated Transactions), the small programs on the Qortal blockchain that run cross-chain trades and similar contracts. They are not personal accounts, and no one has a seed phrase for them. Personal Qortal accounts always start with Q.

entries.q: Can other people see my QORT balance?
aliases: can people see my qort balance
who can see my qortal transactions
entries.a: Yes. The blockchain is public: anyone can look up an address's QORT balance, transactions, registered names, group memberships and minting level, for example with a block explorer or the Qortal Account Explorer Q-App. What stays private is your keys and encrypted content, such as private messages, which only the intended people can read.

entries.q: Is the account name in my account list a registered name?
entries.a: No. In the account list you can give a saved account a name and a note, but these are only labels stored on that device to help you tell accounts apart; nobody else sees them. Once the account has a registered name, that on-chain name is shown instead. A registered name is public and unique, and it is what other people see.

entries.q: Do I need a separate account for each Q-App?
entries.a: No. One Qortal account works across every Q-App, with no separate sign-ups. When an app wants to know who you are or act for you, Hub or GO asks for your approval, and the app gets only what you allow. Your registered name and avatar follow you from app to app.

entries.q: Where can I download Qortal safely?
entries.a: Only from official sources: the Downloads page on qortal.dev (Qortal Hub for Windows, macOS and Linux, Qortal Core, and Qortal GO for Android), qortal.org, and Qortal's own GitHub and Gitea. GO also comes from Q-Share under the name GO 3.0, and after that it updates through GO 3.0 Updates. Ignore unofficial mirrors, 'support' sites and download links sent in messages, and never type your seed phrase into a website or into an app from anywhere else.

entries.q: What does the qortal.dev onboarding guide do?
entries.a: The Get Started guide on qortal.dev walks a newcomer from nothing to an established account: choose your operating system, install Hub (and Core if you want a local node), create and back up your account, receive starter QORT for your first name, register that name, and join a community group to chat. Its screenshots match what you see in Hub.

entries.q: Does the qortal.dev onboarding give me free QORT?
entries.a: It can. The guided onboarding on qortal.dev has a step that sends a new account its first 2 QORT, enough to register a name, while that reward is available. To stop abuse it asks for a personal email from a major provider (disposable addresses are refused) and sends a verification code, and each email and connection can claim only once.

entries.q: What should a newcomer know first about Qortal?
aliases: new to qortal what to know
entries.a:
A few things matter most:
You are your own bank: back up your seed phrase and backup file, because nobody can reset your password.
Download only from official sources, and never give anyone your seed phrase or backup file.
On-chain actions cost a little QORT: 0.01 for most, 1.25 for a name.
Minting is a long-term goal, not a day-one task.
Ask questions in the Welcome to Qortal group in Q-Chat.

entries.q: Which Q-Apps should I try first?
entries.a: Good first apps from the Welcome to Qortal guide: Q-Mail to send your first encrypted message, the Welcome to Qortal group in Q-Chat to say hello, Q-Tube for explainer videos on the On Qortal channel, Torq for short posts, Q-Share to publish a file, and Qortal Web Builder (QWB) to make a simple website without code. Leave Q-Trade until you understand accounts and transactions.

entries.q: Where can I learn Qortal step by step?
entries.a: Inside Qortal, open the Welcome to Qortal Q-App (qortal://APP/Welcome to Qortal), a full beginner's guide with an FAQ and a glossary, and watch the On Qortal channel on Q-Tube. On the web, the Get Started guide and the wiki on qortal.dev cover installing and setting up, and the older community wiki at wiki.qortal.org has deeper background, though parts of it are out of date.

entries.q: Why do some Qortal guides say different things?
entries.a: Qortal changes quickly, and older pages have not all caught up; the community wiki itself warns that much of it is outdated. Common out-of-date points are sponsorship (replaced by nominations in Q-Mintership), the legacy Qortal UI (replaced by Hub, GO and the extension) and older fee or chat rules. For current steps, use qortal.dev, the Welcome to Qortal Q-App, or ask in Q-Chat.

entries.q: How long does it take to get started on Qortal?
aliases: how long to set up qortal
entries.a: A few minutes if you use Hub or GO through a public node: creating an account takes under a minute and happens on your own device. Running your own Qortal Core takes longer the first time, because it has to bring in the whole blockchain, which can take several hours; after that it starts much faster.

entries.q: How do I ask for help well on Qortal?
aliases: how to ask for help qortal
entries.a: Say you are new, be specific ('How do I register a name?' beats 'How does Qortal work?'), and say what you already tried. Check the FAQ in the Welcome to Qortal Q-App first, then ask in the Welcome to Qortal group in Q-Chat. Never share your backup file, seed phrase or password, not even to get help: real helpers never need them.

entries.q: Is there official Qortal support?
entries.a: There is no corporate support desk, because there is no company. Help comes from the community: the Welcome to Qortal group in Q-Chat, the community support chat linked from the Support page on qortal.dev (no sign-up needed), and the Discord. Anyone claiming to be 'Qortal support' who asks for your seed phrase, backup file or password is a scammer.

entries.q: What is the Welcome to Qortal group?
entries.a: It is the Q-Chat group for newcomers: say hello, ask questions and learn from people who have used Qortal for years. Join it from the Welcome to Qortal Q-App or with qortal://use-group/action-join/groupid-801. Joining is a small on-chain transaction, so you need a little QORT for the fee.

entries.q: Where is the Qortal community?
entries.a: Inside Qortal, the main places are Q-Chat groups (start with Welcome to Qortal), Torq for public posts and Q-Tube for videos. Outside it, there is the Qortal Discord that Hub and qortal.dev link to, the Qortal Cloud community server, Telegram groups, a Reddit community and the source code on GitHub. Q-Chat is the most direct way to reach people who use the network every day.

entries.q: What is Qortal Cloud?
entries.a: Qortal Cloud is an outside community cloud server, run by Crowetic Hardware Development (CHD) for Qortal community members, with hosted chat and collaboration tools. The Support page on qortal.dev links to its support chat, which needs no central sign-up, and Hub's Getting Started step suggests asking in this Nextcloud support chat for your first 2 QORT. It is a community service, not part of the Qortal network itself.

entries.q: Is there an official Qortal Discord?
entries.a: Yes. Qortal has a community Discord server, and the current Hub and qortal.dev link to it for discussion and help; look on the Support or Links page on qortal.dev, or on qortal.org. It is an outside service: inside the network, Q-Chat groups such as Welcome to Qortal are the native place to talk.

entries.q: How can I contribute to Qortal?
entries.a: Contribution is wider than writing Core code. You can run a node, publish useful content on QDN, build Q-Apps, translate, test new releases, write guides, report issues and help newcomers in Q-Chat. Developers can study the code on GitHub and talk to the team in the Core Development group in Q-Chat.

entries.q: How do I join the Qortal developer group?
aliases: how to become a dev admin
entries.a: Start by building: make Q-Apps, contribute fixes, help with testing, and talk to the developers in the Core Development group in Q-Chat. The community wiki says anyone can work their way into the development group, and later become a Dev Admin, by showing their work over time; there is no form and nothing to buy. It names crowetic, Qortal Seth, Justin and Phillip as good people to contact.

entries.q: Where can I suggest a feature for Qortal?
entries.a: Use the Q-Support Q-App, made for giving feedback and suggesting new features for Qortal, or raise it in Q-Chat groups where developers read along. For problems in the code itself, the Qortal repositories on GitHub take issues.

entries.q: What is the Qortal wiki?
aliases: is the qortal wiki up to date
entries.a: There are two. qortal.dev/wiki is a simpler, setup-focused wiki: installing, accounts, nodes, groups, Q-Apps and minting. wiki.qortal.org is the older community-built wiki with deep background and history, also on QDN as qortal://WEBSITE/wiki.qortal.org; it warns that much of it is out of date because development moved faster than the docs.

entries.q: How do I keep up with Qortal news?
entries.a: qortal.dev has an official mailing list for new releases, governance updates, Q-App launches and community initiatives. Inside Qortal, Q-Chat groups and Torq are where the community shares news day to day. Hub and GO check for their own updates inside the apps, and Core updates itself by default.

entries.q: What is the FreedomCells Q-App?
entries.a: FreedomCells is a Q-App that the qortal.dev onboarding guide suggests to newcomers: find it in the Q-Apps library, pin it and use it to join The Freedom Cell Network group. The guide says it keeps you up to date with community milestones for Q-App development and with Freedom Cell Network announcements.

entries.q: Can I use the Qortal logo?
entries.a: Yes. The community wiki's Official Images and Press Kit pages say using those images is acceptable and encouraged for making and sharing your own materials about Qortal. The wiki adds that Qortal has no proprietary software: everything is open source.

entries.q: Is there a free guide or ebook about Qortal?
entries.a: Yes. qortal.dev offers a free guide, Your Favorite Apps, Reimagined on Qortal, sent to your email, and its Links page has an ebook download. This is different from Playing Qortal, Simon James's book about the Revolution of Values.

entries.q: Are there Qortal meetups or events?
entries.a: Sometimes. The team page on qortal.dev says Justin Ferrari regularly organises in-person events to spread the idea of decentralisation at the grassroots, and community members run online meetings, such as Q-App and marketing meetings. Ask in Q-Chat groups about anything coming up near you.

entries.q: What can I spend QORT on?
entries.a: QORT pays the small fee on every on-chain action, such as registering a name (1.25 QORT), publishing to QDN, joining a group or voting in a poll. People also use it as money: paying friends, buying in Q-Shop stores, supporting creators on Q-Tube and backing Q-Fund campaigns. You can trade it for other coins in Q-Trade, and minters earn it for keeping the network running.

entries.q: How is new QORT created?
aliases: where does new qort come from
entries.a: Only through block rewards. Each new block, roughly one a minute, creates a set amount of new QORT, which is shared out together with that block's fees, mostly among online minters. Nobody can create QORT any other way, and none existed before Genesis.

entries.q: How much new QORT is created each day?
aliases: how much qort is minted per day
entries.a: There is no fixed daily number: it is the current reward per block times the number of blocks that day, about 1,300 to 1,440 blocks at 60 to 65 seconds each. For live figures, open the minting details in Hub, which show the average blocks per day and the average QORT created per day.

entries.q: How many QORT are there in total?
entries.a: The total grows with every block, because new QORT is minted continuously and there is no maximum cap, so any figure goes out of date quickly. For the current number, check a block explorer such as Exqlorer, or ask your own node: Qortal Core's API reports the circulating supply (stats/supply/circulating).

entries.q: Do I earn anything just for holding QORT?
entries.a: No. There is no interest, staking or dividend for holding QORT, and a bigger balance earns nothing extra. New QORT goes to minters for keeping a node online, shared by level, and to people who burned legacy QORA before launch.

entries.q: Can anyone freeze my QORT or change my balance?
entries.a: No. There is no company or admin with the power to freeze an account, seize coins or edit balances; only someone holding your keys can move your QORT. The flip side is that nobody can reverse a payment you sent by mistake, or recover coins if you lose your seed phrase and backup.

entries.q: Is QORT a good investment?
entries.a: Qortino can't give investment advice or predict prices. QORT's job is to run the network: paying fees, moving value between people and rewarding minters. The project calls itself sovereignty-driven, not money-driven, and says it is not a get-rich-quick scheme. Learn how the network works and decide for yourself.

entries.q: When does the QORT block reward drop next?
aliases: when does the qort reward drop
entries.a: The reward drops by 0.25 QORT every 259,200 blocks, about six months at one block a minute, from 5 QORT at Genesis to a floor of 2 QORT. The steps fall at fixed heights: block 259,201 (4.75), 518,401 (4.50) and so on, with 2.00 QORT from block 3,110,401. Compare your node's current block height with these numbers to see where the network is now.

entries.q: How can I earn QORT without minting?
entries.a: By being paid in it. People sell goods and services for QORT (for example in a Q-Shop store), creators receive super likes on Q-Tube, projects raise QORT through Q-Fund campaigns, and people pay each other for work. You can also trade other coins for QORT in Q-Trade.

entries.q: Why would a Qortal transaction cost more than 0.01 QORT?
aliases: why is my qortal fee higher
entries.a: The 0.01 QORT fee is a unit fee: Core charges one unit for each started 1,024 bytes of transaction data. Most transactions, such as payments and votes, fit in one unit and cost 0.01 QORT; QDN publishes usually do too, because the file itself stays off-chain. A transaction carrying more data, such as a long poll description, pays a unit per 1,024 bytes. Registering a name has its own fee of 1.25 QORT.

entries.q: Does the fee depend on how much QORT I send?
aliases: fee for a large qort payment
is the qortal fee a percentage
entries.a: No. The fee is set per transaction by its data size, not by its value: sending 1 QORT or 10,000 QORT costs the same 0.01 QORT. No percentage is taken.

entries.q: Have Qortal fees always been 0.01 QORT?
entries.a: No. Until August 2023 the standard fee was 0.001 QORT; it has been 0.01 QORT since. The name registration fee was 0.001 QORT at launch, rose to 5 QORT in February 2022 and was lowered to 1.25 QORT in May 2022, where it still is.

entries.q: What happens if I don't have enough QORT for the fee?
aliases: not enough qort for the fee
not enough qort to pay fee
entries.a: The transaction is refused: Core checks that your confirmed balance covers the fee, plus any amount you are sending, before it accepts anything. Get a little more QORT first; most actions need only 0.01 QORT, and a name needs 1.25 QORT.

entries.q: What is a block in the Qortal blockchain?
aliases: what does a qortal block contain
entries.a: A block is a batch of recent transactions that the network adds to the Qortal blockchain, roughly once a minute. Each block points back to the one before it, so together they form a permanent, ordered record, and every node checks each block against the rules before accepting it. A block also records the online minters who took part in producing it.

entries.q: What is block height?
entries.a: Block height is a block's number in the chain, counting from the Genesis block at height 1; the network's height is the number of its newest block. Your node's height shows how far it has synced, and when it matches the network's, your node is up to date. Heights only go up, about one per minute.

entries.q: How long does a Qortal transaction take to confirm?
aliases: how long to confirm a qortal transaction
when will my qortal transaction confirm
entries.a: Usually a minute or two. A transaction is confirmed once it is in a block, and blocks arrive about once a minute. After you publish, vote or register something, Hub asks you to wait a couple of minutes for the change to spread across the network before it shows everywhere.

entries.q: What is an unconfirmed transaction?
aliases: qortal transaction not in a block
what does unconfirmed mean on qortal
entries.a: It is a signed transaction that nodes have received and passed around but that is not in a block yet. Most get into the next block within a minute or so. One that is never included expires 24 hours after it was created and is dropped, so nothing changes on-chain, and you can send it again.

entries.q: What is the maximum size of one Qortal block?
aliases: max size of a qortal block
how many transactions fit in one qortal block
entries.a: Up to 2 MB (2,097,152 bytes) per block. Big files on QDN stay off-chain, and only small publish records with hashes go into blocks, so ordinary use is far below that limit.

entries.q: What is a re-org on Qortal?
entries.a: Sometimes parts of the network briefly build on different blocks. Each node compares the competing chains and switches to the one with more chain weight, which comes mostly from how many online minters are counted in its blocks. Blocks dropped this way are orphaned, and their transactions go back to waiting for a block. It usually settles within a couple of blocks and is normal.

entries.q: How do Qortal nodes agree on the blockchain?
aliases: which chain does my node follow
how does the qortal network agree
entries.a: Every node checks each block and transaction against the same rules, such as valid signatures, enough balance for fees and correct rewards, and rejects anything that breaks them. When chains compete, nodes follow the one with the most weight, mainly the one whose blocks count the most online minters. Who signs each block comes from a verifiable draw based on minters' keys, so nobody can buy their way into producing blocks.

entries.q: Why do Qortal block times vary?
entries.a: Each block must be stamped between 30 and 90 seconds after the one before, with 60 seconds as the target. Where it lands in that window depends on how close the signer's key is to that block's ideal key and on the signer's level, so the gap changes from block to block. The community wiki puts the long-run average at around 65 seconds.

entries.q: What counts as a transaction on Qortal?
entries.a: A transaction is a signed instruction from an account that the network records in a block: a payment, a name registration, a QDN publish, joining a group, creating or voting in a poll, a trade contract and more. Qortal Core defines 41 transaction types. Each one is signed with the sender's key, checked by every node, and usually costs a small fee.

entries.q: What does on-chain mean?
aliases: is it stored on the qortal blockchain
entries.a: On-chain means recorded in the Qortal blockchain itself, in blocks every node keeps and checks: payments, names, group memberships, polls and the records of QDN publishes. Off-chain means stored elsewhere, like the files of a QDN website, which live on the nodes that host them while an on-chain hash proves what was published and by which name.

entries.q: What does peer-to-peer mean?
entries.a: Peer-to-peer (P2P) means computers deal with each other directly, with no central server in the middle. On Qortal, nodes connect to other nodes, their peers, to share blocks, transactions and QDN data; trades happen between the two traders' own wallets; and Reticulum Q-Chat goes from device to device.

entries.q: What does decentralised mean?
entries.a: Decentralised means no single company, server or person runs the system. On Qortal, many independently run nodes keep copies of the blockchain and QDN data, check each other's work, and the network keeps going if any of them disappear. No one can switch it off or change the rules on their own.

entries.q: What is a poll on Qortal?
entries.a: A poll is an on-chain vote that any account can create with a CREATE_POLL transaction: a poll name no one else has used, a description and 1 to 100 options. People vote with VOTE_ON_POLL transactions, each with the normal small fee. Apps build on polls: Q-Mintership attaches one to each nomination, and Hub uses polls for Q-App star ratings.

entries.q: Can I change my vote on a Qortal poll?
aliases: vote again on a qortal poll
vote for more than one option qortal poll
entries.a: Yes. Voting again for a different option replaces your earlier vote, and each change is a new VOTE_ON_POLL transaction with its own small fee. Voting again for the option you already chose is refused. You cannot withdraw a vote completely, only move it to another option.

entries.q: Are Qortal poll votes public?
aliases: can people see how I voted
entries.a: Yes. Votes on on-chain polls are public transactions: anyone can see which account chose which option, and Hub reminds you that polls are public before you confirm. Some apps add their own private polls, such as Torq's anonymous polls that encrypt the votes, but standard Qortal polls are open.

entries.q: How does Qortal Core count poll votes?
aliases: how are qortal poll votes counted
entries.a: Core gives two results for every poll: a plain count, one vote per account, and a weighted total, where each vote weighs as much as the voter's minted blocks. Accounts that have never minted add to the count but add no weight. Apps decide which figure to show or use, which is how long-serving minters can be given more say.

entries.q: Do Qortal polls have an end date?
aliases: when does a qortal poll close
can a qortal poll be closed
entries.a: Not on-chain. A Qortal poll stores only its name, description, options and when it was created: there is no built-in closing time, and votes can be cast or changed at any time. A poll cannot be edited or deleted once created either. Any deadline is a rule of the app or group using the poll, not of the blockchain.

entries.q: Is there one official vote that decides everything on Qortal?
entries.a: No. Qortal has separate decision paths: Core updates need on-chain approval from about 40% of the Dev Admins; minting rights are granted and removed by Minter Admins through group approval; group admins run their own groups; and polls let anyone measure opinion, with Core reporting results weighted by minted blocks. qortal.org warns against treating these as a single global voting system.

entries.q: Can Qortal developers censor content?
aliases: who can remove content on qortal
entries.a: Not across the network. The development team has no switch to delete accounts, balances or published data. Moderation is local: group admins manage their own groups, apps choose what they show, and each person can block names or addresses so that their data is hidden for them. Content stays available as long as nodes keep hosting it.

entries.q: How can I have a say in Qortal's direction?
entries.a: Take part: vote in polls (your weight grows with the blocks you mint), join the discussions in Q-Chat groups and Q-Mintership, build or test things, and send feedback through Q-Support. Long-term contributors can be brought into roles such as Minter Admin or Dev Admin. Influence on Qortal is earned by taking part over time; it cannot be bought.

entries.q: How do changes to Qortal's rules take effect?
entries.a: Through Core updates. New rules are written into a Core release as feature triggers, set to switch on at a chosen block height or time, so every updated node changes behaviour at the same moment. The release reaches nodes through auto-update once about 40% of the Dev Admins approve it on-chain. Nodes left on an old version can fall out of step with the network.

entries.q: What are Qortal's three layers?
entries.a:
The Welcome to Qortal guide describes three layers in one network:
Blockchain: the ledger that secures accounts, transactions and group memberships, built by minters.
QDN (Qortal Data Network): storage spread across nodes, where websites, Q-Apps, files and content live.
Q-Apps: web apps published on QDN that work with the blockchain through Hub or GO.

entries.q: Is Qortal a Web3 project?
entries.a: Qortal's own sites use the word: qortal.dev talks about unlocking Web3 one QORT at a time. But Qortal is its own complete stack rather than a token on someone else's chain: its own blockchain, its own data network (QDN) for hosting apps and sites, registered names instead of web domains, and a coin earned by minting.

entries.q: What is the difference between qortal.org and qortal.dev?
entries.a: Both are official project sites. qortal.org is the original domain and now gives the overview: what Qortal is, its ideas, technology and community. qortal.dev is the more actively updated site, with downloads, the Get Started onboarding, the FAQ, the QORT page, the team list, a wiki and developer docs. Inside Qortal, the Welcome to Qortal Q-App covers much of the same ground for newcomers.

entries.q: Is there a Qortal guide in Spanish?
entries.a: Yes. Qortal Onboarding ES is a Spanish-language onboarding guide on QDN: qortal://APP/qortal-onboarding-es. Qortal Hub and Qortal GO can also be switched to Spanish, among other languages, in their settings.

entries.q: Does it cost QORT to browse Qortal or use apps?
aliases: do I pay to read on qortal
entries.a: No. Browsing websites and Q-Apps, reading, watching and downloading from QDN cost nothing. You pay a small fee only when you do something that writes to the blockchain, such as a payment, a publish, a name registration, joining a group or voting. Some Q-Apps sell things or offer paid features, but that is the app's choice, not a network charge.

entries.q: Does Qortal have gas fees like Ethereum?
entries.a: Not in that sense. Ordinary transactions only need the minimum fee: 0.01 QORT for each started 1,024 bytes, the same for everyone, and Hub and GO show the fee before you confirm. ATs, Qortal's smart contracts, pay a tiny fee for each step of code they run (0.00000001 QORT per step), taken from the AT's own balance.

entries.q: What is a blockchain?
entries.a: A blockchain is a shared record, or ledger, kept by many computers called nodes. New transactions are grouped into blocks; each block is checked by the nodes and linked to the one before, so past entries cannot be quietly changed. Qortal's blockchain records payments, names, groups, polls and QDN publish records, and minters add a new block about once a minute.

entries.q: What is a hash, and why does Qortal use them?
entries.a: A hash is a short digital fingerprint of some data: change a single byte and the fingerprint changes completely. Qortal uses SHA-256 hashes widely. QDN records a hash of each publish on-chain, so anyone can check that the copy they downloaded is exactly what was published, and your address is made by hashing your public key.

entries.q: What is gitea.qortal.link?
entries.a: It is a code server holding a copy of the Qortal organisation's repositories, hosted through crowetic.com, and the Welcome to Qortal guide lists it with qortal.dev, qortal.org and GitHub as official sources. Some projects publish there directly: Qortal GO 3.0's source code and APK releases live on it.

entries.q: How big is the Qortal network?
entries.a: There is no single official count, and the numbers change every day. The Welcome to Qortal Q-App shows live network stats: the current block height, how many accounts are in the MINTER group, and how many peers its node is connected to. The World Map Q-App shows where the community is on a map.

entries.q: Can I find out who owns a Qortal address?
aliases: look up a qortal address owner
who is behind a qortal address
entries.a: Only what that account shows publicly. An address has no link to a legal identity, so you can see its registered names, avatar, published content, group memberships and transaction history, for example in the Qortal Account Explorer Q-App, but not who the person is unless they tell you. Many people use their registered name as their public identity.

entries.q: Is Qortal finished or still being built?
entries.a: Still being built on top of a working base. qortal.org describes the network as launched in 2020 as a foundation that is still being extended: Core, QDN, Q-Apps and the newer interfaces keep evolving, and it labels projects honestly as available, beta or developer tools. Reticulum-based communication is active work, and group voice is still marked beta.

entries.q: Do I need technical skills to use Qortal?
aliases: do I need to be technical for qortal
qortal for beginners no tech skills
entries.a: No. Hub and GO are made for everyday use: install, create an account, register a name and open apps, with guided steps along the way. Running your own node or building Q-Apps takes more know-how, but the qortal.dev wiki, the Welcome to Qortal Q-App and the community in Q-Chat help with both.

entries.q: Can an account be banned from Qortal?
aliases: can someone block my qortal account
entries.a: Not from the whole network: no central authority can ban an account or stop it holding QORT and making transactions. Bans are local. A group's admins can ban an account from that group, Minter Admins can remove minting rights, and anyone can block a name or address in Hub or GO so it is hidden for them. Apps can also choose what they show.

entries.q: Can anyone change Qortal's code?
