entries.a: No. An admin can send you an invite, but you only become a member when you accept it with your own join transaction. An invite you don't want can simply be ignored: nothing happens and it costs you nothing. The only time an invite adds you at once is when you had already asked to join that group.

entries.q: What do the globe and lock icons next to a group mean?
entries.a: The globe marks an open group: anyone can join it. The lock marks a closed group, which Find groups calls a Reticulum Encrypted Group: joining needs an admin's approval, and its chat is shared only with members.

entries.q: Why did someone's name change in my chats?
entries.a: Names can change hands: the person may have renamed their name, or sold it, in which case their account now shows another of its names or just its address. The account's address never changes, so if it matters, check the address in User search.

entries.q: Why doesn't my name show in Names for sale yet?
entries.a: The listing has to confirm first, usually within a minute or two, and the Names Q-App reloads the market list every couple of minutes. Refresh it if your name still doesn't show after that.

entries.q: Why can't I see the Join requests tab on a group's Members screen?
entries.a: That tab only shows for admins and the owner of a closed (private) group, because only closed groups have join requests to review. In an open group people simply join, and regular members never see other people's requests.

entries.q: Can I get a Qortal name for free?
entries.a: No. Registering a name costs a one-time fee, currently 1.25 QORT, paid from your own balance. New accounts can get their first 2 QORT, enough for a name, by finishing the onboarding on qortal.dev, asking in the Nextcloud support chat, or buying with Q-Trade.

entries.q: Has the name registration fee always been 1.25 QORT?
aliases: why did my friend pay less for a name
entries.a: No. The fee is part of Qortal Core's rules: it was tiny at first, rose to 5 QORT in February 2022 and has been 1.25 QORT since May 2022. A future Core update could change it again, so go by the fee the confirmation window shows.

entries.q: What does Qortal Core do while it is running?
aliases: what does core do all day
core running in background what for
entries.a: Qortal Core is the node program. While it runs it keeps a full copy of the Qortal blockchain and checks every new block and transaction, passes them on to other nodes (its peers), stores and shares QDN data for names you follow or view, and serves a local API on port 12391 that Hub, GO and Q-Apps use. If you add a minting account, it also mints blocks. Your account's private keys stay in Hub or GO, which sign transactions and send only the signed result to Core.

entries.q: What is the difference between Qortal Core and Qortal Hub?
aliases: are hub and core the same
do i need both core and hub
entries.a: Qortal Core is the node: a Java program that syncs the blockchain, talks to peers and serves the API. It has no main window, only a tray icon on desktops. Qortal Hub is the desktop app you use for your account, chat and Q-Apps. Hub can work with Core on the same computer (Local Node), with a node elsewhere that you add (Custom Nodes), or with a public node, so Hub alone is enough to get started.

entries.q: Does closing Qortal Hub stop my node?
aliases: core still running after closing hub
hub closed is node still on
entries.a: No. Core runs as its own program, so it keeps running, syncing and minting after you close Hub. To stop it, use Stop Core in Hub's Set up Qortal Core window (under Advanced), choose Exit from the Qortal tray icon on Windows, or run ./stop.sh in the qortal folder on Linux and macOS.

entries.q: What is the difference between Local Node, Public Node and a custom node in Hub?
aliases: public node or local node hub
entries.a: These are the choices in Hub's Connection Mode window. Local Node is Qortal Core on this computer; Hub marks it Recommended for full decentralized access, faster performance and keeping your data local. Public Node is a shared node run by someone else: quick to start, but with limited decentralization. A custom node is any other node you add by its URL and API key, such as your own Core on another machine.

entries.q: Who runs the Qortal public node?
entries.a: Hub describes it as a privately operated node that has been made publicly accessible. It is convenient for getting started, but it is someone else's machine, it has limits compared with your own node, and you depend on it staying online. Running your own Core removes that dependence.

entries.q: What can I not do while using a public node?
aliases: features that need a private node
entries.a: Minting needs your own node; Hub says Minting requires a private node. Node admin actions, such as those in the Q-Node app (stop, restart, bootstrap, peers, minting accounts), are refused with this action cannot be done through a public node. Blocking users and editing follow or block lists also need your own node. Big files and some apps can load slowly or stall there, because the public node often drops data again after a while.

entries.q: Why does Hub recommend using my local node?
aliases: why use local node instead of public
entries.a: Hub lists three advantages of your local node: full decentralized access, faster downloads and user-controlled data. With your own node you also don't depend on someone else's public node being up, and you can mint once you are a minter. You can still use the public node while your node catches up.

entries.q: Can I use the public node while my own node is still syncing?
aliases: hub public node until core synced
wait for core sync or use public
entries.a: Yes. Hub's Core setup says you can use a public node while Core starts and syncs. Core keeps catching up in the background, and when it is synced Hub shows Local node ready with a Switch to local button. You can also stay on Local Node while it syncs; Hub then shows how many blocks you are behind.

entries.q: What is inside the qortal.zip download?
aliases: what comes in qortal core zip
entries.a: Unzipping qortal.zip gives a folder called qortal with qortal.jar (Core itself), settings.json (a few starter settings), start.sh and stop.sh (to start and stop Core), qort (a helper for calling the API from a terminal) and log4j2.properties (logging settings). Core creates the rest as it runs: db for the blockchain, data for QDN, lists, qortal.log, and apikey.txt once an app asks for a key.

entries.q: What is the qortal.jar file?
entries.a: qortal.jar is Qortal Core itself, the program that Java runs. It sits in your Core folder: qortal in your home folder on Linux and macOS, or C:\Program Files\Qortal on Windows. Auto-update replaces it with a newer one. If you ever update by hand, stop Core first, swap the file and start Core again.

entries.q: How do I install Qortal Core on Windows?
aliases: set up qortal core on windows
entries.a:
1. On qortal.dev open Downloads, and under Qortal Core (Optional) choose Windows. This downloads the official installer (qortal.exe).
2. Run it and follow the steps.
3. A splash screen shows Core downloading and extracting the bootstrap, a ready-made copy of the blockchain.
4. Core then runs in the background with a Qortal icon in the taskbar tray and finishes syncing.
Hub can do the same for you: Set up Qortal Core, then Download Core.

entries.q: Do I need to install Java for Qortal Core on Windows?
entries.a: No. The Windows installer brings its own 64-bit Java and Core uses that, so there is nothing else to install. A separate Java is only needed for the qortal.zip version used on Linux and macOS, and even there Hub can fetch one for you.

entries.q: Where does Qortal Core keep its files on Windows?
aliases: where is qortal installed on windows
entries.a: The program is in C:\Program Files\Qortal: qortal.exe, qortal.jar and a small settings.json that only points to your data folder. Your node data is in %LOCALAPPDATA%\Qortal (C:\Users\<your name>\AppData\Local\Qortal): the settings.json you edit, the db folder (blockchain), the data folder (QDN), lists and wallets. To open it, right-click Start, choose Run, type %localappdata%\qortal and press Enter.

entries.q: How do I start Qortal Core on Windows?
entries.a: Open the Start menu, type Qortal and run the Qortal app; that is Core. Or in Hub use Set up Qortal Core and Start Core. Core starts in the background, and a Qortal icon appears in the taskbar tray.

entries.q: How do I stop Qortal Core on Windows?
entries.a: Right-click the Qortal icon in the taskbar tray and choose Exit. Or in Hub open Set up Qortal Core, then Advanced, and use Stop Core. Let it finish closing before you shut down the PC or touch its files.

entries.q: What does the Qortal Core tray icon show?
entries.a: Hover over it to see Core's state, its number of connections, the block height, the blocks remaining while syncing, and the build version. The state reads Synchronizing clock, Connecting (fewer than 3 peers), Synchronizing with a percentage, Minting or NOT minting. Guides describe the icon as red until Core is fully synced and blue once it is. Right-click for Check time accuracy, Synchronize clock (Windows only), Build version and Exit.

entries.q: How do I install Qortal Core on Linux by hand?
entries.a:
1. Install Java 11 or newer (an OpenJDK package) and unzip.
2. Download qortal.zip from qortal.dev Downloads (Qortal Core, Linux) into your home folder.
3. In a terminal run unzip qortal.zip, then cd qortal, then chmod +x *.sh
4. Start Core with ./start.sh
On first start Core downloads the bootstrap and then syncs the rest.

entries.q: What does the Linux install script on qortal.dev do?
entries.a: On qortal.dev Downloads, Linux (Script) copies a one-line command; paste it into a terminal and press Enter. The script, written by crowetic, installs Java (21, or 17 as a fallback) and the tools it needs, puts Core in ~/qortal and Hub in ~/qortal-hub, adds Qortal launchers and icons to your menu, and finally offers automation that keeps Core running, updated and synced. It asks for your system password once.

entries.q: Which Linux systems does the Qortal install script support?
aliases: does the qortal script work on my linux
entries.a: It recognizes the Debian family (Debian, Ubuntu, Mint, Raspberry Pi OS and similar), the Red Hat family (Fedora, RHEL, CentOS, Rocky, Alma), Arch and Manjaro, openSUSE, and Alpine. On other systems it asks you to install the parts yourself: Java 21 or newer, curl or wget, unzip, jq, zlib development headers, ImageMagick and FUSE2, which Hub's AppImage needs.

entries.q: Can I run the Qortal Linux script on a server with no desktop?
entries.a: Yes. Over SSH or without a desktop it skips the Hub test launch but still downloads Hub and creates its launchers for later. Core itself runs fine without a screen. With the automation on, a server starts Core at boot from cron instead of at login.

entries.q: Should I accept the automation offer at the end of the Qortal Linux script?
aliases: install qortal automation yes or no
entries.a: The automation is crowetic's auto-fix script. It keeps Core running, updates Core and possibly its settings, recovers from common problems, and bootstraps the database if your node falls far behind the network, using autostart or cron entries. If you don't answer within 20 seconds it installs itself; type n to decline. You can add it later from the same scripts.

entries.q: How do I install Qortal Core on a Mac?
entries.a: The simplest way is from Hub: Set up Qortal Core, then Download Core. Hub fetches Core, and Java if your Mac has none, into your home folder and starts it. By hand: install Java 11 or newer, then in Terminal download qortal.zip (the Mac uses the same zip as Linux), unzip it, run cd qortal and chmod +x *.sh, then ./start.sh. A splash screen shows the bootstrap, then a Q icon appears.

entries.q: Which Java should I install on a Mac for Qortal Core?
entries.a: An OpenJDK build, version 11 or newer. The community guide suggests Eclipse Temurin from Adoptium (download the .pkg for your Mac) or Homebrew with brew install temurin --cask. Check it with java -version in Terminal. If you let Hub install Core, it can fetch its own Java copy instead.

entries.q: Which Java version does Qortal Core need?
entries.a: Java 11 or newer. Core is built for Java 11, and its start.sh refuses to run with anything older. Hub installs a Java 17 copy when it finds none, the qortal.dev Linux script installs Java 21 (or 17), and the Windows installer brings its own Java. Any of these works.

entries.q: Can I run Qortal Core with Oracle Java?
entries.a: Use an OpenJDK build instead, such as Eclipse Temurin or your Linux system's OpenJDK package. Core's own code notes that it is critical to use OpenJDK and not Oracle's Java SE: Core repacks the BouncyCastle security library, and Java SE then rejects it as a security provider.

entries.q: How do I check which Java version I have?
aliases: how to see my java version
entries.a: Open a terminal (Command Prompt on Windows), type java -version and press Enter. The first line shows the version, for example openjdk version "17.0.2". Core needs 11 or newer. On Linux and macOS, start.sh does the same check and prints Passed Java version check, or tells you to install or upgrade Java.

entries.q: Why does start.sh say Please su to non-root user before running?
entries.a: Core's start script refuses to run as the root user for security reasons; Core doesn't need root. Log in as, or switch to, your normal user and run ./start.sh from that user's qortal folder. That user should own the qortal folder and its files.

entries.q: How do I start Qortal Core on Linux or macOS?
entries.a: In a terminal run cd ~/qortal and then ./start.sh. It checks Java, starts Core in the background and prints qortal running as pid followed by a number, so you can close the terminal afterwards. Hub can also start it for you with Start Core in Set up Qortal Core.

entries.q: How do I stop Qortal Core on Linux or macOS?
entries.a: In a terminal run cd ~/qortal and then ./stop.sh. The script asks Core to shut down through its API using the key in apikey.txt, falls back to a normal stop signal if that fails, then waits and prints Qortal ended gracefully. Hub's Stop Core button (Set up Qortal Core, Advanced) does the same job.

entries.q: Can Qortal Hub install Qortal Core for me?
entries.a: Yes. Open Set up Qortal Core and use Download Core, then Start Core. On Windows Hub downloads and runs the official Core installer. On Linux and macOS it downloads Core into a qortal folder in your home folder, and if it finds no Java it first fetches a Java 17 copy (you see setting up Java... please wait). Core then starts and syncs in the background.

entries.q: How do I open the Core setup in Qortal Hub?
aliases: where is set up qortal core
entries.a: On Hub's login screen, use the gear button at the bottom right (Core controls) to open Set up Qortal Core. It also opens when you pick Local Node in Connection Mode while Core is not installed, and when another window offers to open node settings. There you can download, start and stop Core, set its folder and bootstrap the chain.

entries.q: What does Local node installed mean in Hub?
aliases: hub asks to start local core
entries.a: Hub found Qortal Core on this computer, but it is not running while you use the public node. It asks whether to start it: Start, Later or Ignore. If you start it, Core syncs in the background and Hub tells you when you can switch to it.

entries.q: Hub says Local node ready. What should I do?
entries.a: It means your own Core has finished syncing. Click Switch to local and Hub stops using the public node and talks to your node instead. You can stay on the public node if you prefer, but your own node is the more independent choice.

entries.q: My Qortal Core is in a different folder. How do I tell Hub?
aliases: chosen directory does not contain a qortal.jar
entries.a: Open Set up Qortal Core and find Core location. Click Choose (or Change) and pick the folder that contains qortal.jar; if it has none, Hub says chosen directory does not contain a qortal.jar. Hub then runs Core from that folder. Clear puts it back to the default location.

entries.q: Where does Hub put Qortal Core on Linux and macOS?
aliases: where is the qortal folder on mac
entries.a: In a folder called qortal in your home folder (~/qortal), with qortal.jar, settings.json, start.sh and stop.sh inside. If Hub had to fetch Java, that copy sits in ~/jdk-17.0.2. Core's own data folders (db, data, lists) are created inside ~/qortal as well.

entries.q: How long does Qortal Core take to start?
aliases: how long until core is ready
waiting for qortal core to start
entries.a: Core first loads its database and checks the blockchain, and only then opens its API; the log line is Starting API on port 12391, and Hub waits for it. The very first start takes longer because Core downloads and extracts the bootstrap first. On slow hardware a start can take a long time: crowetic's automation waits up to about 35 minutes before treating it as failed.

entries.q: What does Core not fully started mean in Hub?
aliases: qortal core has yet to be fully started
entries.a: Hub can see Core, but Core hasn't finished starting, so Hub says The Qortal Core has yet to be fully started. Please wait. Leave it running; when it is done Hub shows Qortal Core is ready. On a first start this includes the bootstrap download, which can take a while.

entries.q: What is the qort command in the qortal folder?
entries.a: qort is a small helper script shipped with Core for calling its API from a terminal. It sends your API key from apikey.txt automatically. For example, in the qortal folder ./qort admin/status shows the node's status, and ./qort -p blocks/last shows the latest block neatly formatted. Run ./qort with nothing after it to see its options.

entries.q: What does admin/status tell me about my node?
entries.a: admin/status is the node's quick health report (localhost:12391/admin/status on the node, or ./qort admin/status). height is your node's latest block, syncPercent how far it is synced, and isSynchronizing whether it is catching up right now. numberOfConnections counts blockchain peers and numberOfDataConnections QDN peers. isMintingPossible turns true when the node is synced, has enough up-to-date peers and has a minting account. It needs no API key.

entries.q: How do I see which version of Qortal Core I am running?
aliases: which core version do i have
entries.a: In Hub, hover over the sync status icon to open Core information; it lists the Core version. On a desktop you can also right-click the Core tray icon and choose Build version. From a terminal, ./qort admin/info in the qortal folder shows it as buildVersion.

entries.q: Who approves Qortal Core auto-updates?
aliases: who signs a qortal core update
entries.a: The Qortal development group, on chain. A member of the dev group publishes an update transaction that names the exact build, and the group's admins (the Dev Admins) approve it until it passes the group's approval threshold. Only then do nodes start downloading and applying it, so no single person can push an update to every node.

entries.q: How does Qortal Core know an auto-update is genuine?
aliases: is the qortal auto update safe
entries.a: The approved update transaction contains the build's commit and the SHA-256 hash of the update file. Core downloads the file from one of several mirrors, checks that its hash matches the approved one, and throws the file away if it doesn't; the log then says the downloaded JAR's hash doesn't match. Core also only takes an update that is newer than the version it is running.

entries.q: How often does Qortal Core check for updates?
entries.a: About every 20 minutes, Core looks on chain for a newly approved update. Nodes don't all switch at the same moment; the community wiki says it takes about 2 hours for the whole network to update. You don't need to do anything while auto-update is on.

entries.q: Why did my Qortal node restart by itself?
entries.a: Usually an auto-update: Core downloads the new version, a helper stops the node, swaps qortal.jar and starts it again, and the tray says Applying automatic update and restarting... A bootstrap (Applying bootstrap and restarting node) or a restart from the Q-Node app works the same way. If you use crowetic's automation, it can also restart Core when it finds the node stuck. Give it a few minutes to come back.

entries.q: How do I turn off automatic Qortal Core updates?
entries.a: Add "autoUpdateEnabled": false to Core's settings.json and restart Core. The community wiki does not recommend it: auto-update keeps all nodes on compatible versions and avoids forks. With it off you must install every new release yourself, or your node will sooner or later stop syncing with newer peers.

entries.q: What is new-qortal.jar in my qortal folder?
entries.a: It is a Core update that has been downloaded and checked but not yet swapped in. During the automatic restart, Core's update helper moves it over qortal.jar and starts the new version. If an update can't be applied, Core deletes the download and tries again on a later check.

entries.q: What happens if my Qortal Core version is too old?
entries.a: Newer nodes refuse to sync with peers below a minimum Core version (their minPeerVersion setting), and by default they don't even keep the connection. A node that falls several versions behind therefore finds fewer and fewer peers and stops syncing. Leave auto-update on, or update by hand soon after each release.

entries.q: Does updating Qortal Core also update Hub or GO?
entries.a: No. Core's auto-update only replaces Core on that machine. Qortal Hub and Qortal GO are separate apps with their own updates, so check those in the apps themselves. Hub's Core information shows the Core version and the Hub version as two separate lines.

entries.q: Does a Core auto-update change my settings or data?
entries.a: No. An auto-update only replaces qortal.jar. Your settings.json, the db folder (blockchain), QDN data, lists, apikey.txt and minting accounts stay as they were, and Core starts again with them. Separate tools, such as crowetic's automation, may adjust settings.json, but Core's own update doesn't.

entries.q: Where is the Qortal Core log file?
entries.a: Core writes its log to qortal.log in the folder it runs from: ~/qortal/qortal.log on Linux and macOS, and C:\Program Files\Qortal\qortal.log on a standard Windows install. When it reaches 10 MB it is compressed into a dated file such as qortal.04-Nov.log.gz and a fresh qortal.log starts. Older installs wrote log.txt files instead.

entries.q: What are run.log and run.pid in the qortal folder?
entries.a: start.sh writes both. run.pid holds the process number of the running Core, which stop.sh uses to find and stop it; it is removed after a clean stop. run.log catches what Java prints to the console. Core only prints errors there, so run.log is where startup errors and crashes show up, while the normal running log is qortal.log.

entries.q: What are the qortal .log.gz files in my qortal folder?
aliases: can i delete qortal log gz
entries.a: They are older parts of Core's log. Each time qortal.log reaches 10 MB, Core compresses it into a file named after the date, like qortal.04-Nov.log.gz. They are only there for reading later; Core doesn't need them to run, and crowetic's recovery script deletes them when it resets a node.

entries.q: Which log lines show that Qortal Core started properly?
aliases: tell core is running from log
entries.a: In qortal.log a healthy start goes roughly: Starting repository, Validating blockchain..., Chain height at start-up followed by a number, Starting networking on port 12392, Starting second network (QDN) on port 12394, and finally Starting API on port 12391. Once that last line appears, Hub and Q-Apps can talk to the node.

entries.q: How can I tell from the log that Core is bootstrapping?
entries.a: Look for lines such as Downloading full node bootstrap from (a bootstrap server), Extracting bootstrap..., Moving files to output directory... and Starting repository from bootstrap... If a download fails you see Bootstrapping failed. Retrying in a number of minutes; Core keeps retrying with longer waits each time. After that the normal startup lines follow and the node syncs the newest blocks.

entries.q: How do I know if UPnP opened my Qortal ports?
aliases: did my router open the qortal port
entries.a: Check qortal.log after Core starts. UPnP Mapped for P2P, port: 12392 means your router opened the port for Core. Unable to map P2P port: 12392 with UPnP, port in use? means it didn't, so forward TCP 12392 and 12394 to the node yourself if you want incoming connections. UPnP is on by default (the uPnPEnabled setting).

entries.q: Is it safe to share my Qortal Core log?
aliases: what is in the qortal log
does the qortal log show my ip
entries.a: Share it only with people you trust to help. qortal.log lists peer IP addresses, your node's external IP address once Core learns it, and account addresses, for example of the accounts it mints for. It does not contain your seed phrase, but never send apikey.txt or anything from the qortal-backup folder along with it.

entries.q: How do I change how much Qortal Core writes to its log?
entries.a: Logging is set in log4j2.properties in the Core folder. The default level is info, and chatty libraries are already turned down. You can raise one part of Core to debug while a developer helps you, then restart Core; set it back afterwards, because debug logs grow fast.

entries.q: What does Synchronize clock in the Qortal Core tray menu do?
entries.a: It appears on Windows only. It runs a small script that asks for administrator rights, sets the Windows Time service to use public internet time servers (pool.ntp.org) and sets it to start automatically, because Core needs an accurate clock. Check time accuracy, in the same menu, opens a time-check website so you can compare your clock.

entries.q: What does the Qortal Core splash screen show?
entries.a: On a desktop, Core shows a splash window while it starts. On a first start or after a bootstrap it shows progress such as Downloading full node bootstrap... with a percentage, then Extracting bootstrap... When the splash closes, Core keeps running in the background with its tray icon, and it may still need to sync the newest blocks.

entries.q: Core says Database upgrade needed. Please restart the core. What do I do?
aliases: please restart the core to complete the upgrade
entries.a: Do what it says: stop Core and start it again. Core shows this when its database still needs some internal tables built, which can happen right after a bootstrap, and it won't start fully until it has been restarted once.

entries.q: How do I restart Qortal Core?
entries.a: Stop it, wait until it has fully ended, then start it again: ./stop.sh then ./start.sh in the qortal folder on Linux and macOS, or Exit from the tray icon and run Qortal again on Windows. With your own node you can also use restart in the Q-Node app, which asks you to approve it and can take up to 5 minutes.

entries.q: Can I start Qortal Core with a different settings file?
entries.a: Yes. Core reads settings.json from the folder it starts in, or the file you name after qortal.jar on the command line (java -jar qortal.jar mysettings.json). A settings file can also contain userPath, which tells Core to read the real settings.json from another folder; the Windows installer uses this to point at %LOCALAPPDATA%\Qortal.

entries.q: How do I open Qortal Core's API documentation?
entries.a: Add "apiDocumentationEnabled": true to settings.json and restart Core, then open localhost:12391/api-documentation in a browser on the node machine. It lists the API calls with descriptions and examples and lets you try them. Admin calls still need your API key.

entries.q: What does the Core information panel in Hub show?
aliases: where hub shows peers and height
entries.a: Hover over the sync status icon in Hub to see Core information: Core version, block height, connected peers, QDN (data) peers, Hub's Reticulum details (connected remote interfaces, P2P Hub peers and P2P Hub health), which node you are using, and the Hub version. It tells you at a glance whether your node is synced and well connected.

entries.q: Does Qortal Core start automatically when my computer starts?
entries.a: Not on a plain install: on Windows, macOS and Linux you start Core yourself, or Hub offers to start it when you open Hub. QORTector devices and nodes set up with crowetic's automation start Core by themselves. If your computer restarts for system updates, set Core to start automatically, or minting stops until you start it again.

entries.q: How do I make Qortal Core start at boot on Linux?
aliases: qortal core start at boot linux
entries.a: The easiest way is crowetic's automation, which adds a cron @reboot line for its start-qortal-core.sh script (and, on desktops, a login autostart entry). To do it yourself, run crontab -e and add an @reboot line that changes into your qortal folder and runs ./start.sh. The folder change matters, because cron does not start in your qortal folder.

entries.q: How do I make Qortal Core start automatically with Windows?
aliases: qortal core run at windows login
qortal core automatic after windows update restart
entries.a: Add Qortal to your startup apps, as the community wiki suggests, so Core comes back after Windows restarts for updates. Press Win+R, type shell:startup and press Enter, then put a shortcut to the Qortal app (the Core shortcut from the Start menu) in the folder that opens. Core then starts each time you log in.

entries.q: How often does crowetic's auto-fix script run?
entries.a: It runs shortly after the machine starts (about 7 minutes after login on a desktop, or 399 seconds after boot on a server) and then at 01:01 on every third day of the month; the cron line for that is 1 1 */3 * *. Each run first updates the script itself.

entries.q: How do I turn off crowetic's auto-fix automation?
entries.a: Run crontab -e and delete the lines that run auto-fix-qortal.sh (and the @reboot start line too if you don't want Core started at boot), then remove its entry from ~/.config/autostart if there is one. Running the auto-fix script again later re-creates its schedules.

entries.q: Where does crowetic's auto-fix write its logs?
entries.a: On a headless node its cron runs write to ~/auto-fix-startup.log (the run after boot) and ~/log-auto-fix-cron.log (the regular runs). On a desktop it usually runs in a terminal window you can watch; let it finish once it has started.

entries.q: Can I undo settings changes made by crowetic's auto-fix?
entries.a: Yes. Before it merges its recommended values into settings.json, auto-fix saves a timestamped copy of your old file in qortal-backup/auto-fix-settings-backup inside the qortal folder, and latest-good.json points at the newest good copy. Stop Core, copy the backup over settings.json and start Core. When merging, it keeps the higher of two numbers and forces a few thread-priority settings.

entries.q: What is the autoRestartEnabled setting in Qortal Core?
aliases: core auto restart with no peers
entries.a: When set to true in settings.json, Core checks every 10 minutes and restarts itself if it has no connected peers at all. It is off by default. It is meant for a node that sometimes loses all its peers and doesn't recover on its own.

entries.q: What does Qortal Core do the first time it starts?
aliases: what happens when core starts first time
entries.a: It creates its folders, sees there is no blockchain database yet and downloads the bootstrap instead of syncing from block one. It loads a starting list of well-known peers, makes its own certificate for the API, and once the API is up it syncs the blocks made since the bootstrap. The first app that needs it then has Core create an API key in apikey.txt.

entries.q: What is QortalKeyStore.jks in the qortal folder?
entries.a: It holds the certificate Core uses to serve its API over HTTPS. Core creates it by itself on first start and makes a new one if the file goes missing or gets damaged. It has nothing to do with your account, but keep it private like the rest of the node's files.

entries.q: Does Qortal Core's API use HTTPS?
entries.a: Yes. Current Core serves both HTTPS and plain HTTP on the same API port, 12391, using a certificate it makes for itself. Hub on the desktop talks to your local node over HTTPS and trusts that certificate. GO uses plain HTTP for a node on your home network.

entries.q: What does Qortal Core save when it shuts down?
entries.a: A clean stop shuts Core's parts down in order: syncing, the API, wallets, networking and the rest. On the way it logs Backing up local data and writes your minting accounts and trade-bot states to the qortal-backup folder, then closes the database and logs Shutdown complete! That is why stopping Core properly beats pulling the plug. Hub waits up to 2 minutes for Core to finish.

entries.q: What is a bootstrap in Qortal?
entries.a: A bootstrap is a ready-made, compressed copy of the blockchain database. Instead of downloading and checking every block from peers one at a time, a node downloads the bootstrap, unpacks it into its db folder and then syncs only the blocks made since. Core does this by itself on first start, and the community wiki says a new bootstrap is made every 12 hours.

entries.q: Can I sync my node from the genesis block instead of using a bootstrap?
entries.a: Yes. Before the first start, add "bootstrap": false to settings.json. With no database and bootstrapping off, Core syncs from block one using its peers. Expect it to take far longer than a bootstrap; the community FAQ says a full sync can take up to a few days.

entries.q: Where does Qortal Core download its bootstrap from?
entries.a: From one of the Qortal bootstrap servers, picked at random: bootstrap.qortal.org, or bootstrap2, bootstrap3 or bootstrap4.qortal.org. On a normal node the file is bootstrap-archive.7z (testnet nodes use a testnet- version). The list is the bootstrapHosts setting, so it can be changed in settings.json if ever needed.

entries.q: What happens step by step during a bootstrap?
aliases: what happens when a node bootstraps
entries.a:
1. Core downloads the bootstrap archive from a bootstrap server.
2. It closes its database and deletes the old db folder.
3. It extracts the archive and moves the new database into place as db.
4. It starts the database again, restores your minting accounts and trade data from qortal-backup, and opens the API.
5. It syncs the blocks made since the bootstrap was created.
If a download fails, Core waits and tries again.

entries.q: What does a bootstrap replace and what does it keep?
entries.a: It only replaces the db folder, which holds the node's copy of the blockchain. settings.json, apikey.txt, your follow and block lists, hosted QDN data and the wallets folder stay. Your minting accounts and trade-bot data are in the database too, but Core saves them to qortal-backup and restores them after the bootstrap, so minting carries on.

entries.q: What exactly does Bootstrap chain in Hub do?
entries.a: It is one tool with two paths. If your local Core is running, Hub asks Core, with your API key, to bootstrap itself from the snapshot, then watches the log until the API is back. If that isn't possible or fails, Hub stops Core if needed, deletes the local chain database (the db folder) and starts Core, which then bootstraps on start. Wallet files are left alone either way.

entries.q: How do I bootstrap a Windows node by hand?
entries.a:
1. Right-click the Qortal tray icon, choose Exit and wait for Core to close.
2. Right-click Start, choose Run, type %localappdata%\qortal and press Enter.
3. Delete the db folder in the window that opens.
4. Start Core again from the Start menu. It downloads and applies a fresh bootstrap, then syncs the newest blocks.

entries.q: How do I bootstrap a Linux or Mac node from the terminal?
entries.a: In a terminal run cd ~/qortal, then ./stop.sh, and wait for Qortal ended gracefully. Then rm -rf db deletes the database folder, and ./start.sh starts Core, which bootstraps by itself. Delete only the db folder: the rest of the qortal folder holds your settings, API key, lists and QDN data.

entries.q: Hub says my local node is not synchronized when I log in. What can I do?
entries.a: Hub shows how many blocks behind your node is and asks you to wait until it is synchronized. You can wait, choose continue with public node to use the public node for now, or continue with Local anyway if you know your node is behind. Once the node has caught up, Hub says you are now synchronized and you may continue.

entries.q: How does Qortal Core catch up when it is behind?
entries.a: Core asks its up-to-date peers for the blocks it is missing and checks each one before adding it. Since Core 6, a node more than 200 blocks behind asks for 200 blocks at a time, which the developers describe as up to a 300% speed-up. It needs at least 3 peers with recent blocks before it syncs or mints.

entries.q: What is the block archive in Qortal Core?
entries.a: To keep the database smaller, Core moves older blocks out of the main database into compact archive files (the archiveEnabled setting, on by default). The node still keeps every block back to genesis and can still serve them; they are only stored more compactly. That is also why normal nodes download the bootstrap-archive file.

entries.q: How do I control when Core runs database maintenance?
entries.a: Core picks a random time between repositoryMaintenanceMinInterval and repositoryMaintenanceMaxInterval after it starts: 3 and 14 days by default, written in milliseconds in settings.json. Setting the maximum to 0 turns scheduled maintenance off. You can also start it on demand with a DELETE request to admin/repository and your API key while Core runs; it needs enough free disk space to rebuild the database and pauses the node for a while.

entries.q: What do the maxPeers, minOutboundPeers and minBlockchainPeers settings do?
aliases: how many peers does core connect to
entries.a: maxPeers is the most blockchain peer connections Core allows (32 by default). minOutboundPeers is how many connections Core tries to make out to others itself (16). minBlockchainPeers is how many peers with recent blocks it needs before it will sync or mint (3), and it must be at least 1. QDN data peers are counted separately, up to maxDataPeers (64).

entries.q: Which peers does a new Qortal node start with?
aliases: first peers of a new node
entries.a: When its peer list is empty, Core adds a built-in list of well-known nodes, such as node1 to node15.qortal.org and a few community nodes, and connects to some of them. From there it learns about more peers from the nodes it talks to, so it doesn't rely on that list for long.

entries.q: Why does my node keep switching to different peers?
entries.a: That is on purpose. Core stays connected to each blockchain peer for a random time between 2 and 6 hours (minPeerConnectionTime and maxPeerConnectionTime), then drops it and finds others. Rotating peers stops nodes from forming isolated islands and keeps the network well mixed. QDN data peers are only kept for up to 30 minutes.

entries.q: Can I clear my node's list of known peers?
entries.a: Yes. The API has a call that removes all known peers from the node's database; with the qort helper it is ./qort -l DELETE peers/known in the qortal folder, and your API key is sent automatically. When Core next finds its peer list empty, for example after a restart, it adds its built-in starting peers again and rebuilds the list.

entries.q: How do I tell Qortal Core my public IP address?
entries.a: Core normally works it out itself from its peers or from UPnP. If it gets it wrong, Core 6 added a setting for it: put your public address in settings.json as "ourExternalIpAddress" (the address in quotes) and restart Core. It tells other nodes where yours can be reached.

entries.q: Can I stop Qortal Core from using UPnP?
entries.a: Yes: add "uPnPEnabled": false to settings.json and restart Core. UPnP is on by default, and Core uses it at startup to ask your router to open its peer ports, 12392 and 12394. With it off, forward those TCP ports to the node yourself if you want incoming connections.

entries.q: What is port 12391 on a Qortal node?
entries.a: It is Core's API port, where Hub, GO, Q-Apps and scripts talk to the node, over HTTPS or plain HTTP. Don't forward it on your router or open it to the internet; only the peer ports 12392 and 12394 need that. To reach your node's API from elsewhere, use a VPN or an SSH tunnel. The settings shipped with Core let devices on your own network reach this port, but sensitive calls still need the API key.

entries.q: How do I change the ports Qortal Core uses?
entries.a: Set them in settings.json and restart Core: "apiPort" for the API (default 12391), "listenPort" for blockchain peers (12392) and "listenDataPort" for QDN data peers (12394). If you change the API port, also change the address Hub or GO use for this node. Running a second node on the same network is the usual reason to change the peer ports.

entries.q: What is the Qortal testnet and which ports does it use?
entries.a: The testnet is a separate Qortal network with its own chain, used for testing. A node joins it when settings.json has "isTestNet": true. Its ports are 62391 for the API, 62392 for peers, 62394 for QDN data and 62393 for the developer proxy. The scripts know it too: ./stop.sh --testnet and ./qort -t use the testnet API port.

entries.q: How do I use Hub with my Qortal node on another computer?
aliases: connect hub to node on another pc
hub use node on raspberry pi
entries.a:
1. Core on the node must accept API calls from your computer. The settings shipped with Core already do; if you turned the whitelist on, add your computer's address to apiWhitelist and restart Core.
2. In Hub open Connection Mode, go to Custom Nodes and choose Add custom node.
3. In Manual node setup enter a Name, the Node URL (the node's address with port 12391) and the API key from the node's apikey.txt.
4. Save it, pick it, and reload Hub when it asks.

entries.q: How do I connect Hub to a remote node through an SSH tunnel?
entries.a:
1. On your computer run ssh -L 12398:localhost:12391 you@192.168.1.20, using your own user and the node's address, and keep that terminal open. The first number can be any free port.
2. In Hub add a custom node with the Node URL 127.0.0.1 and port 12398, plus the node's API key from its apikey.txt.
3. Choose that node and log in as usual.
For a node outside your home network, its SSH port (usually 22) must be reachable.

entries.q: Does Hub need my node's API key?
aliases: hub custom node api key optional
where hub gets the api key
entries.a: For your local node, Hub reads the key from Core's apikey.txt by itself, and asks Core to create one if there is none. For a custom node you type it into the API key (optional) field. Without it Hub can still read the chain and QDN, but actions that need the key, such as publishing, node admin actions and changing lists, are refused.

entries.q: What is the Qortal Core API key?
entries.a: It is a long random code, kept in a file called apikey.txt, that works like a password for your node's sensitive API calls. Apps such as Hub send it when they need to control the node or act through it; reading public chain and QDN data doesn't need it. It is not your account password or seed phrase and gives no access to your QORT account, but it does give control over the node.

entries.q: Where is my node's apikey.txt?
aliases: find the qortal api key file
entries.a: Core keeps it in the folder set by apiKeyPath, which by default is the folder Core starts from: ~/qortal/apikey.txt on Linux and macOS, and C:\Program Files\Qortal\apikey.txt on a standard Windows install. To check on any system, open localhost:12391/admin/settings on the node and look for apiKeyPath. The file only appears once something has asked Core to create a key.

entries.q: What does my node's API key protect?
aliases: which core calls need the apikey
entries.a: Calls that control the node or act through it: stopping, restarting and bootstrapping Core, adding or removing minting accounts and peers, database maintenance, building QDN publishes and uploads, changing follow and block lists, foreign-coin wallet calls such as balances and sends, trade-bot actions, and making a new key once one exists. Reading blocks, names, balances and QDN content needs no key.

entries.q: How is my node's API key created?
aliases: first api key for a node
entries.a: Core doesn't make one by itself. The first app that needs it, usually Hub talking to your local node, calls Core's admin/apikey/generate, which works without a key only while none exists. Core then saves a fresh random key in apikey.txt, and from then on generating another key requires the current one.

entries.q: How do I change my node's API key if it leaked?
aliases: new api key for my node
entries.a: Make a new one, which makes the old one useless. In Hub you can use reset apikey: it deletes apikey.txt and has Core generate a new key. Without Hub, stop Core, delete apikey.txt, start Core and let your app create a new key, or call admin/apikey/generate with the current key, which replaces it. Then enter the new key everywhere else you use this node, such as GO and your scripts.

entries.q: What is localAuthBypassEnabled in Core settings?
aliases: api key not needed on same computer
entries.a: When set to true, Core accepts requests from the same machine (loopback addresses such as 127.0.0.1) without the API key. It is off by default. Be careful with it: if a web server or proxy on that machine passes outside traffic to Core, those visitors look local too and skip the key. GO only trusts it for a node it reaches over 127.0.0.1, localhost or ::1.

entries.q: What is the apiWhitelist setting?
aliases: who can connect to the core api
entries.a: It lists the addresses allowed to use the API at all. With the whitelist on, Core's default is only the node itself (::1 and 127.0.0.1), while "apiWhitelistEnabled": false lets any address connect; the settings.json shipped with Core sets exactly that. To allow only your home network, set "apiWhitelistEnabled": true and, for example, "apiWhitelist": ["::1", "127.0.0.1", "192.168.0.0/24"], then restart Core. Sensitive calls still need the API key either way.

entries.q: What does apiRestricted mean in Core's settings?
entries.a: When it is on, Core refuses a group of API calls meant for testing and development, such as building certain raw transactions for you or signing one with a private key sent to the node. If the setting is missing it is on for the main network and off on testnet. The settings.json that comes with Core sets it to false.

entries.q: Can I put the API key in the address instead of a header?
aliases: api key in the url qortal
how to send the qortal api key
entries.a: Yes. Core takes the key from the X-API-KEY header or from an apiKey parameter in the address, and Core's own stop.sh uses the address form. The header is the better habit, because addresses end up in browser history, logs and screenshots. The qort helper sends the header for you.

entries.q: How do I check that an API key is correct?
entries.a: Call admin/apikey/test with the key in the X-API-KEY header: a correct key answers true. A wrong one is refused with API key invalid, and no key at all with Missing 'X-API-KEY' header. In the qortal folder, ./qort admin/apikey/test does this with the key from apikey.txt. Hub and GO run the same check on custom and private nodes.

entries.q: Why does Core say API key not generated?
aliases: core has no api key yet
entries.a: Your node has no API key yet, so it refuses every call that needs one. Let Hub create it by using the node as your Local Node, or call admin/apikey/generate yourself; that works without a key only while none exists. The new key is saved in apikey.txt.

entries.q: Can I keep the API key in settings.json?
entries.a: Not any more. The apiKey setting is a legacy option from before November 2021. If an old settings.json still has one (at least 8 characters), Core copies it into apikey.txt and uses it; otherwise the key lives only in apikey.txt.

entries.q: Where is Qortal Core's settings.json?
entries.a: On Linux and macOS it is in the qortal folder, ~/qortal/settings.json. On Windows the one you edit is %LOCALAPPDATA%\Qortal\settings.json; the settings.json in C:\Program Files\Qortal only points Core to that folder. Core logs which file it used at startup, as Using settings file followed by the path.

entries.q: Why are there two settings.json files on Windows?
entries.a: The Windows installer writes a tiny settings.json in C:\Program Files\Qortal that only holds userPath, the folder with your real settings. That real settings.json is in %LOCALAPPDATA%\Qortal, together with the db, data, lists and wallets folders it points to. Edit the AppData one; the wiki says the Program Files copy is for advanced users only.

entries.q: Should I change Qortal Core's settings.json?
aliases: do i need to edit settings.json
entries.a: Usually not. The community wiki's advice is to leave it alone unless you have a specific reason, because Core's defaults are chosen to suit general use. If you do change something, restart Core afterwards, since settings only apply when Core starts.

entries.q: What is in the settings.json that comes with Qortal Core?
aliases: what settings does core ship with
entries.a: Very little. The Linux and macOS zip has four settings: balanceRecorderEnabled true, apiWhitelistEnabled false, allowConnectionsWithOlderPeerVersions false and apiRestricted false. The Windows installer's copy has apiDocumentationEnabled true, apiWhitelistEnabled false, apiRestricted false and allowConnectionsWithOlderPeerVersions false, plus the paths of your data folders. Every other setting uses Core's built-in default.

entries.q: Do changes to settings.json take effect right away?
entries.a: No. Core reads settings.json only when it starts, so stop Core, make your change and start it again. The community wiki gives exactly that order: stop, edit, start.

entries.q: Can Qortal Core's settings.json contain comments?
entries.a: Current Core skips any line that starts with #, and it also tolerates a comma right before a closing } or ]. Older Core versions and most guides expect strict JSON, so the safe habit is still plain JSON: no comments and no comma after the last setting.

entries.q: How can I see the settings my node is actually using?
aliases: show all settings of my node
check a setting value in core
entries.a: Open localhost:12391/admin/settings in a browser on the node, or run ./qort -p admin/settings in the qortal folder. It lists every setting with the value Core is using, including built-in defaults you never set. For a single one, add its name, for example admin/settings/maxPeers.

entries.q: What happens if a setting is not in settings.json?
entries.a: Core uses its built-in default for it. settings.json only needs the settings you want to change, and a file containing just {} is valid; the Core README starts developers off with exactly that. If the file is missing entirely, though, Core stops with a Settings file not found error.

entries.q: Where can I find the full list of Qortal Core settings?
entries.a: In Core's source code: the file Settings.java in the Qortal/qortal repository on GitHub lists every setting with its default value and a short note. The community wiki's settings page explains the common ones, and on a running node admin/settings shows them all with their current values.

entries.q: What is the wallets setting in Qortal Core?
aliases: turn off ltc wallet in core
qortal node foreign coin wallets off
entries.a: Since Core 6 you can switch off individual foreign-coin wallets in Core (ARRR, BTC, DGB, DOGE, LTC and RVN) with the wallets setting, to save memory and bandwidth on a node that only serves data or mints. A wallet switched off at startup can still be started later through the API. Leave them on if you trade or use coin wallets through this node.

entries.q: How do I turn on Qortal Core's QDN gateway?
entries.a: Set "gatewayEnabled": true in settings.json and restart Core. The gateway serves QDN websites and apps to ordinary web browsers, on port 80 by default (gatewayPort changes it). Public gateways usually sit behind a web server such as nginx with HTTPS. Anything visitors open through your gateway is fetched and stored on your node and uses your bandwidth.

entries.q: Can I change Qortal Core's language?
entries.a: Core's own texts, such as the tray menu and its pop-ups, follow your computer's language by default. To choose one, set "localeLang" in settings.json to a language code such as de or fr, and restart Core. The tray texts exist in 17 languages, including English, German, Spanish, French, Russian, Japanese and Chinese.

entries.q: Can I run two copies of Qortal Core on one computer?
aliases: two qortal nodes on one computer
entries.a: Yes, if they share nothing: give each its own folder (with its own settings.json, db and data) and its own ports for the API, blockchain peers and QDN peers (apiPort, listenPort, listenDataPort). Two copies pointed at the same database fail, with Core reporting Repository in use by another process? A testnet node already uses different ports from a mainnet node.

entries.q: What does allowConnectionsWithOlderPeerVersions do?
entries.a: It decides what happens with peers older than minPeerVersion. When true, they can still connect and sync from your node, and show in your peer list, but your node won't sync from them. When false, as in the settings.json shipped with Core, syncing is blocked both ways and they don't appear at all.

entries.q: What does apiLoggingEnabled do in Core's settings?
entries.a: When set to true, Core writes every API request it receives to a file called API-requests.log, in the standard web-server log format with times in UTC. It is off by default. Turn it on only while you investigate something, because the file grows quickly and keeps a record of every request made to your node.

entries.q: What does the bindAddress setting do?
entries.a: It sets which local address Core listens on for both its API and its peer connections. The default, ::, means every address on the machine, with 0.0.0.0 as a fallback where IPv6 isn't available. Changing it affects peers as well as the API, so to limit who can use the API use apiWhitelist instead.

entries.q: What does tradebotSystrayEnabled do?
entries.a: When set to true, Core shows a pop-up from its tray icon each time one of its trade-bot entries, a Trade Portal trade it is running, changes state. It is off by default and only matters on a desktop where Core's tray icon is visible.

entries.q: What are the folders inside my qortal folder?
aliases: what is in the qortal directory
entries.a: db holds the node's copy of the blockchain; data holds the QDN files the node hosts; lists holds its follow and block lists; qortal-backup holds exported minting accounts and trade-bot data; wallets holds encrypted caches for coin wallets that need them; uploads-temp holds unfinished uploads and is cleared at start. Next to them sit qortal.jar, settings.json, apikey.txt, QortalKeyStore.jks, the logs and the start and stop scripts. On Windows the data folders are in %LOCALAPPDATA%\Qortal.

entries.q: What should I back up from my Qortal node?
aliases: what to save from the qortal folder
entries.a: First and most important is your account backup and seed phrase, which stay with you, not on the node. From the node itself, keep a private copy of the qortal-backup folder (minting accounts and trade data), the lists folder (follows and blocks), settings.json, and apikey.txt if other devices use this key. The db folder doesn't need backing up, since a bootstrap rebuilds it. QDN data can usually be fetched again from peers, unless your node is the only one hosting something you published.

entries.q: What is in the qortal-backup folder?
entries.a: Core's own copy of data that lives only on this node: MintingAccounts.json with the node's minting accounts, TradeBotStates.json with the trades it is running, and TradeBotStatesArchive.json with older ones, plus a few other node files. Core writes them when it shuts down, and loads the minting accounts and trades back in when it starts. That is why a bootstrap or a fresh database doesn't lose them.

entries.q: Is the qortal-backup folder sensitive?
aliases: is my minting key in the backup folder
entries.a: Yes. MintingAccounts.json contains the private key of your minting key, and the trade-bot files hold the keys for trades in progress. Keep the folder private: don't post it, send it to anyone or store it anywhere public. Core itself calls this export sensitive, node-local data.

entries.q: Do I need to back up the db folder?
aliases: should i back up the blockchain
entries.a: No. The db folder is only your node's copy of the public blockchain, and a bootstrap or a sync rebuilds it. Copying it can save time when you move a node, but copy or restore it only while Core is stopped.

entries.q: What does the repositoryBackupInterval setting do?
entries.a: It makes Core back up its own database regularly; the value is the time between backups in milliseconds, and 0, the default, means off. Each backup replaces the previous one in a backup folder inside db, and when it is on Core also makes one before an auto-update or a bootstrap. If the database gets damaged, Core can try to recover from that backup.

entries.q: Which files should I copy when moving my node to a new computer?
aliases: copy my node to a new pc
transfer the qortal folder to a new computer
entries.a: Install Core on the new machine first. Then, with both Cores stopped, copy over the qortal-backup folder (minting accounts and trade data), the lists folder (follows and blocks) and settings.json if you changed it. Copy the data folder too if you want to keep hosted QDN files without fetching them again. Start Core and let it bootstrap; if you mint, you can instead simply add your minting key again from Hub on the new node.

entries.q: What happens to my old node when I run the Linux install script again?
aliases: linux script with an existing node
qortal script backs up old install
reinstall qortal with the linux script
entries.a: If Core is running and synced, the script keeps it as it is. Otherwise it moves your old qortal folder to ~/backups/qortal-<number>, installs a fresh Core, and copies back qortal-backup (minting and trade data), lists (follows and blocks), the data folder if it was in the default place, apikey.txt and a custom dataPath setting. Check your other custom settings afterwards.

entries.q: How do I uninstall Qortal Core?
entries.a: Stop Core first. On Windows, remove Qortal from your installed apps, then delete %LOCALAPPDATA%\Qortal if you also want the node's data gone. On Linux and macOS, delete the qortal folder in your home folder (and jdk-17.0.2 if Hub fetched Java for it), and remove any auto-fix lines from your crontab. Your account isn't stored in Core, but keep qortal-backup if you mint or have trades open.

entries.q: What is the wallets folder in the qortal folder?
entries.a: It is where Core keeps encrypted wallet caches for the foreign coins that need one, such as Pirate Chain (ARRR), so it doesn't have to rebuild them each time. You can move it with the walletsPath setting. It is not where your coins are: those are on their own blockchains, controlled by your keys.

entries.q: What is in the db folder?
entries.a: It is Core's database: the node's own copy of the Qortal blockchain, stored as HSQLDB database files whose names start with blockchain. Don't edit or open it while Core runs. If it ever gets damaged, delete it with Core stopped and let a bootstrap rebuild it.

entries.q: How do I install Qortal Core on a Raspberry Pi?
entries.a: Use a 64-bit Raspberry Pi OS, or another 64-bit Linux, and install it like any Linux machine. The Linux (Script) command from qortal.dev Downloads installs Java, puts Core in ~/qortal and fetches the arm64 build of Hub. Or follow the qortal.zip steps with Java 11 or newer. Then start Core with ./start.sh and let it bootstrap.

entries.q: Which memory settings does crowetic's automation give Qortal Core?
aliases: core java memory by ram size
entries.a: It swaps in a start.sh chosen for the machine's RAM. Up to about 6 GB it lets Java use up to 80% of the memory, from 6 to 16 GB up to 70%, and above 16 GB up to 40%. On a 32-bit ARM board it uses a fixed 1750 MB instead. Core's own start.sh uses 50%.

entries.q: Can I run Qortal Core on Qubes or Whonix?
aliases: qortal core in an app qube
entries.a: Yes, the community wiki has a Qubes guide. Install Java 11 or newer in the template (or a standalone qube) and Core in the app qube as on Linux. On Whonix, add "testNtpOffset": 0 to settings.json so Core works with Whonix's own time sync. Over Tor the bootstrap servers can fail to connect; a new Tor circuit, or a manual bootstrap, gets around that.

entries.q: Do I need a Qortal account or QORT to run a node?
aliases: run a node without an account
does a node need a name
entries.a: No. Qortal Core syncs the chain, shares data and serves its API without any account, name or QORT. You need an account only to use Hub or GO with it, and minting needs an account that has been accepted into the MINTER group.

entries.q: Can several people use the same Qortal node?
aliases: use one node for many accounts
entries.a: Yes. Each person signs in with their own account in their own Hub or GO, pointed at the node, and the node never holds their account keys. Some things are shared, though: the node's follow and block lists apply to everyone using it, and anyone you give the API key to can control the node. Give out the key only to people you trust with that.

entries.q: Can other Qortal nodes see my IP address?
entries.a: Yes. Like any peer-to-peer network, the nodes yours connects to see its IP address, and peers pass addresses around so others can find yours. The chain doesn't record IP addresses, but anyone running a node yours talks to can see it. If you don't want your home address in peer lists, run the node somewhere else, such as a VPS, and connect to it from home.

entries.q: Where can I learn more about running a Qortal node?
aliases: learn to run a qortal node
entries.a: Start with the Running a Node page in the qortal.dev wiki, which covers installing Core on each system and bootstrapping. The community wiki at wiki.qortal.org has deeper pages on settings, port forwarding, SSH tunnels and Raspberry Pi. Inside Qortal, the Q-Minter guide has node recommendations and the Welcome to Qortal Q-App has a Nodes page.

entries.q: Why does stop.sh say Stop command failed - not running?
aliases: stop.sh not running with process id
entries.a: stop.sh could not reach Core through its API and found no running Core process to signal, so as far as it can tell Core isn't running. Check whether it is (for example with localhost:12391/admin/status); if it started from another folder or as another user, stop it there.

entries.q: Why does Core say Unable to start networking?
entries.a: Core couldn't open its peer port, so it shuts itself down again; desktops show a Networking failure message, and the log adds Can't create listen socket with the reason. The usual cause is another program, often a second copy of Core, already using port 12392 or the QDN port 12394. Stop the other one, or give this node different ports with listenPort and listenDataPort.

entries.q: Why does Core say Unable to start API?
entries.a: Core couldn't open its API on port 12391 and shuts down again; desktops show an API failure message. Most often another program, or a second copy of Core, is already using that port. Stop the other program, or set a different apiPort in settings.json and use that port in Hub and GO.

entries.q: How do I see the peers my node is connected to from a terminal?
entries.a: In the qortal folder run ./qort -p peers for the blockchain peers, with each one's address, Core version and last block height, and ./qort -p peers/data for the QDN data peers. The Q-Node app shows the same lists in tables, and Hub's Core information shows the counts.

entries.q: How do I see how long my node has been running?
aliases: how long has core been running
entries.a: Run ./qort admin/uptime in the qortal folder; it answers in milliseconds. admin/info also includes it, and the Q-Node app has a node uptime widget.

entries.q: How do I see what happened on the chain in the last 24 hours?
entries.a: Ask your node: ./qort -p admin/summary in the qortal folder returns the past 24 hours of activity, with the number of blocks, the transactions counted by type, and names registered and assets issued. admin/summary/alltime gives the same since genesis.

entries.q: Can Core tell me when it backs up or maintains its database?
entries.a: Yes, on a desktop where its tray icon is visible. Set "showMaintenanceNotification": true to get a Performing scheduled maintenance... pop-up, "showBackupNotification": true for database backups, and "showCheckpointNotification": true for its regular saving of database changes. All three are off by default.

entries.q: Does my node help the network even if I don't mint?
aliases: why run a node if not minting
entries.a: Yes. A node that doesn't mint still checks and passes on blocks and transactions, hosts and relays QDN data so apps and sites load faster for others, and gives other nodes more peers to connect to, especially with its ports open. The Minter Guide says every extra healthy node helps Qortal, whether or not it is minting.

entries.q: What is the difference between qortal.zip and qortal.jar?
aliases: which core download zip or jar
do i need the zip or the jar
qortal jar download for an update
entries.a: qortal.zip is the full package for a first install on Linux or macOS: it unpacks into a qortal folder with qortal.jar, the start and stop scripts, a starter settings.json, the qort helper and the logging settings. qortal.jar on its own is just the Core program, which is what you replace when updating by hand. Windows uses the qortal.exe installer instead.

entries.q: Should Qortal Core run on the same computer as Hub?
aliases: core and hub on the same computer
hub on one pc core on another
best machine to run qortal core
core on a different machine than hub
entries.a: Either works. Running Core and Hub together locally is the setup qortal.org calls the preferred one. Many minters instead keep Core on a small always-on machine and open Hub on their everyday computer only when needed, adding the node there as a custom node. What matters is that Core stays online and synced.

entries.q: Do I need a full JDK or is a JRE enough for Qortal Core?
aliases: is a jdk needed for qortal
entries.a: A Java runtime (JRE) is enough to run Core. The qortal.dev Linux script installs just the runtime packages, such as openjdk-21-jre, and falls back to the headless versions. You only need a full JDK, together with Maven, if you want to build Core from its source code.

entries.q: Does Hub's own Java copy change the Java on my computer?
aliases: does hub install java system wide
entries.a: No. On Linux and macOS, when Hub finds no Java it unpacks a Java 17 copy into ~/jdk-17.0.2 and uses it only to run Core. Your system's own Java, if you install one later, is left alone: Hub checks for its own copy first and otherwise uses the system java command.

entries.q: How can I tell whether Qortal Core is running?
aliases: is my qortal node switched on
how to know qortal core started
entries.a: On a desktop, the Qortal tray icon is there while Core runs. Hub's Connection Mode shows Core running for a local node, and the sync icon's Core information shows its version and height. In a browser on that machine, localhost:12391/admin/status answers only when Core's API is up; on Linux and macOS, ./qort admin/status in the qortal folder does the same check.

entries.q: start.sh says qortal running as pid, but Core doesn't answer. Why?
aliases: qortal running as pid but not working
core started but api not responding
entries.a: That line only means Java was started in the background. Core may still be loading or bootstrapping, or it may have stopped with an error. Give it some minutes, then look at the end of qortal.log to see what it is doing, and at run.log for startup errors such as a broken settings.json or a port already in use.

entries.q: How do I bootstrap my node from the terminal while Core is running?
aliases: bootstrap core from the command line
trigger a bootstrap in the terminal
entries.a: In the qortal folder run ./qort admin/bootstrap; the helper sends your API key. Core answers true, then restarts itself to delete the old database, download a fresh bootstrap and sync from there, and the log shows Bootstrapping node... and Restarting node with:. Hub's Bootstrap chain and Q-Node's bootstrap use the same call.

entries.q: What do inbound and outbound peers mean?
entries.a: Outbound peers are nodes yours connected to itself; Core aims for at least 16 of them (minOutboundPeers). Inbound peers are nodes that connected to yours, which only happens when others can reach your peer ports through UPnP or port forwarding. Q-Node's peer list shows this as each connection's direction. No inbound peers is fine for using Qortal, but open ports help the network.

entries.q: What does a peer's handshake status mean?
entries.a: Before two nodes trust each other they go through a short handshake: they exchange hello messages with their versions and node IDs, then each proves itself with a challenge and response that includes a small proof of work. Only a peer whose handshake is COMPLETED is used for syncing and data; peers at an earlier stage are still connecting.

entries.q: What does the ntpServers setting do?
entries.a: It is the list of internet time servers Core asks for the exact time; by default these are the pool.ntp.org servers for each region of the world. Core relies on that time to judge blocks and transactions. Change the list only if those servers are blocked where you are. Whonix users set testNtpOffset to 0 instead.

entries.q: Core says topOnly mode is no longer supported. What do I do?
aliases: topOnly mode is no longer supported
entries.a: Open settings.json, delete the "topOnly" line (an old setting for nodes that kept only recent blocks), and start Core again. Current Core refuses to start while that setting is there.

entries.q: What do Core errors like minBlockchainPeers must be at least 1 mean?
aliases: apiKey must be at least 8 characters
entries.a: Core checks a few values in settings.json when it starts and stops if one is wrong: minBlockchainPeers must be at least 1, a legacy apiKey must be at least 8 characters, and storagePolicy must be one of FOLLOWED_OR_VIEWED, FOLLOWED, VIEWED, ALL or NONE. Fix the value named in the message, or remove that line to use the default, and start Core again.

entries.q: Does Qortal Core restart itself after a crash?
entries.a: Not by itself. Core restarts on purpose for updates and bootstraps, and the autoRestartEnabled setting restarts it when it has no peers, but if the Java process stops, nothing in Core starts it again. crowetic's automation checks after each boot and every third day, and starts Core again when it isn't running or responding.

entries.q: Should I run Qortal Core as its own user on Linux?
aliases: run core as a non root user
entries.a: It is a good habit on servers. Core must not run as root (start.sh refuses), and the community guides for a VPS or a gateway node create a separate user, such as one named qortal, and install Core in that user's home folder. On a desktop, your normal user account is fine.

entries.q: How do I open the qortal folder on a Mac?
aliases: where is the qortal folder macos
entries.a: In Finder choose Go, then Home, and open the folder named qortal. Or in Terminal type open ~/qortal and press Enter. For a Core installed by Hub or from the zip, that folder holds qortal.jar, settings.json, apikey.txt, the logs and the db and data folders.

entries.q: Does Qortal Core slow down my computer?
aliases: core uses a lot of ram
entries.a: It is built to stay in the background: start.sh and Hub start Java at the lowest CPU priority (nice), so your other programs come first, and by default Java may use at most half of the RAM. It works hardest during the first sync or a bootstrap and during its database maintenance every few days. Many minters prefer a separate small machine that runs all the time.

entries.q: What is qortal.exe on Windows?
entries.a: qortal.exe is the Windows launcher for Core: it starts qortal.jar with the Java the installer brought along. It sits in C:\Program Files\Qortal next to qortal.jar, and the Start menu entry, Hub's Start Core button and Core's own restart after an update all go through it. The installer you download from qortal.dev is also called qortal.exe.

entries.q: I changed apiPort. How does Hub find my local node?
aliases: changed api port hub cannot connect
entries.a: Hub's Local Node choice always looks for Core on port 12391. If you moved the API to another port, add the node under Custom Nodes instead, with the Node URL 127.0.0.1 and your new port, plus the API key from apikey.txt.

entries.q: Does Qortal Core run on Apple Silicon Macs?
entries.a: Yes. Core is a Java program, so it runs on both Intel and Apple Silicon Macs. When Hub installs Core on an Apple Silicon Mac and finds no Java, it fetches the Apple Silicon (aarch64) build of Java 17 for it.

entries.q: What is the Qortal Core API?
aliases: how apps talk to qortal core
entries.a: It is the local web interface that Qortal Core offers on port 12391. Hub, GO, Q-Apps and scripts send it requests, for example for the block height, a name, a QDN file or the node's status, and Core answers, mostly in JSON. Anyone who can reach it may read public chain data; calls that control the node need the API key. With apiDocumentationEnabled on, Core also serves a page that lists every call.

entries.q: Can my node work as my own block explorer?
aliases: look up block on my node
entries.a: For simple lookups, yes. On the node, open these in a browser or run them with ./qort -p in the qortal folder: blocks/height for the latest height, blocks/last for the newest block, blocks/byheight/ followed by a number for any block, and transactions/signature/ followed by a signature for one transaction. Each answer comes from your own copy of the chain.

entries.q: How do I check an address's QORT balance with my own node?
entries.a: Open localhost:12391/addresses/balance/ followed by the address in a browser on the node, or run ./qort addresses/balance/ followed by the address in the qortal folder. The answer is the address's QORT balance from your node's copy of the chain, so make sure the node is synced first. addresses/ followed by the address gives more about the account.

entries.q: Does the Windows Core installer change my clock settings?
entries.a: It can. The installer checks the Windows Time service, and if it isn't already using the pool.ntp.org time servers it can set it to use them and to start automatically, because Core needs an accurate clock. Later, Synchronize clock in Core's tray menu does the same.

entries.q: Where are the Qortal launchers after running the Linux script?
aliases: where is qortal in my linux menu
entries.a: The script adds a Qortal submenu to your desktop's applications menu, with a Qortal Hub launcher and a Qortal Core launcher, and puts a Qortal Hub shortcut on your Desktop. The Core launcher starts Core from ~/qortal. If the launchers show up under Internet instead, log out and back in.

entries.q: When does crowetic's auto-fix bootstrap my node?
entries.a: In the current version, when your node is more than 2,500 blocks behind the public API node after a fresh check, or when its height hasn't moved since the last run and stays stuck through two more checks five minutes apart. Before bootstrapping it stops Core, copies and checks the db folder and keeps the original aside; if Core then fails to start, it puts the original database back. Older copies of the script used 1,500 blocks.

entries.q: How do I run crowetic's auto-fix without it updating itself?
entries.a: Start it as AUTO_FIX_SELF_UPDATE=0 bash ~/auto-fix-qortal.sh. That keeps the installed script version, but everything else still runs: it can still update Core, merge settings, change schedules, restart Core or bootstrap. There is no dry-run mode, so only run it when you want real maintenance.

entries.q: Is it safe to forward the Qortal peer ports on my router?
entries.a: Yes, they are meant for that: 12392 and 12394 only talk Qortal's peer protocol, and every connection goes through a handshake before it is used. Forward only those two. Never forward the API port 12391, and don't put the node in the router's DMZ, which opens everything.

entries.q: Does a node behind CGNAT or a mobile connection still work?
entries.a: Yes. Core makes its own outbound connections to peers, so it syncs and can mint without anyone connecting in. It just gets no inbound peers. For QDN, Core 6 can relay data through better-connected nodes for nodes that others can't reach directly.

entries.q: What does Connecting mean on the Qortal Core tray icon?
entries.a: Core has fewer than 3 connected peers, the minimum it needs before it syncs or mints (minBlockchainPeers), so it is still finding them. After a start this usually clears as peers connect. If it stays on Connecting, check the internet connection, the computer's clock and the firewall.

entries.q: What is my node's ID?
entries.a: Since Core 6, each node has its own identity, an Ed25519 key pair it makes for itself, and other nodes use its node ID to tell nodes apart even when an IP address or port changes. You can see it as nodeId in admin/info (./qort admin/info in the qortal folder). It is not linked to your account.

entries.q: How do I list my node's minting accounts from the terminal?
aliases: check minting key on node terminal
which accounts mint on my node
entries.a: In the qortal folder run ./qort -p admin/mintingaccounts. For safety Core only shows public keys: each entry has the minting account and the recipient account it mints for. Hub's Minting panel shows the same list as Node minting accounts.

entries.q: What does Rebuilding all names... mean in the Core log?
entries.a: It is a normal startup step. Each time a full node starts, Core rebuilds its table of registered names from the chain before it validates the blockchain and opens the API. Let it finish.

entries.q: Hub says error downloading Java. What can I do?
entries.a: Hub could not fetch its Java copy, which it gets from Qortal's own download servers. Check your internet connection and any firewall or proxy, then try Download Core again. Or install Java 11 or newer yourself, such as an OpenJDK package; Hub then finds and uses the system Java.

entries.q: Does Hub use start.sh when it starts Qortal Core?
entries.a: No. On Linux and macOS, Hub runs Java on qortal.jar directly from the Core folder, with its own options and settings.json, and writes the console output to run.log.
