Your node can collect different chunks from different peers and checks each one against its hash.

entries.q: Why is there a .qortal folder in my website files?
aliases: hidden qortal folder in my website
entries.a: Qortal Core adds a small hidden .qortal folder to multi-file resources such as websites and apps, for its own bookkeeping. It doesn't count towards the size limit, and you don't need to add, edit or remove it.

entries.q: Does QDN keep the original file name?
aliases: download name of a qdn file
entries.a: Yes, when the app sends one: a publish can carry a file name, and the metadata lists the file names inside a resource and its file type. So downloads usually come back with their names. If an app published data without one, you choose a name when you save it.

entries.q: Does following a name protect its data from cleanup?
aliases: followed data deleted when storage is full
followed content removed when node full
entries.a: Not fully. When storage passes 90% of its limit, your node deletes chunks at random from everything except your own uploads, followed names included. It downloads followed names again only once usage is back under 80%.

entries.q: Does following someone on Torq make my node host their content?
aliases: does a torq follow download posts
entries.a: No. A Torq follow is a social follow that Torq publishes, so their posts show in your Following feed. Hosting is a separate setting: to have your node keep someone's QDN data, follow their name with the Follow button in an app such as Q-Share or Q-Tube.

entries.q: Why do some names with spaces or symbols fail to open on QDN?
aliases: name with spaces breaks qdn link
special characters in a name qdn
name with a slash wont load
qortal name with a plus sign
non latin name qdn app error
entries.a: Names can contain spaces, a plus, a slash and letters from many languages, and some apps and links don't encode them properly, so the address breaks. Hub's own copy link writes a space as %20. If content from such a name won't open in one app, the app's handling of the name is usually the cause, not the data.

entries.q: How does Qortal Core 6 make QDN downloads faster?
entries.a: Core 6 moved QDN onto its own network connections, separate from block syncing. It also remembers how fast each peer has sent data before and prefers peers that keep up, and it builds Q-Apps faster by decrypting while it unpacks.

entries.q: How many QDN data peers can my node have?
aliases: how many data peers on qortal
entries.a: By default Qortal Core keeps up to 64 slots for QDN data peers, set with maxDataPeers in settings.json. A peer connected for QDN data is also dropped after about 30 minutes, so data connections keep changing.

entries.q: Can I host QDN data without minting?
aliases: do i need to mint to host data
qdn node that does not mint
entries.a: Yes. Hosting and minting are separate: any node with QDN turned on stores what it follows and opens, whether it mints or not. Minting needs minting rights; hosting needs only disk space and bandwidth.

entries.q: Can I turn off QDN relay mode?
entries.a: Yes. Close Qortal Core, add "relayModeEnabled": false to its settings.json and start Core again. Your node then passes on only data it hosts itself. Relaying is optional, but it helps data reach nodes that can't connect directly, including publishers without port forwarding.

entries.q: Can my internet provider see what QDN data my node handles?
aliases: can my isp see qdn data
can my isp see my qortal data
can someone see what my node relays
entries.a: They can see that your node exchanges encrypted data with other Qortal nodes, but not what it is at a glance. For public data, though, the decryption keys are on the public blockchain, so someone who runs Qortal and looks hard enough could match and decrypt it. Private data stays unreadable to them. A VPN hides the traffic from your provider, but then the VPN provider sees it.

entries.q: Can a QDN website run PHP or a database?
aliases: server side code on a qortal site
can qdn run a web server
entries.a: No. A QDN website is static: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, images and other files that the visitor's Hub or GO shows as they are. Nothing runs on a server, so PHP, server databases and server-side forms don't work. A Q-App can still use the Qortal API through qortalRequest, for example to sign in with a Qortal account, take payments or store data on QDN.

entries.q: Can I put my WordPress site on QDN?
aliases: convert my website to static for qortal
move my existing site to qortal
static copy of a website for qdn
entries.a: Only as a static copy. Export the site to plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript (WordPress plugins such as Simply Static can do this), zip it with index.html at the top and publish it as a website. Anything that needs the WordPress server, such as comments, forms, shops or logins, won't work, and some sites convert better than others.

entries.q: Why won't my website zip publish?
aliases: why does my website zip fail
entries.a: Check three things. index.html, or another index file, must be at the top level of the zip, not inside a folder. The zip must be a normal .zip: some archive programs write older formats that don't work, while 7-Zip in zip format and Windows' own archiver are known to work. And Hub's website form takes zips up to 400 MB.

entries.q: Do private Q-Apps get updates like other Q-Apps?
entries.a: Yes, when the group admin who published it publishes a new zip to the same identifier; it is encrypted for the group again and replaces the old version. Members get the new version the next time they open it, and in GO, Refresh builds the app again from the latest copy.

entries.q: Can I publish on QDN for free?
entries.a: Not any more. Publishing once had a free option that used a proof-of-work calculation instead of a fee, but since 2023 every publish has to pay the fee, about 0.01 QORT, which goes to the minters. Keeping your content hosted afterwards costs nothing.

entries.q: Why doesn't Qortal store files on the blockchain itself?
aliases: why is qdn data off chain
why not put files on the blockchain
why are files not on the blockchain
entries.a: Because every node would then have to hold every file. QORA, the project Qortal grew from, stored data on its chain, which would have bloated it beyond what normal computers can hold and put everyone's uploads, unwanted ones included, on every node. QDN keeps only small records and hashes on the chain, while each node hosts just what it follows or opens.

entries.q: Is a QDN publish usable before it is in a block?
aliases: do i wait for a block after publishing
entries.a: Yes. As soon as nodes receive your unconfirmed publish transaction, they know the resource exists and can fetch it, so it can open before a block includes it. That is why a publish can show up within minutes.

entries.q: What is the difference between a public and a private QDN gateway?
entries.a: A public gateway lets ordinary browsers reach anything published on QDN. A private gateway is set up for one resource only, such as a single website mapped to its own domain, so people can visit that site through it but can't use it to reach other QDN content.

entries.q: Where do I see the apps and websites I published?
aliases: see what i published in hub
entries.a: In the Q-Apps library's My apps tab in Hub or GO. It lists your published apps and your published websites for your names, with buttons to update them or publish something new.

entries.q: Does my node share QDN data while my computer sleeps?
aliases: does qdn work when pc is off
does my node host while my computer sleeps
entries.a: No. Qortal Core has to be running for your node to share data, so while the computer sleeps or is off, other nodes can't get anything from it. The Hub window itself doesn't need to be open, only Core.

entries.q: Can I make a public QDN resource private later?
entries.a: Not the copy that is already out. You can publish an encrypted version to a _PRIVATE service and replace the public one with a delete marker, so nodes stop serving it. But anyone who opened or saved the public version may still have it, and the record of the public publish stays on the blockchain.

entries.q: Can I change who can open a private QDN resource?
aliases: add someone to a private qdn file
remove access to private qdn data
share private file with new person
change who can open private qdn
who can open my private file change
entries.a: Only by publishing it again. To add or remove people, the app encrypts the data again for the new list of keys and publishes it as a new version; nodes then drop the old version. Someone you remove can't open the new version, but whatever they already opened or saved, they keep.

entries.q: What does "Data unavailable. Please try again later." mean?
aliases: data unavailable please try again later
entries.a: Your node tried several times to collect the resource's files from peers and gave up for now, so it shows this instead of the item. It isn't an error with your account. Try again later; if it keeps happening, no reachable node is hosting that content right now.

entries.q: Why does a page say "QDN is disabled in settings"?
entries.a: The node you use has QDN switched off with "qdnEnabled": false in its settings.json, so it doesn't load or publish any QDN content. If it's your node, change the value to true, or remove the line, and restart Qortal Core.

entries.q: Why does sharing several files cost more than publishing one website zip?
aliases: why multiple fees for one share
one fee for a website zip
entries.a: Each QDN resource is one publish with one fee. A website or app zip, however many files it holds, is a single resource, so it costs one fee. Q-Share publishes every shared file as its own FILE resource plus a document describing the share, so a share with three files costs four fees.

entries.q: What is the IMAGE service on QDN?
entries.a: IMAGE holds one picture of up to 10 MB. The community GIF library, for example, keeps its GIFs as IMAGE resources, and Torq publishes the cover picture of an attached video or file as one. For bigger pictures use FILE, and for small avatars and previews THUMBNAIL (500 KB). IMAGE_PRIVATE is the encrypted version.

entries.q: How do I see how much disk space QDN uses on my node?
aliases: how big is my qdn storage
how much space does qdn use
qdn space used on my node
entries.a: Check the size of the data folder inside Qortal Core's folder. Core also writes a line with "Total used" and "Total capacity" for its QDN storage to its log about every 10 minutes, which shows how close it is to its limit.

entries.q: How is QDN like a torrent network?
aliases: qdn peer to peer like torrent
entries.a: Like torrents, nodes share data they have downloaded, in chunks, with other peers, so popular content spreads by itself. Unlike torrents, every item sits under a registered name and is recorded on the blockchain with its hashes, only the name's owner can update it, everything is encrypted, and your node hosts only what you follow or open.

entries.q: What is a data node on Qortal?
aliases: is my node a data node
what is a qortal data node
entries.a: Every Qortal node is a data node by default: it stores and shares the QDN data it follows or opens, and relays data for others, unless its operator turns QDN off. There is no separate data node program; Qortal Core does both jobs.

entries.q: What does "Downloading from network..." mean on a QDN loading page?
entries.a: Your node is collecting the resource's chunks from peers right now. The count under it, such as 5 / 14 files, shows how many pieces have arrived, and a peer count shows how many nodes are sending. The page switches to the app or site by itself once everything is in and built.

entries.q: Can I see how big a QDN item is before I download it?
aliases: how big is this qdn file
entries.a: Yes. The publish record holds the resource's size, so apps such as Q-Share can show file sizes in their lists before you download anything, and Q-Share's Follow button shows the total size of a name's content.

entries.q: How can I help QDN work better?
entries.a: Run your own node and leave it on, follow the names whose content you value so your node keeps a copy, keep relay mode on so data can pass through you, and give your node enough disk space. Each of these adds copies or paths, which makes content load faster for everyone.

entries.q: What happens if a node sends me corrupted QDN data?
entries.a: Your node checks every chunk against its hash. A chunk that doesn't match is thrown away, and that peer is skipped for that file for about 10 minutes while your node gets the piece from someone else. So a bad peer can slow a download down, but it can't slip in changed data.

entries.q: Does QDN scan files for viruses?
entries.a: No. Qortal Core checks only that the data matches its publish record and fits the service's rules, not what a file contains. Anyone with a name can publish, so treat downloaded files like any file from the internet and open them with care.

entries.q: Can I publish a file on QDN without a Q-App?
aliases: publish a file in hub without an app
hub publish only apps and websites
how to upload a file to qdn from hub
entries.a: Hub's own publish form in the My apps tab handles only apps and websites. For files, videos, images and other kinds of content, use a Q-App made for them, such as Q-Share for files or Q-Tube for videos; the app picks the right service and identifier for you.

entries.q: Which Q-App should I use to publish on QDN?
aliases: which app to publish on qdn
where to publish a video on qortal
app for publishing a website qortal
how to publish different content qdn
entries.a:
Files and documents: Q-Share.
Videos: Q-Tube.
Posts with pictures, polls and short videos: Torq.
Blogs: Q-Blog.
A website without coding: Qortal Web Builder, or your own zip through Hub's My apps tab.
Mail with attachments: Q-Mail.

entries.q: Can I make a QDN website that only some people can see?
aliases: hide my qdn website from public
entries.a: Not as a normal WEBSITE: anyone can open those. For something only certain people should use, a private group's admin can publish a private Q-App, which is encrypted for the group so only members can open it. Qortal Web Builder can also limit a site to a group's members, but that is only a gate: the site's files stay public on QDN.

entries.q: What is Reticulum?
entries.a: Reticulum is open networking software that lets devices find each other and exchange encrypted data without central servers. It runs over almost any link: the internet, Wi-Fi, LoRa radios, serial cables and more, even very slow ones. It is a tool for building many independent networks, not one network you sign up to. Qortal Hub and Qortal GO use it for Q-Chat, online status and voice calls.

entries.q: Who made Reticulum?
entries.a: Reticulum was created by Mark Qvist, who also maintains its reference implementation: the Python code that defines the protocol. It is an independent open project, not a Qortal product. Its home is reticulum.network, where the Reticulum manual lives.

entries.q: Is Reticulum part of Qortal?
entries.a: No. Reticulum is a separate open-source project by Mark Qvist that anyone can use. Qortal builds on it: Qortal Hub and Qortal GO run Reticulum to carry chat, online status and calls between devices, and Qortal developers are also testing it inside Qortal Core.

entries.q: Why does Reticulum exist?
entries.a: Its goal is to let anyone be their own network operator, and to make it cheap and easy to cover large areas with many independent networks that can link up with each other. The project describes these as networks without kill-switches, surveillance, censorship or central control. It is built to keep working over slow, unreliable links that normal internet tools struggle with.

entries.q: Is Reticulum one big network like the internet?
entries.a: No. Reticulum is a tool for building networks, and there can be thousands of them. They can join up, split apart and work with each other without any central oversight. Qortal Hub and GO, for example, join a Reticulum network segment named qortal-hub, carried by Qortal's community hubs.

entries.q: Do I need an account to use Reticulum?
entries.a: No. Reticulum is free software, not a service you subscribe to. There are no accounts, phone numbers or email addresses: each device makes its own cryptographic identity, which works as its address. In Qortal Hub and GO this happens by itself in the background; you just sign in with your Qortal account as usual.

entries.q: Is Reticulum open source?
entries.a: Yes. The reference implementation is published under the Reticulum License, and the Reticulum protocol itself was dedicated to the public domain in 2016. Anyone can read the code, run it, or build their own compatible version.

entries.q: Does Reticulum need the internet?
entries.a: No. Reticulum does not depend on the internet or on IP at all: it can run directly over LoRa radios, packet radio, serial lines, Wi-Fi or Ethernet. It can also use the internet as one of its links, which is easy and common. Qortal Hub and GO currently reach each other through Qortal's Reticulum hubs over a normal internet connection.

entries.q: Does Reticulum use IP addresses?
entries.a: Not for addressing. A Reticulum address is a short hash made from a public key and an app name, so it works on any kind of link and needs no central registry. Reticulum can still travel over IP networks such as your Wi-Fi or the internet, but it does not rely on IP addresses to find anyone.

entries.q: How slow a link can Reticulum work on?
entries.a: Reticulum needs very little: a link of at least 5 bits per second that can carry 500-byte packets, even if it only sends one way at a time. Its usable range today is roughly 150 bits per second up to about 500 megabits per second; the goal is 250 bits per second to 1 gigabit.

entries.q: What can Reticulum run over?
entries.a: Almost any medium that can carry data: LoRa radios (using RNodes), packet radio modems and TNCs, amateur radio digital modes, serial lines, Wi-Fi, Ethernet, free-space optical links, and the internet over TCP or UDP. It can also talk to other programs through pipes. One network can mix several of these at once.

entries.q: Can one Reticulum network mix LoRa, Wi-Fi and the internet?
entries.a: Yes, that is one of its strengths. A device with several interfaces, say a LoRa radio, a packet radio modem and Wi-Fi, joins them into one network: once the interfaces are set up, Reticulum handles the routing, so a device on the Wi-Fi can reach nodes on the radio side and the other way round.

entries.q: What programming language is Reticulum written in?
entries.a: The reference implementation is written in Python and runs as a normal program: no kernel modules or drivers are needed, and it works on practically any system with Python 3. Other compatible versions exist, such as reticulum-kt in Kotlin for Android and Java systems.

entries.q: Is there a written specification for Reticulum?
entries.a: No separate one, by design. The Python reference implementation and its manual are the authoritative definition of the protocol. Other software counts as Reticulum only if it fully works together with that reference implementation and uses the same cryptographic building blocks.

entries.q: What is reticulum-kt?
entries.a: reticulum-kt is a Kotlin version of Reticulum for Android and Java systems. It is tested against the Python reference implementation so the two can talk to each other, and it adds Android-only extras such as Bluetooth LE links. Qortal GO no longer uses it: GO runs the Python Reticulum inside the app as its only Reticulum stack.

entries.q: Has Reticulum been security audited?
entries.a: Not externally, according to its own README. It was built with cryptography best practice in mind, but the project calls itself relatively young software and says there could still be privacy or security bugs. By default it uses well-tested building blocks (X25519, Ed25519, AES-256, SHA-256) from OpenSSL.

entries.q: How is Reticulum different from the normal internet?
entries.a: The normal internet relies on providers, central services and IP addresses, and much of it is unencrypted by default. Reticulum is peer to peer, encrypts its traffic, addresses devices by cryptographic keys instead of IP addresses, and is designed to keep working over slow or broken links during outages. It can also run on top of the internet when that is available.

entries.q: What does self-configuring mean in Reticulum?
entries.a: You don't set up routes by hand. Devices announce themselves, and the nodes that pass traffic learn the way to each address on their own, across several hops and mixed link types. Once the interfaces are configured, Reticulum takes care of the rest.

entries.q: Can Reticulum handle long delays?
entries.a: Yes. Reticulum is built to work even with very high latency and extremely low bandwidth. Messaging apps on top of it, such as LXMF messengers, are delay tolerant: if no path to the recipient exists yet, the message waits and goes out once one appears. A quiet Reticulum app usually means no traffic, not a failure.

entries.q: Can Reticulum run on a Raspberry Pi?
entries.a: Yes. Reticulum runs on practically any system with Python 3, and a Raspberry Pi is a common choice for an always-on node. The Reticulum README gives the example of a Pi with a LoRa radio, a packet radio modem and Wi-Fi that joins all three into one network.

entries.q: How do I install Reticulum on a computer?
entries.a: Qortal Hub users don't need to: Hub ships its own Reticulum and needs no Python install. To install Reticulum by itself, use Python's package tool: pip install rns, or pipx install rns for an isolated install. On first start Reticulum writes a default config file with basic settings for reaching peers nearby.

entries.q: What is rnsd?
entries.a: rnsd is the Reticulum daemon: it runs Reticulum as an always-available background service, and other Reticulum programs on the same machine can share it. Qortal Hub starts its own rnsd when it opens and shares it between all open Hub windows, stopping it when the last one closes.

entries.q: What tools come with Reticulum?
entries.a: Reticulum comes with command-line tools: rnsd (run it as a service), rnstatus (interface status), rnpath (path tables), rnprobe (reachability check), rncp (file copy), rnid (identities and file encryption), rnsh and rnx (remote shell and commands), rnodeconf (RNode radio setup) and rngit (Git over Reticulum). They work even over slow links like LoRa.

entries.q: What does rnstatus show?
entries.a: rnstatus is Reticulum's status tool: it shows information about the interfaces of the running Reticulum instance, so you can see whether a node is connected. Qortal Hub shows similar details for its own Reticulum in Settings, on the Reticulum tab.

entries.q: What is rnprobe for?
entries.a: rnprobe is Reticulum's connectivity test: it sends a probe to a destination and shows whether, and how quickly, it answers. A transport node only answers probes if its operator turns on respond_to_probes in its config; it is off by default.

entries.q: What is rncp?
entries.a: rncp is a simple file transfer program that copies files between machines over Reticulum. Like the other Reticulum tools, it works even over very low-bandwidth links such as LoRa or packet radio.

entries.q: What is rnodeconf?
entries.a: rnodeconf is the RNode configuration and firmware tool that comes with Reticulum. It changes an RNode's settings and startup modes, and it can install, flash and update the firmware on supported LoRa devices.

entries.q: What is rnid?
entries.a: rnid is Reticulum's identity and encryption tool. You can use it to create and manage Reticulum identities, and to encrypt or decrypt files with them.

entries.q: What are rnsh and rnx?
entries.a: Both let you work on another computer over Reticulum. rnsh opens a fully interactive remote shell session, and rnx runs single commands or programs on a remote system and brings back their output. Both work even over slow links like LoRa.

entries.q: What is rngit?
entries.a: rngit is a Git node for Reticulum: it serves one or more Git repositories over a Reticulum network. The included git-remote-rns helper lets ordinary Git work with those repositories over Reticulum.

entries.q: Where is the Reticulum config file?
entries.a: Standalone Reticulum keeps its config in a folder called .reticulum in your home folder (or in /etc/reticulum or ~/.config/reticulum if one of those exists), and writes a default config there on first start. Qortal Hub uses its own folder inside Hub's app data instead; Settings, Reticulum tab, shows it and has Reveal in file explorer.

entries.q: What is a shared instance in Reticulum?
entries.a: The first program on a computer to start Reticulum opens all the configured interfaces and becomes the shared instance; other Reticulum programs on that machine connect to it over a local socket instead of opening their own. This happens automatically. Qortal Hub runs one shared instance, named qortal-hub-shared, for all its windows, while GO runs its own instance inside the app.

entries.q: What is the rnspure package?
entries.a: rnspure contains exactly the same Reticulum code as the normal rns package, but lists no dependencies. Without the PyCA/cryptography library, Reticulum falls back to its own pure-Python crypto, which is much slower and has had less review. Use it only on systems that cannot install the normal package, and read the README's warning first.

entries.q: What does Reticulum need installed to run?
entries.a: The normal rns package needs just two Python libraries: PyCA/cryptography (crypto through OpenSSL) and pyserial (serial devices such as RNodes). Reticulum loads them only when they are needed, so on a system without serial support it still runs, just without serial interfaces.

entries.q: How does a Reticulum node connect to the wider Reticulum network?
entries.a: Reticulum is not a network you join automatically. You add interfaces that reach other nodes: a TCP connection to a public entry point, a LoRa radio, local Wi-Fi and so on. Reticulum can also discover public interfaces announced over the network itself, and the community keeps directories of public entry points. Qortal Hub and GO do this for you with a built-in list of Qortal hubs.

entries.q: Is there a public Reticulum testnet?
entries.a: Not any more. The Reticulum project used to run a public testnet, including an Amsterdam entry point, but it has been shut down now that there are many independent public nodes. New setups use the distributed backbone and Reticulum's built-in interface discovery instead.

entries.q: What is LXST?
entries.a: LXST is a protocol and toolkit from the Reticulum project for real-time audio and signals over Reticulum. It has building blocks for voice apps and hardware, such as the rnphone program for building telephones. Columba uses it for voice calls. Qortal Hub and GO calls use Qortal's own call system instead.

entries.q: Can Reticulum carry large files?
entries.a: Yes. Reticulum can move anything from a few bytes to files of many gigabytes, and it handles the splitting, ordering, compression and checksums automatically while reporting progress. Qortal Hub and GO also send chat attachments between devices over Reticulum links.

entries.q: Does Reticulum work on phones?
entries.a: Yes. Reticulum runs on Android: apps such as Sideband and Columba use it, and reticulum-kt is a version made for Android. Qortal GO runs a full Reticulum inside the app, so you don't need any other Reticulum app for Qortal chat.

entries.q: Is Reticulum a blockchain?
entries.a: No. Reticulum is a networking stack: it moves encrypted data between devices. It has no blockchain or ledger. In Qortal, the blockchain is Qortal Core's job; Reticulum carries real-time traffic such as chat, online status and calls between Hub and GO.

entries.q: What is a Reticulum identity?
entries.a: A Reticulum identity is a set of cryptographic keys: a 256-bit Ed25519 key for signing and a 256-bit X25519 key for setting up encryption, 512 bits together. It is made on your device, its public half can be shared, and it takes the place of a username or phone number. Qortal Hub and GO each create one per installation, separate from your Qortal account keys.

entries.q: How is a Reticulum identity created?
entries.a: It is generated on the device from fresh random keys, with no registration and no server. Apps such as Columba create one on first launch. Qortal Hub and GO create theirs on first start, keep it in a file in the app's data, and reuse it every time after that.

entries.q: What is a Reticulum destination?
entries.a: A destination is an endpoint you can send to on a Reticulum network, a bit like an address plus a service. It is named by an app name and some extra words called aspects, and is usually tied to an identity. A destination can announce itself, which shares the keys others need to reach it securely. Qortal Hub and GO each run a presence destination of their own.

entries.q: What does a Reticulum address look like?
entries.a: It is a destination hash: 16 bytes, usually written as 32 hexadecimal characters (0 to 9 and a to f). It is calculated from the app name, its aspects and the identity's public key, and it cannot be turned back into the key. Hub shows its own under Destination hash in Settings, Reticulum tab, Reticulum details.

entries.q: Why don't Reticulum addresses need a central registry?
entries.a: Each address is derived from keys made on the device itself, so nobody has to hand addresses out, and the chance of two devices getting the same one is negligible. The project calls this coordination-less, globally unique addressing.

entries.q: What types of destinations does Reticulum have?
entries.a: Four: SINGLE (one identity; data is encrypted to its keys), GROUP (a shared symmetric key held by a group of nodes), PLAIN (no encryption, for open broadcasts) and LINK (an established encrypted link between two endpoints).

entries.q: What is an announce in Reticulum?
aliases: what does an announce do reticulum
entries.a: An announce is a small signed message a destination sends out to say it exists. It carries the destination's public key and optional app data, and as it spreads, nodes learn which way leads back to it. That is how others can find and encrypt to a destination without any directory. Qortal Hub and GO announce themselves this way so other Hubs and phones can find them.

entries.q: How do Reticulum devices find a route to each other?
entries.a: Through announces and path requests. When a destination announces, transport nodes pass the announce on and remember which side it came from, building a table of next hops. Traffic to that address then follows the remembered path. A node that has no path yet can send a path request, and a node that knows the way answers.

entries.q: What is a path request in Reticulum?
entries.a: It is how a node asks the network for a way to reach a destination it has no path for. Nodes that know a path answer, and the requester can then send its traffic. By default a client waits up to 15 seconds for an answer.

entries.q: How long does Reticulum remember a path?
aliases: how long are reticulum paths kept
entries.a: Normally one week. Paths learned through an interface in access point mode expire after one day, and through a roaming interface after 6 hours. A destination that keeps announcing keeps its paths fresh, and entries that go unused are cleaned up.

entries.q: How many hops can a Reticulum packet travel?
entries.a: Up to 128 hops. Reticulum also limits how much bandwidth announces may use and gives priority to announces from fewer hops away, so large fast networks don't swamp small slow ones.

entries.q: How much bandwidth do Reticulum announces use?
entries.a: At most 2% of an interface's bandwidth by default. If sending an announce would go over that, it waits in a queue, and announces with fewer hops go first, so distant large networks on fast links don't overwhelm small networks on slow radios. An announce that waits too long is dropped.

entries.q: What is a Reticulum link?
entries.a: A link is an encrypted, verified connection between two destinations, used when they need to talk back and forth, transfer files or stream data. Setting one up takes only 3 packets (297 bytes in total), and keeping it open costs about 0.44 bits per second. Qortal Hub and GO keep links to a limited number of other Hub and GO devices to pass chat and online status along.

entries.q: What encryption does Reticulum use?
entries.a: Every identity has an Ed25519 key for signatures and an X25519 key for key exchange. Each packet or link gets fresh keys from an X25519 exchange; data is encrypted with AES-256 in CBC mode and checked with HMAC-SHA256, and keys are derived with HKDF. SHA-256 and SHA-512 are used for hashing. By default OpenSSL does the heavy lifting.

entries.q: Is all Reticulum traffic encrypted?
entries.a: Traffic to a normal (SINGLE) destination and everything inside a link is encrypted end to end, with fresh keys each time. Reticulum also has PLAIN destinations, which are deliberately unencrypted for open broadcasts, and GROUP destinations, which use a shared key. Apps choose which to use; Qortal Hub and GO carry chat and presence over encrypted links.

entries.q: Does Reticulum have forward secrecy?
entries.a: Yes, for all kinds of communication. Forward secrecy means traffic recorded today stays safe even if keys leak later. Links get fresh keys from every key exchange, and single packets can have it too through ratchets: extra keys a destination rotates, at most every 30 minutes, with old ones expiring after 30 days.

entries.q: What is initiator anonymity in Reticulum?
entries.a: Reticulum packets carry no source address. A packet names where it is going but not who sent it, so you can talk to a destination without revealing your own identity, unless your app chooses to identify itself on a link.

entries.q: What are delivery proofs in Reticulum?
entries.a: When a destination receives a packet, it can send back a small proof signed with its own key. Nobody else can fake that signature, so the sender knows for certain the packet arrived. The project calls these unforgeable delivery confirmations.

entries.q: What are channels and buffers in Reticulum?
entries.a: They are tools for apps that need a steady stream over a link. A channel delivers messages reliably and in order, with flow control and resending of lost packets, and a buffer lets an app read and write over a channel like an ordinary data stream.

entries.q: What is the request and response feature in Reticulum?
entries.a: A destination can register request handlers for named paths. Another node opens a link, sends a request to one of those paths and gets the answer back over the same link. Reticulum describes it as a lightweight, flexible request/response mechanism; Qortal's bridge uses one to set up chat file sessions.

entries.q: What is the Reticulum MTU?
entries.a: Reticulum's packet size limit (MTU) is 500 bytes, which lets it run over very slow radio links. On a link, Reticulum can discover and use a bigger size when the path allows it, which speeds up fast connections a lot. Apps such as Qortal chat cut their messages into pieces that fit.

entries.q: What is IFAC in Reticulum?
entries.a: IFAC (Interface Access Code) makes an interface part of a named, protected network. You give the interface a network name and/or a passphrase; Reticulum then adds an access code to every packet it sends there, and drops packets that arrive without the right code. That gives authentication and separate virtual networks on any interface type. Qortal's hubs use the network name qortal-hub.

entries.q: What is a transport node in Reticulum?
entries.a: A transport node routes traffic for others: it passes announces along, forwards packets and answers path requests. It is turned on with enable_transport in the config. Reticulum advises it only for machines that stay in one place and are always on, such as a home server. Qortal's community hubs do this job for Hub and GO.

entries.q: Should my laptop or phone be a Reticulum transport node?
aliases: should my phone be a transport node
entries.a: Usually not. Reticulum recommends transport only for systems that stay put and are always on, because the network starts relying on them for routes. A phone or laptop that comes and goes is better as a plain client. Qortal GO always runs with transport off, and Hub's Community transport switch stays off unless you turn it on.

entries.q: What are interface modes in Reticulum?
entries.a: Each interface can run in a mode that tells a transport node how to treat it: full (the default), point to point, access point, roaming, boundary or gateway. For example, paths learned over an access point interface expire after a day and over a roaming one after 6 hours, instead of a week. Qortal Hub's mesh listen interface can run in gateway mode.

entries.q: What is interface discovery in Reticulum?
entries.a: Transport nodes can announce their public interfaces over the network, with details such as type, address and port, and for radios the frequency and other settings. Nodes with discover_interfaces on collect these, and autoconnect_discovered_interfaces sets how many they join automatically. Each announced interface needs a valid cryptographic stamp, which keeps spam down. Qortal Hub turns discovery on with a small autoconnect limit.

entries.q: What is a blackhole list in Reticulum?
entries.a: It is a list of identities whose announces a node blocks. Operators of public entry points can keep their own, or pull lists that other transport nodes publish, to keep spammy or excessive announces off their network.

entries.q: What happens to a Reticulum network when a node goes offline?
entries.a: The rest of the network keeps working. Nodes keep learning paths from fresh announces, so if another route to a destination exists, traffic can use it. Delay-tolerant apps such as LXMF messengers hold messages until a path is available again.

entries.q: What is a Reticulum interface?
entries.a: An interface is one way a Reticulum node sends and receives data: a network card, a TCP connection to another node, a LoRa radio, a serial port and so on. You list your interfaces in the config, and Reticulum uses all of them together, passing traffic between them when transport is on.

entries.q: Which interface types does Reticulum include?
entries.a: The built-in interfaces cover: AutoInterface (local networks, no setup), UDP, TCP server and client, Backbone (fast TCP on Linux and Android), I2P, RNode (LoRa radios), KISS (packet radio modems), AX.25 KISS (amateur radio), plain serial ports, and Pipe (talking to other programs). You can also load custom interfaces.

entries.q: What is AutoInterface in Reticulum?
entries.a: AutoInterface finds other Reticulum nodes on the same local network by itself, over link-local IPv6 and UDP. It needs no router setup or DHCP server, only IPv6, which is on in almost every system. It is on in Reticulum's default config, but Qortal Hub and GO leave it off and use their list of Qortal hubs instead.

entries.q: Can two devices on the same Wi-Fi use Reticulum without internet?
entries.a: Yes. With Reticulum's AutoInterface (or a UDP interface), devices on the same local network find each other with no internet and no setup; apps like Columba work this way. Qortal Hub and GO don't do this by default: they connect through Qortal's hubs over the internet.

entries.q: What is the UDP interface in Reticulum?
entries.a: The UDP interface sends Reticulum traffic in UDP packets: usually as broadcasts across a local network (port 4242 in the example config), or to one specific IP address. It is a simple way to link machines on the same network or over a plain IP connection.

entries.q: What are the TCP server and client interfaces in Reticulum?
entries.a: A TCP server interface listens for incoming connections from other Reticulum nodes, and a TCP client interface connects out to one, by IP address or hostname. This is the usual way to carry Reticulum over the internet. Qortal Hub and GO connect out to Qortal's hubs over TCP, so chat works without opening ports on your router.

entries.q: What is the Backbone interface in Reticulum?
entries.a: BackboneInterface is a fast TCP interface for Linux and Android, built for high-throughput links between nodes. Qortal's community hubs are reached with it: Hub on Linux and GO on Android connect to them through BackboneInterface, while Hub on Windows and macOS uses a TCP client interface instead.

entries.q: What is the I2P interface in Reticulum?
entries.a: It carries Reticulum over the I2P anonymity network. You need an I2P router running on the same system with its SAMv3 API enabled; the interface can then connect to I2P peers and, when set as connectable, accept connections too.

entries.q: What is an RNode for Reticulum?
entries.a: An RNode is an open-source LoRa radio designed for Reticulum. You can build one yourself or buy a complete transceiver that only needs a USB connection to a computer, and some can also connect over Bluetooth LE. With RNodes, Reticulum nodes can reach each other by radio, without internet or a mobile network.

entries.q: What is the KISS interface in Reticulum?
entries.a: The KISS interface runs Reticulum over packet radio hardware: KISS-compatible TNCs and software modems, connected by a serial port. You set the serial speed, preamble, TX tail and similar modem settings, and can have it send a callsign ID at set intervals.

entries.q: What is the AX.25 KISS interface in Reticulum?
entries.a: It wraps Reticulum traffic in AX.25 frames and marks transmissions with your station callsign and SSID, for use on amateur radio spectrum. The Reticulum config notes that Reticulum doesn't need AX.25 for anything and that it adds overhead to every packet, so the plain KISS interface with callsign beaconing is the more efficient choice.

entries.q: Can Reticulum use amateur radio?
entries.a: Yes. Reticulum runs over packet radio TNCs and amateur radio digital modes through its KISS and AX.25 KISS interfaces, and both can send your callsign as station identification at set intervals.

entries.q: Can Reticulum use a serial port?
entries.a: Yes. Reticulum can run over any device with a serial port, such as a data radio or a direct cable between two machines, using its serial interface. KISS modems and RNodes also connect through serial ports. Serial support needs the pyserial library.

entries.q: What is the Pipe interface in Reticulum?
entries.a: The Pipe interface connects Reticulum to an external program through stdin and stdout or pipes. That lets you carry Reticulum over almost anything another program can pass bytes through, custom hardware included.

entries.q: Can I write my own Reticulum interface?
entries.a: Yes. Reticulum can load custom interface types written by users or the community, so you can make it talk over hardware it doesn't support yet. The project accepts new interfaces when they are generally useful and well tested in real use.

entries.q: Can Reticulum run over Bluetooth between phones?
entries.a: Some apps do this. Columba uses an Android version of ble-reticulum to message over Bluetooth LE with other Android and Linux devices, and reticulum-kt has its own Bluetooth LE mesh interface. The standard Python Reticulum uses Bluetooth LE to reach RNode radios. Qortal GO does not use Bluetooth for chat.

entries.q: Can Reticulum run over the internet?
entries.a: Yes, easily. Reticulum can be tunnelled over the internet or any private IP network with its TCP or UDP interfaces, and it works just as well there. That is how Qortal Hub and GO users reach each other today: each device connects out to Qortal's community Reticulum hubs.

entries.q: What is LXMF?
entries.a: LXMF (Lightweight Extensible Message Format) is a messaging format and delivery protocol built on Reticulum. It gives end-to-end encrypted messages with forward secrecy and routing that needs no setup, over any medium Reticulum supports, and is light enough for LoRa or packet radio. Apps such as Sideband, Nomad Network, MeshChat and Columba use it.

entries.q: What is an LXMF propagation node?
entries.a: A propagation node stores and forwards LXMF messages for people who can't be reached when a message is sent. Propagation nodes peer with each other and keep their stores in sync, forming an encrypted, distributed message store, and users collect messages meant for them from any available one. They can also host bulletin or discussion boards.

entries.q: How does LXMF reach someone who is offline?
entries.a: The message can go to a propagation node, which keeps it encrypted and syncs it with other propagation nodes. When the recipient comes online, their app collects it from any available propagation node. Without one, the sending app keeps the message and delivers it once a path to the recipient appears.

entries.q: What are LXMF paper messages?
entries.a: An encrypted LXMF message can be written as a QR code or as a text link starting with lxm://, so it can travel on paper or any other analog way. The recipient scans or opens it in an LXMF app, such as Sideband on Android, which decrypts it and adds it as a message.

entries.q: How much overhead does an LXMF message add?
entries.a: Only 111 bytes in total, mostly a 16-byte destination, a 16-byte source and a 64-byte Ed25519 signature. In return every message is timestamped, signed, end-to-end encrypted and routed with no setup, which is why LXMF works over very slow radio links.

entries.q: What is lxmd?
entries.a: lxmd is the LXMF daemon that comes with the lxmf package: a lightweight message router that can also run as a propagation node (lxmd -p). It can run a program each time a message arrives, and lxmd --exampleconfig prints a fully commented example configuration.

entries.q: Is LXMF encrypted?
entries.a: Yes, end to end by default, using Reticulum's encryption. Messages sent over a Reticulum link (the default) use ephemeral keys with forward secrecy, messages sent as a single packet are encrypted per packet, and messages to a GROUP destination use that group's shared key.

entries.q: What can LXMF be used for besides chat?
entries.a: LXMF is flexible. Short SMS-like messages use only the content; email-like mail uses a title and content, with attachments in the fields; machines can exchange commands or sensor readings in the fields; and with propagation nodes it can carry USENET-style discussion groups or broadcast bulletins.

entries.q: What is Sideband?
entries.a: Sideband is a Reticulum app for Android, Linux, macOS and Windows with a graphical interface. It does LXMF messaging plus file transfers, image and voice messages, real-time voice calls, a distributed telemetry system, maps and plugins. It is a separate app from Qortal and doesn't show Q-Chat.

entries.q: What is Nomad Network?
entries.a: Nomad Network (NomadNet) is an off-grid, encrypted and resilient communications platform built on Reticulum and LXMF. Its nodes host pages that people browse over Reticulum, a bit like small websites, and apps such as Columba and MeshChatX include a browser for them.

entries.q: What is Columba?
entries.a: Columba is a messaging and voice app for Reticulum on Android. It sends LXMF messages and makes LXST voice calls without needing the internet, cell towers or central servers, connecting over Bluetooth LE, Wi-Fi, LoRa radios (through an RNode) or TCP. There are no accounts: it creates your identity on the phone. It is a separate project, not part of Qortal.

entries.q: What can Columba do?
entries.a: Besides messages and voice calls, Columba can share your location with others on a map, download or import offline maps (MBTiles), browse Nomad Network pages, relay traffic for others to grow the mesh, manage several identities, export and import identities (including from Sideband), share your identity as a QR code, and use custom colour themes.

entries.q: How do I start a chat in Columba?
entries.a: Open Announces, tap a contact's name and choose Start Chat. Or open Chats, choose New Conversation, add the contact by scanning their QR code or pasting their destination, then type and press Send. If they are reachable it arrives at once; if not, Columba keeps it and delivers it when they come within reach.

entries.q: How do I install Columba?
entries.a: Columba is an Android app installed from an APK. Get the latest release from the Columba project's Releases page (or through Obtainium), allow your browser or file manager to install unknown apps, then open the APK. Its guide recommends Android 12 or newer and about 100 MB of free space. A copy is also offered on a Nomad Network page.

entries.q: Why didn't my Columba message arrive right away?
entries.a: That is normal on a delay-tolerant network: the message is delivered once a path to the recipient exists. If no peers show up, check that both devices are running Columba and share a medium, such as the same Wi-Fi, Bluetooth range or a radio, then restart the app. Silence often just means no traffic, not a failure.

entries.q: What is MeshChat?
entries.a: MeshChat and MeshChatX are LXMF clients for Reticulum. MeshChatX is described as full-featured: it supports image and voice messages, file transfers and voice calls, and has a built-in browser for Nomad Network pages.

entries.q: Can I message Sideband or Columba users from Q-Chat?
aliases: talk to sideband users from qortal
entries.a: No. Q-Chat in Hub and GO uses Qortal's own signed chat protocol over Reticulum, tied to Qortal accounts and groups, while Sideband, Columba, Nomad Network and MeshChat use LXMF. The two kinds of app don't read each other's messages, so each app only talks to its own users.

entries.q: Do Qortal Hub and GO use LXMF?
entries.a: Not for Q-Chat. Hub and GO send chat as signed Qortal chat events, using Qortal's own RCHAT protocol over Reticulum links, and keep them in a local database on each device. Hub's bundled Reticulum runtime includes the LXMF package, which Reticulum can use for things like interface discovery stamps, but Q-Chat itself is not LXMF.

entries.q: Do I need Sideband or another Reticulum app to use Qortal chat?
entries.a: No. Qortal Hub and Qortal GO each include their own Reticulum and connect to Qortal's hubs by themselves, so chat, online status and calls work with nothing else installed. Hub doesn't need a Python install either.

entries.q: Can I use my Qortal account in Sideband or Columba?
entries.a: No. Sideband and Columba create their own Reticulum identities and use LXMF, while Qortal chat signs everything with your Qortal account keys and needs Qortal groups and names. Your Qortal account belongs in Hub or GO; never type your seed phrase into another app.

entries.q: Can I move my Reticulum identity between Columba and Sideband?
entries.a: Yes. Columba can export your identity as a backup or to move to a new device, and it can import identities from other Reticulum clients such as Sideband. You can also share your identity with others as a QR code. Keep identity backups private: the file holds your private keys.

entries.q: Why is the Columba app called Columba?
entries.a: Columba is Latin for dove, and also the name of a constellation in the southern sky that depicts a dove. Doves are symbols of peace and hope and have carried messages throughout history.

entries.q: Why does Qortal use Reticulum?
entries.a: Qortal wants communication that doesn't depend on central servers and, in time, less on internet providers. Reticulum fits: it is open, encrypts traffic between devices, needs no central coordination and runs over many kinds of links. Qortal's wiki calls it the mesh networking protocol that could one day make ISPs unnecessary; qortal.org describes it as an evolving layer, not a finished replacement. Today Hub and GO use it for real-time chat, online status and calls.

entries.q: What does Reticulum do in Qortal Hub?
aliases: what is reticulum in qortal hub
entries.a: In Hub 3.0, Reticulum carries Q-Chat (groups, channels and direct messages), chat attachments, online status, voice calls (always the set-up, and the audio whenever a direct link isn't used), group calendars, Qortal Land, and the syncing of read marks and notification settings between your devices. The blockchain, names and QDN still run through Qortal Core.

entries.q: What does Reticulum do in Qortal GO?
entries.a: The same as in Hub: GO runs a full Reticulum inside the app for Q-Chat groups and DMs, attachments, Saved Messages, online status, calls and syncing with your other devices. It connects to Qortal's community hubs over Wi-Fi or mobile data, and the badge in GO's top bar shows its Reticulum status.

entries.q: Who works on Reticulum for Qortal?
entries.a: siddi leads the Reticulum work: the qortal.dev team page lists siddi as Core Network (Reticulum) Developer, working on Reticulum integration and networking infrastructure. The Reticulum chat and call features are part of the Qortal Hub code, which Qortal GO is built from.

entries.q: When did Q-Chat move to Reticulum?
aliases: when did q-chat switch to reticulum
entries.a: With Hub 3.0, in 2026. Legacy Q-Chat (2022) recorded chat messages through Qortal transactions; Reticulum Q-Chat sends them as fast, real-time conversations over Reticulum, and added channels, Group Score, message expiry and calls. Qortal GO 3.0 uses the same Reticulum chat.

entries.q: What is Reticulum Q-Chat?
entries.a: It is the Q-Chat in Hub 3.0 and GO 3.0, where messages travel over Reticulum instead of being recorded as Qortal transactions. It keeps Qortal accounts, names and group membership at its centre, and adds channels and categories inside groups, Group Score for finding communities, message expiry you choose, replies, mentions, attachments, edits, calls and Qortal Land.

entries.q: How is Reticulum Q-Chat different from legacy Q-Chat?
entries.a: Legacy Q-Chat recorded messages through Qortal transactions and centred each group on one text conversation. Reticulum Q-Chat sends messages over Reticulum in real time, so they arrive faster, and adds channels and categories, search, previews and Group Score, mentions, direct chat, calls and proximity voice in Qortal Land.

entries.q: Does Reticulum Q-Chat still need 4 QORT in my account?
aliases: need qort to chat on reticulum
entries.a: No. Holding a small QORT balance before you could post was a rule of legacy Q-Chat, where messages went through Qortal transactions. With Reticulum chat on, Hub and GO don't check your balance before sending. You still need QORT for blockchain actions, such as joining or creating a group.

entries.q: Are Reticulum Q-Chat messages stored on the blockchain?
aliases: is qortal chat on the blockchain
entries.a: No. Each message is a signed event kept in a local database on the devices of the people in the chat, and devices fetch missing messages from each other. Nothing goes on the blockchain and there is no central chat server. The blockchain still decides who is a member and who is an admin of a group.

entries.q: How does Reticulum chat use the Qortal blockchain?
aliases: powered by reticulum validated on qortal blockchain
entries.a: For identity and permissions. Every message, edit, reaction and online-status update is signed with your Qortal account key, so others can check it really came from you. Who may read and post in a group, and who is an admin, comes from the group's membership on the Qortal chain, which devices check with their Qortal node. Hub's Q-Chat card puts it as: powered by Reticulum, validated on Qortal blockchain.

entries.q: Is Reticulum replacing Qortal Core?
aliases: does hub still need core with reticulum
is core still needed with reticulum
entries.a: No. Qortal Core still runs the blockchain, names, groups, trades and QDN, and Hub and GO still talk to a Qortal node for those. Reticulum runs beside it and carries real-time traffic: chat, online status and calls. Qortal developers are separately testing a Core build that can also use Reticulum for its own peer network.

entries.q: How does Reticulum relate to QDN?
entries.a: They are separate. QDN, the Qortal Data Network, is run by Qortal Core: websites, Q-Apps and published files spread between nodes over Core's own peer network. Reticulum is what Hub and GO use for chat, online status and calls. Chat can still show QDN content: a qortal:// link gets a preview card, and a GIF from the GIF library is sent as a QDN reference that each reader loads from their own node.

entries.q: Are Reticulum chat attachments stored on QDN?
entries.a: No. Files and pictures you attach in Reticulum Q-Chat are sent over Reticulum between devices and kept on the devices of the people in the chat; they are not published to QDN. Each file is identified by its hash and checked when it arrives, and a device can fetch it from any other device in the chat that has it.

entries.q: Does Qortal Core run over Reticulum?
entries.a: Not in the normal Core release: Core syncs the blockchain and QDN over its own peer-to-peer network on the internet. Qortal developers have been testing a Reticulum-enabled Core that runs Reticulum as a second network beside the usual one, carrying the same blockchain and QDN traffic. Hub and GO already use Reticulum for chat and calls.

entries.q: How does the Reticulum test build of Qortal Core work?
entries.a: It adds Reticulum as a second network stack that runs alongside Core's normal IP networking. Reticulum peers are treated like ordinary peers, so blockchain sync and QDN work over either. Its Reticulum config is generated from Core's settings.json, or can be edited by hand in a .reticulum folder inside the Qortal folder, and Core builds and manages the mesh by itself. It is a test build, not the normal Core release.

entries.q: What are Qortal's Reticulum hubs?
entries.a: They are community-run Reticulum servers on the internet that Hub and GO connect to. Each device dials out to them, and the hubs pass Reticulum traffic between everyone connected, so phones and computers behind home routers can reach each other. Hub and GO come with a built-in list of them. The hubs only pass encrypted traffic along; your messages are kept on the devices in the chat.

entries.q: What is the qortal-hub network name?
entries.a: It is the name of the Reticulum network segment Qortal uses. Hub and GO set it on their connections to Qortal's hubs, so they only exchange traffic with devices on that same named network. GO's Reticulum details show it as Network; a different name there means a different network, whose peers you can't see.

entries.q: Do I need to open a port on my router for Reticulum chat?
entries.a: No. Hub and GO connect outward to Qortal's Reticulum hubs, which works behind normal home routers. Hub also listens on TCP port 4243 and tries to open it with UPnP, so other Hubs can connect to it directly; that helps the network but isn't needed for your own chat. Hub's Community transport switch does need UPnP or a forwarded Reticulum port.

entries.q: Which ports does Hub use for Reticulum?
entries.a: Hub dials out to Qortal's hubs (they listen on ports such as 4400 and 4444), listens for other Hubs on TCP port 4243 (opened with UPnP when the router allows), and, with Community call support on, offers a STUN service on UDP port 47321. Its own Reticulum daemon also uses local ports from 37428 up, on the computer itself only.

entries.q: Is my Q-Chat on Reticulum encrypted?
aliases: who can read my reticulum messages
entries.a: Yes, while it travels: messages go over Reticulum links that are encrypted between the two devices at each end, so the hubs in between only pass on scrambled data. Each message is also signed with your Qortal account key. Group messages are handed only to devices of the group's members, checked with the Qortal node, and DMs only to the two people's own devices. On those devices messages are stored readable, without an extra group key, so a group is as private as its members.

entries.q: Can the Qortal hubs read my messages?
entries.a: No. Your device and the device it talks to set up an encrypted Reticulum link with keys only those two hold, and the hubs only forward that encrypted traffic. The hubs don't keep copies of chats either: messages live on the devices of the people in the conversation.

entries.q: Can people outside my group read its Reticulum chat?
aliases: who can see group messages reticulum
entries.a: No. A device only hands out a group's messages to someone the Qortal node confirms as a member of that group, and messages from non-members are rejected. Devices that only pass network traffic along learn that something new exists, not what it says. Keep in mind that every member's device keeps a readable copy.

entries.q: Who stores my Reticulum DMs?
aliases: who has a copy of my dm
is my dm stored on a server
entries.a: Only the devices of the two accounts in the conversation: yours, including your other signed-in devices such as your Hub, and the other person's. A device answers a request for DM history only when the requester is one of those two accounts. There is no server holding DMs in between.

entries.q: Can someone fake a message from me on Reticulum chat?
entries.a: Not without your private key. Every message, edit, delete and reaction is signed with your Qortal account key, and other devices check the signature, and your group membership, before accepting it. A message that reuses a known message ID with different content is rejected as a conflict.

entries.q: Does Reticulum hide my IP address?
entries.a: Reticulum packets carry no sender address, and when chat or a call goes over Reticulum the other person doesn't see your IP address. Calls are the exception to watch: GO's Direct (faster) call setting connects you straight to the other person, who can then see your IP, while Private (Reticulum only) keeps it hidden. Hub's Community call support shares your public IP anonymously with other Hub users.

entries.q: Can I copy my Hub data folder to a new computer?
aliases: move hub to new computer reticulum
entries.a: It is better to install Hub fresh and sign in with your account. Copying Hub's whole app data folder also copies that installation's Reticulum identity and chat author stream, so two computers would look like one device to the network, and Hub can't detect a copied profile yet. A fresh install gets its own identity and fetches chats from your other devices and group members.

entries.q: Is my Reticulum identity the same as my Qortal account?
entries.a: No. Your Qortal account (address, keys, seed phrase) is who you are on Qortal. Each Hub or GO installation has its own Reticulum identity, made on first start and kept in the app's data, which is just its network address. While you are signed in, your account signs a short-lived, renewed statement linking it to that address, so one account can use several devices and one device can switch accounts. A device's Reticulum identity never holds your QORT.

entries.q: What happens to my Reticulum identity if I reinstall GO?
entries.a: GO makes a new one. The Reticulum identity lives in GO's app data, which is removed on uninstall and is not backed up to Google, so a reinstalled GO starts with a fresh identity. Your Qortal account is not affected: restore it from your backup file or seed phrase, and GO links the account to the new identity when you sign in.

entries.q: How does Qortal know someone is online?
aliases: how does online status work qortal
entries.a: Through presence messages over Reticulum. While you are signed in, Hub or GO sends a small online-status message signed with your account key, and repeats it every 25 seconds. Other devices see it and show you as online, busy or idle. If nothing arrives from a device for about a minute and a half, it counts as offline.

entries.q: What does Idle mean in Qortal chat?
entries.a: Idle means the account is signed in but not in use. Hub or GO switches to Idle by itself after 30 minutes without activity, and also while the app is locked, then goes back to your chosen status as soon as you are active again. Idle is set per device and can't be picked by hand.

entries.q: Who can see that I'm online on Qortal?
entries.a: Other Qortal Hub and GO users on the Reticulum network: your presence messages spread across it, so contacts and group members see your status. If you don't want that, pick Offline in your status menu to appear offline. Group voice calls need your status set to Online.

entries.q: How is someone's status shown when they use several devices?
aliases: why does contact show online and idle
entries.a: Each device sends its own presence, and Hub and GO combine them into the most available status: Busy wins over Online, and Online over Idle. So a phone in use plus an idle desktop shows as Online, and one device going offline doesn't hide the others.

entries.q: How long after closing Hub or GO do I show as offline?
entries.a: Logging out sends an offline notice right away. If a device simply stops sending presence, for example because it lost its connection, other devices show it as offline after about 95 seconds without a presence message (presence repeats every 25 seconds).

entries.q: What does the online count in GO mean?
entries.a: It is how many Qortal accounts your phone currently sees as present on the Reticulum network. The same number shows on Home and on the Reticulum badge in the top bar. It is not the number of hubs or Reticulum nodes.

entries.q: What do the colours of GO's Reticulum badge mean?
entries.a: Green, online: your phone sees at least one Qortal account on the network. Orange, connecting: Reticulum is starting or still reaching the hubs. Red, offline: the phone has no network, or Reticulum failed. Grey, idle: Reticulum hasn't started yet, for example before you sign in. Tap the badge for details.

entries.q: What does Hubs mean in GO's Reticulum details?
entries.a: It is how many links your phone has open right now to Qortal's community Reticulum hubs: the TCP connections that put it on the network. 0 means the phone is not on the network yet; 2 is typical and healthy.

entries.q: What does Known paths mean in GO's Reticulum details?
entries.a: It is how many destinations Reticulum currently knows a route to. Each announce your phone hears teaches it a way to reach an identity, and a few hundred is normal on a busy network. It is not the number of people chatting right now.

entries.q: What does IFAC mean in GO's Reticulum details?
entries.a: IFAC is the Interface Access Code size: the shared network filter that comes from the network name. 16 B means your phone is on the named Qortal network; 0 B would mean an open, unfiltered interface.

entries.q: What do Received and Sent mean in GO's Reticulum details?
entries.a: They are the total data your phone has received from and sent to the hubs since Reticulum started this session. They reset when the Reticulum stack restarts, not when you close a chat.

entries.q: What does Chat engine mean in GO's Reticulum details?
aliases: what does chat engine starting mean
entries.a: It shows whether GO's local chat database and chat worker are ready: "ready" is good; "starting" means it is still booting, with the time so far; "failed" shows the error; "idle" means it hasn't been asked to start yet (chat off or not signed in). The green badge only covers the network, so check this line when chats won't load or send.

entries.q: Why is GO's Reticulum badge green but my chats don't load?
aliases: go chat not loading green badge
entries.a: Green only means the network side is up: GO is linked to the hubs and sees other accounts. Loading and sending chats also need GO's chat engine. Tap the badge and look at the Chat engine line; if it isn't ready, use Copy diagnostics and send the text with your problem report.

entries.q: What does Reticulum offline in GO's notification mean?
entries.a: It means GO can't reach the network, most often because the phone has no Wi-Fi or mobile data at that moment. If it also says, for example, 4 unsent, those are your messages waiting on the phone; they go out once the connection is back.

entries.q: What do Reticulum starting, connecting and online mean in GO's notification?
entries.a: Starting: GO's Reticulum bridge is booting. Connecting: it is up but hasn't seen any Qortal account on the network yet. Online: it sees at least one account. Offline: no network, or a failure. Chat paused means the phone stopped GO's chat engine in the background; open GO to sync.

entries.q: Why does a DM need both people online on Reticulum?
entries.a: Because nothing in between stores it. A Reticulum DM stays on the sender's devices until the recipient's device fetches it, which can only happen while a device holding it and the recipient are online together. An always-on Hub signed in with the sender's account can do this for a phone.

entries.q: Is there a server that keeps Q-Chat messages for people who are offline?
entries.a: No. Qortal's Reticulum chat has no store-and-forward server, and the hubs only pass traffic along. Group messages are kept by the members' devices, so a member who comes back fetches what they missed from any member who has it. DMs are kept by the two people's devices.

entries.q: Do Qortal voice calls go over Reticulum?
entries.a: Partly. Setting up a call (ringing, joining, keys) always travels over Reticulum. For the audio, a one-to-one call first tries a direct WebRTC connection between the two devices and switches to Reticulum by itself if that fails. Group calls also prefer direct WebRTC links between participants and use Reticulum on any link that can't connect. GO's Private (Reticulum only) setting sends all call audio over Reticulum.

entries.q: How does a Qortal group call carry everyone's audio?
entries.a: Through forwarders, rather than everyone sending to everyone. One participant, chosen by a fixed rule from the account addresses and the call room, is the root forwarder: the others send their encrypted audio to it, and it passes the audio on to the rest. Calls of more than 10 people add cluster forwarders, and a standby forwarder can take over. Forwarders pass the audio on without decrypting it.

entries.q: Are Qortal voice calls encrypted?
entries.a: Yes. In a group call the room's root creates a room key and sends it to each participant, and every audio packet is encrypted with that key before it leaves the device, so forwarders and hubs only pass on scrambled audio. One-to-one calls show Encrypted on GO's call screen, whether the audio goes direct or is relayed over Reticulum.

entries.q: What is STUN and why do Qortal calls need it?
entries.a: A STUN server helps a device learn the public address its router shows to the internet, which two devices behind home routers need in order to set up a direct (WebRTC) call. When a direct call can't connect, Qortal calls fall back to Reticulum. Hub doesn't use big public STUN servers: it uses small STUN services run by other Hub users and found over Reticulum.

entries.q: What is Community call support in Hub?
entries.a: It is a Hub setting, on the System tab of Settings and on by default, that makes your Hub offer a small STUN service on UDP port 47321 so other people's direct calls can connect. Your Hub announces it over Reticulum under a throwaway identity that is replaced every day, so your public IP address is shared with other Hub users but not tied to your account. Only one Hub per computer runs it.

entries.q: How does Hub find STUN servers for calls?
entries.a: Hubs with Community call support announce their STUN service over Reticulum, and other Hubs collect these announcements. Each Hub checks the servers with its own test probes, ranks them, and gives a call at most 6 of the best. After a one-to-one call, Hub notes how well that set worked. The old list of public STUN servers is switched off.

entries.q: Why does a call say Reticulum is not ready yet?
aliases: calls get ready half a minute
entries.a: Calls need Reticulum connected first, because ringing and joining travel over it. Right after Hub or GO starts, Reticulum is still reaching the hubs and finding other devices; in GO, calls get ready about half a minute after it connects. Wait a moment and try again.

entries.q: What is P2P Hub health in Hub?
entries.a: It is Hub's measure of its Reticulum peer links, shown in the Core information popover next to the number of P2P Hub peers. Bad means no Reticulum peer is sending data to Hub yet, Low means peers are linked but not yet steady for 30 seconds, and Good means at least one has been steady that long. Group voice calls wait for a healthy connection.

entries.q: Can I be in the same group call from two devices?
aliases: join call from phone and hub
same account twice in a call
move group call to other device
entries.a: Not at once: a group call allows one active device per account. If you join from a second device, that device takes your place and the first one leaves the call.

entries.q: Does Qortal Land use Reticulum?
aliases: is qortal land peer to peer
entries.a: Yes. Qortal Land, the shared social space in Q-Chat, runs over Reticulum: your avatar's moves, room, mood and status, Land chat, proximity voice, and games such as Chess, Checkers and Qonnect Four travel between devices over it, signed with your account. If you turn Reticulum off in Hub, Qortal Land is unavailable.

entries.q: Are group calendar events shared over Reticulum?
entries.a: Yes. Group calendar events in Q-Chat are signed events sent between members' devices over Reticulum, much like messages, and they can carry a cover image. Only members of the group can see its events.

entries.q: Where are Hub's Reticulum settings?
aliases: where are reticulum settings in hub
entries.a: Open Hub's Settings and choose the Reticulum tab. It has Enable Reticulum, Managed Reticulum config, Community transport, Reticulum details (this computer's destination hash and its overlay peers) and a Config editor. The Reticulum group chat switch, Attachment storage and Community call support are on the System tab. GO doesn't show these tabs.

entries.q: What happens if I turn off Reticulum in Hub?
aliases: what happens if i disable reticulum
entries.a: Hub asks you to confirm first. With Reticulum off, Q-Chat goes back to legacy chat, and calls and Qortal Land are unavailable until you turn Reticulum on again. The switch applies to that computer only; it doesn't change your other devices.

entries.q: What is Managed Reticulum config in Hub?
entries.a: When it is on (the default), Hub writes its own Reticulum daemon config at startup, with Qortal's hubs and its mesh settings. Turn it off if you want to keep a config you edited by hand; Hub then leaves the file alone. Community transport can only be switched while it is on.

entries.q: How do I edit Hub's Reticulum config?
entries.a: In Settings, Reticulum tab, open the Config editor, make your change and save; it takes effect after Reticulum or Hub restarts. Reset to Hub default loads Hub's standard config for you to review and save, and Reveal in file explorer shows where the file is. All Hub windows on the computer share this config.

entries.q: What is Community transport in Hub?
entries.a: It makes your Hub a Reticulum transport node that helps relay traffic for other users. It is off by default, needs Managed Reticulum config on, and works with UPnP or a Reticulum port you forward on your router yourself. Restart Hub after changing it. It suits a computer that stays on most of the time.

entries.q: What does Reticulum details show in Hub?
entries.a: It shows this Hub's Reticulum destination hash and the overlay peers it has links with right now: each peer's hash and Qortal address, whether the link is inbound or outbound, and how long it has been connected.

entries.q: What do the Reticulum daemon states in Hub mean?
entries.a: hub-connected: at least one of Qortal's Reticulum hubs is online for this computer. lan-only: only local discovery is available. disconnected: the hubs are set up but none can be reached right now. unknown: Hub hasn't worked it out yet.

entries.q: What is Attachment storage in Hub?
entries.a: It sets how much disk space Hub may use for Reticulum chat files: 2, 5, 10, 25 or 50 GB, with 10 GB as the default. It is on the System tab of Hub's Settings, next to how much is in use now.

entries.q: What is the Reticulum group chat switch in Hub?
entries.a: It is on the System tab of Hub's Settings and turns the Reticulum transport for group chat on or off; it is on by default. With it off, groups use legacy Q-Chat. The Enable Reticulum switch on the Reticulum tab turns all Reticulum features on or off.

entries.q: What is RCHAT?
entries.a: RCHAT is the chat protocol Qortal Hub and GO speak over Reticulum. It doesn't sync chat screens; it copies a log of signed events (messages, edits, deletes, reactions, channel changes) between devices. Each device keeps the events in its own local database, which is the source of truth, and the chat you see is built from it.

entries.q: How does Reticulum chat find messages a device missed?
entries.a: Devices swap short summaries of what they hold, compare them, and then ask a peer only for the pages they are missing, in small batches that fit Reticulum's packet size. Each author's messages are also numbered in order, so a gap, say message 39 then 42, shows exactly what to fetch.

entries.q: What is an author stream in Reticulum chat?
entries.a: Each installation of Hub or GO numbers the messages it writes in its own sequence, called an author stream. With several devices on one account, each device has its own stream, so peers can tell the devices' messages apart and spot a missing one, while edits, deletes and reactions still belong to the account.

entries.q: How much chat history does a new device get?
aliases: why no old messages new device
entries.a: A new device fills in history from other members' devices as you open chats. Desktop Hub 3.0 accepts chat events from other devices only up to 30 days old, and GO hands other devices only the last 29 days (though GO takes older history from Hubs). So expect a fresh install to show about the last month; older messages stay on the devices that already had them.

entries.q: Does my device clock matter for Reticulum chat?
aliases: does my clock matter for chat
entries.a: Yes. Messages and online-status updates carry signed timestamps, and devices refuse ones that look too far in the future (more than about 5 minutes for chat events), so a wrong clock can get your messages or status dropped by others. Keep your device's date and time set automatically.

entries.q: What are overlay peers in Hub and GO?
entries.a: Overlay peers are the other Hub and GO installations your device keeps direct Reticulum links with, to pass chat notices, online status and other small messages along. A desktop Hub keeps up to 12 outgoing and 8 incoming; a phone keeps up to 6 of each, and more while charging on Wi-Fi.

entries.q: Does Hub relay chat traffic for other people?
entries.a: Yes, by default: a desktop Hub passes group notices and other small chat messages on to its neighbours, which helps them spread. That is separate from Community transport, which also makes Hub a Reticulum transport node that routes traffic for others.
