entries.q: Why does GO reconnect after I switch between Wi-Fi and mobile data?
entries.a: When the phone moves to another network, its old connections to the hubs stop working. GO notices the switch and reconnects to the hubs as soon as the phone settles on the new network, instead of waiting a couple of minutes for the dead links to time out.

entries.q: What happens to Reticulum when I swipe GO away or log out?
entries.a: GO pauses its Reticulum network connection, so it doesn't keep running with nothing attached to it. When you open GO and sign in again, it connects to the hubs again.

entries.q: How does GO keep Reticulum light on battery?
entries.a: GO runs one Reticulum stack, keeps fewer links than a desktop (6 out and 6 in), doesn't relay other people's group traffic on battery, and slows its timers and keepalives when you aren't chatting or calling. Opening a chat or a call brings everything back to full speed.

entries.q: Can Qortal chat work without the internet?
entries.a: Not today. Hub and GO reach each other through Qortal's Reticulum hubs on the internet, and they also ask a Qortal node about group membership. Reticulum itself can run over radios and local networks, which is part of Qortal's longer-term mesh plans, but Hub and GO don't set that up.

entries.q: Can two Hubs on the same local network chat without internet?
entries.a: Not with the default setup. Hub's managed config connects through Qortal's hubs and leaves Reticulum's local network discovery off, and Hub also checks group membership with a Qortal node. Advanced users can turn off Managed Reticulum config and add local interfaces in the Config editor, but Hub doesn't do this for you.

entries.q: How often is Group Score updated?
entries.a: It is worked out in six-hour slots based on Qortal network time, so it can refresh four times a day, and saved score data is reused for up to 24 hours when a new fetch fails. A group seen for the first time can get an extra refresh, with a five-minute cooldown. The activity part comes from a public-group activity directory shared over Reticulum, the holdings part from the Qortal node.

entries.q: Why does GO keep a link free for my own Hub?
entries.a: So your own devices can always reach each other. GO's Reticulum bridge reserves an incoming link slot for your own devices, so Saved Messages and settings sync still get through when the phone's other link slots are full of other peers.

entries.q: What happens to Reticulum chat when my Qortal node is down?
entries.a: Messages still travel over Reticulum, but anything that needs the node waits: devices confirm group membership and admin rights with it, so accepting new messages, calendars and admin changes can be slower until it answers. GO keeps serving recent history to members the node confirmed within the last hour, and a not-a-member answer from the node always wins.

entries.q: Is Reticulum Q-Chat still experimental?
entries.a: It is the main Q-Chat in Hub 3.0 and GO 3.0 and is on by default, but it is still developing fast. qortal.org calls Reticulum-backed communication an evolving layer, marks group voice as beta, and notes that the hosted web version of Hub is still on an older build. Hub's own setting still describes the Reticulum group chat transport as experimental.

entries.q: Can a Reticulum address move to another network?
entries.a: Yes. A Reticulum address belongs to a key, not a place, so a device can take it from Wi-Fi to a LoRa mesh to the internet, or even to a different Reticulum network. It only has to send a new announce where it is now, and after a short while it can be reached there.

entries.q: Does any Reticulum node know the full route to a destination?
entries.a: No. Each transport node only knows the best next hop that brings a packet one step closer to its destination, and nothing about the rest of the way. Paths are pieced together hop by hop from announces.

entries.q: Can Reticulum transport nodes see who is talking to whom?
entries.a: No. Transport nodes forward traffic blindly, using cryptographic proofs, and know only their immediate surroundings, while packets carry no source address. They can't read the encrypted contents either, or pick out traffic by sender or type.

entries.q: How quickly does a Reticulum network learn about a new device?
aliases: how fast reticulum finds a device
entries.a: Quickly. A new device's announce spreads in a predictable way, and the manual says even very complex networks using the full 128 hops reach end-to-end connectivity in about a minute, given enough bandwidth. Slow parts of a network, such as LoRa, catch up over time and look up the paths they actually need.

entries.q: Can Reticulum work without any transport nodes?
entries.a: Yes. Without transport nodes, devices within range of each other, for example on the same radio channel or local network, can still talk directly. Transport nodes are only needed to carry traffic over several hops.

entries.q: Can anyone filter or slow down certain kinds of Reticulum traffic?
entries.a: Not by content or sender. All Reticulum traffic is encrypted with fresh keys and carries no source address, so the transport and routing layers can't inspect it, prioritise it or throttle one kind over another: they pass all traffic equally. Only announces follow their own bandwidth rules.

entries.q: Can I make a private, closed Reticulum network?
entries.a: Yes. You can add authentication to any interface, even old devices such as modems, with a network name and passphrase, so only nodes that know them get in. Open and closed interfaces can be mixed on the same system. Qortal Hub and GO use a named network, qortal-hub, on their hub links.

entries.q: What is a network identity in Reticulum?
entries.a: It is an ordinary Reticulum identity that several transport nodes share to show they belong to the same network, like one flag flown by a fleet of ships. Today it is used mainly for interface discovery: it signs discovery announces, and can encrypt them so only nodes holding that identity can read the connection details.

entries.q: What is the mesh network identity that Qortal Hub ships with?
entries.a: Every Hub comes with the same bundled Reticulum network identity and community mesh passphrase. Hub uses them for its mesh listen interface: a Hub that can be reached from the internet announces itself as a gateway in encrypted discovery announces, which only other Hubs holding that identity can read, so Hubs can find and connect to each other's gateways.

entries.q: What is a bootstrap-only interface in Reticulum?
entries.a: It is an interface Reticulum uses mainly to find better connections. With interface discovery and auto-connect on, a bootstrap_only interface, such as a TCP tunnel to a wider network, helps your node discover nearby or more relevant interfaces and is dropped once enough have been found. That keeps the network from leaning on a few central entry points.

entries.q: Why shouldn't everyone connect to the same few Reticulum entry points?
entries.a: Because it brings back the centralisation Reticulum is meant to avoid: if everyone dials the same handful of public servers, the network becomes brittle. The manual suggests temporary bootstrap links plus interface discovery instead, so devices find local infrastructure and form more direct links.

entries.q: Should I run my own Reticulum node at home?
entries.a: The Reticulum manual encourages it. Rather than connecting every phone and computer straight to a distant public gateway, use an old computer, a Raspberry Pi or a supported router as your own transport node, on your Wi-Fi and perhaps with a radio such as an RNode, with interface discovery on. For Qortal, an always-on Hub with Community transport is the simplest way to help.

entries.q: How much does it cost to set up a Reticulum node?
entries.a: Very little. The manual's reference setup, a LoRa radio with open-source firmware on USB plus any Linux computer such as a Raspberry Pi, should get you on a Reticulum network for around 100 dollars even if you buy everything. Over Wi-Fi or the internet you already have, it costs nothing extra.

entries.q: What is the Zen of Reticulum?
aliases: why reticulum is designed this way
entries.a: It is the essay in the Reticulum manual on the system's philosophy. Its main ideas: there is no cloud, only other people's computers; an address should name who you are, not where you are; assume every link is hostile, so encryption is built in rather than added on; trust math, not institutions; treat low bandwidth as a design discipline; and build your own personal infrastructure.

entries.q: Why can't Reticulum run without encryption?
entries.a: Because its routing depends on it. Transport nodes use the per-packet encryption and signatures to verify paths and keep them alive, so plain, unencrypted packets can't travel over several hops at all; they only reach nodes in direct range. The Zen of Reticulum puts it as: encryption is not a feature.

entries.q: What is Reticulum Relay Chat?
entries.a: Reticulum Relay Chat (RRC) is a live chat system on Reticulum, close in spirit to IRC: you connect, join a room and talk. It keeps no message history on purpose; if you weren't there, you didn't see it. The rrcd program runs an RRC hub, and clients include Nomad Network and MeshChatX. It is separate from Qortal's Q-Chat.

entries.q: What is Partyline?
entries.a: Partyline is a group voice app for Reticulum, built on LXST and inspired by Mumble. It offers real-time group voice over any Reticulum link faster than about 6 kilobits per second, LXST dial-in, and listen-only rooms for music or broadcasts.

entries.q: What is Retipedia?
entries.a: Retipedia lets you host all of Wikipedia, StackExchange or any other .zim file and serve it to Nomad Network clients over Reticulum.

entries.q: What is RNS FileSync?
entries.a: RNS FileSync keeps files in sync between devices over Reticulum, with no central servers, internet or cloud services needed. It works over any medium Reticulum supports, such as radio, LoRa, Wi-Fi or the internet.

entries.q: What is Ren Browser?
entries.a: Ren Browser is a standalone browser for Nomad Network pages built on Reticulum-Go, an implementation of Reticulum in the Go language. It can run its own embedded Reticulum or use a shared Reticulum instance already running on the computer. It is alpha software, still under active development.

entries.q: What is Modem73?
entries.a: Modem73 is an open-source software modem for Reticulum that works with any HF, VHF or UHF radio able to pass 2400 Hz of bandwidth. Besides the radio you only need a sound card and an audio cable; its companion Modem73Interface connects it to Reticulum.

entries.q: How do I run Reticulum as a service at boot?
entries.a:
Install rnsd as a systemd service:
1. With a pip install, link rnsd into a system path: sudo ln -s $(which rnsd) /usr/local/bin/
2. Create /etc/systemd/system/rnsd.service that runs rnsd --service as your user.
3. Start it with sudo systemctl start rnsd and turn it on at boot with sudo systemctl enable rnsd.
A per-user service under ~/.config/systemd/user works too.

entries.q: Can I manage a Reticulum node remotely?
entries.a: Yes. Set enable_remote_management = yes in the [reticulum] section and list the identity hashes allowed to query it in remote_management_allowed. Tools such as rnstatus and rnpath can then check that node from another machine over Reticulum.

entries.q: What does rnpath do?
aliases: how many hops to reticulum destination
entries.a: rnpath looks up and manages paths to destinations: give it a destination hash and it tells you how many hops away it is and through which interface. It can also list the whole path table (-t), show announce rates (-r) and drop a path (-d).

entries.q: How do I see which interfaces my Reticulum node has discovered?
entries.a: With discover_interfaces on, run rnstatus -d to list discovered interfaces with their type, status, when they were last heard and their stamp value. rnstatus -D followed by a name shows full details, including a ready-to-paste config entry, and --json exports the list.

entries.q: How big are common Reticulum packets?
entries.a: Small. On the wire, without access codes, a path request is 51 bytes, an announce 167, a link request 83, a link proof 115, a link RTT packet 99 and a link keepalive 20. A single packet carries up to 465 bytes of data.

entries.q: Do Hub and GO join the same Reticulum network?
aliases: hub and go same reticulum network
entries.a: Yes. GO connects to hubs from the same list the desktop Hub uses, on the same qortal-hub network name, so phones and computers see each other. GO's hub list is kept in step with Hub's for exactly this reason.

entries.q: How does GO run Reticulum without installing Python?
entries.a: GO carries its own Python runtime inside the app and runs the same Reticulum code and Qortal bridge as Hub, inside GO's own process. Unlike Hub, which starts a separate Reticulum daemon, GO runs Reticulum standalone and connects straight to the Qortal hubs.

entries.q: Does the hosted web version of Hub have Reticulum chat?
entries.a: Not yet. qortal.org says Hub and Q-Chat are being rebuilt around Reticulum quickly, and hosted access stays on an earlier version until a new hosted build is ready. For Reticulum Q-Chat, use the installed Qortal Hub or Qortal GO.

entries.q: Can I edit or delete a message from my other device?
aliases: delete message from hub sent on go
entries.a: Yes. Edits and deletes are checked against your Qortal account, not the device, so any device signed in with your account can change or remove that account's messages. Reactions also count once per account across your devices.

entries.q: Does Hub sign Reticulum messages without asking me?
aliases: does go ask to sign messages
entries.a: Yes, for chat traffic: Hub and GO sign your messages, online status and similar Reticulum messages with your account key automatically. They only sign message types on a fixed list, with the expected fields and size limits, and refuse anything else. Payments and other blockchain transactions still need your approval.

entries.q: Where are Hub's Reticulum logs?
entries.a: Hub writes its Reticulum log to reticulum.log, in the logs folder inside Hub's app data folder. Include it, or the relevant part, when you report a Reticulum problem in Hub.

entries.q: Why does Hub need a Qortal node if chat goes over Reticulum?
aliases: why hub needs node for chat
entries.a: Because the node holds the blockchain's facts. Hub and GO ask it who is a member or admin of each group and look up names, and they use it for everything else on chain, such as your wallet, Q-Apps and QDN. Reticulum only carries the messages.

entries.q: Why do my devices show different online counts?
entries.a: Each device counts the Qortal accounts it currently hears on the Reticulum network through its own links, so two devices can show slightly different numbers at the same moment. The count also includes your own account.

entries.q: Why does my contact show offline even though they use GO?
aliases: why is my friend offline qortal
entries.a: Online status only reaches you while their device is connected to the Reticulum network and sending it. A phone whose GO is closed, paused in the background or without network, or set to appear Offline, shows as offline, and calls to them can't start.

entries.q: What happens if one of Qortal's Reticulum hubs goes down?
aliases: what if a reticulum hub fails
entries.a: Hub and GO keep links to several hubs from their built-in list, so traffic carries on through the others. A hub that stays down is retried with growing pauses, up to a minute apart, instead of every few seconds.

entries.q: What does UPnP do for Hub's Reticulum?
entries.a: Hub asks your router through UPnP to open TCP port 4243 for its Reticulum mesh listener, and learns your public address from the router so it can tell other Hubs where to reach it. If your router doesn't allow UPnP, Hub still works through the Qortal hubs, and you can forward the port yourself instead.

entries.q: Does Reticulum chat use a lot of mobile data?
entries.a: It is light, but a phone on a busy network keeps a steady trickle going: online status, chat notices and summaries from its links. GO keeps it down by limiting links and not relaying for others on battery or mobile data. GO's Reticulum details show the Received and Sent totals since Reticulum started, so you can check.

entries.q: Why can't I send files in Q-Chat with Reticulum chat off?
entries.a: Q-Chat attachments travel only over Reticulum, so with Reticulum chat off Hub shows that file attachments require Reticulum chat. Turn Reticulum, or the Reticulum group chat switch, back on to send files.

entries.q: What does "Reticulum image file is not available" mean?
entries.a: The picture's file isn't on this device and couldn't be fetched from another device right now, often because the members who have it are offline. It can load once a device that holds the file is reachable again.

entries.q: What does RNS stand for?
entries.a: RNS stands for Reticulum Network Stack, the full name of Reticulum's reference software. You'll see it as the name of the Python package (rns) and in Qortal's Reticulum settings and logs.

entries.q: Do I need a radio to use Reticulum?
aliases: do i need an rnode for reticulum
entries.a: No. Reticulum works over ordinary Wi-Fi, Ethernet and the internet; radios such as LoRa RNodes or packet radio are optional, for places without internet. Two devices on the same Wi-Fi are enough to start, and radio interfaces can be added later. Qortal Hub and GO use internet links only today.

entries.q: Do I need to set up Reticulum myself to use Qortal?
entries.a: No. Hub and GO start Reticulum by themselves, create their network identity, connect to Qortal's community hubs and link up with other devices once you sign in. Hub's Reticulum settings are optional, for advanced users.

entries.q: Is Qortal's Reticulum network a mesh?
entries.a: Not in the radio sense, yet. Reticulum can build real meshes over radios and local links, but today Hub and GO form a network of Qortal devices linked through community hubs on the internet, each device keeping direct Reticulum links to a few others. A wider mesh is part of Qortal's longer-term plans.

entries.q: How is Reticulum different from Qortal's normal peer network?
entries.a: Qortal Core's peer network links nodes over the internet by IP address to sync the blockchain and QDN. Reticulum is a separate network used by Hub and GO: devices are addressed by cryptographic keys, traffic is encrypted end to end, and it carries chat, online status and calls. Your node and your Reticulum connection run side by side.

entries.q: How do I check that Reticulum is working in Hub?
entries.a: In Hub's Reticulum settings, the Reticulum daemon line should say hub-connected, and the status line shows how many Qortal hubs are linked out of those configured (for example Hubs 2/6) and how many overlay links Hub has. The Core information popover also shows P2P Hub health and P2P Hub peers; Good means chat and calls can work.

entries.q: How do I check that Reticulum is working in GO?
entries.a: Look at the badge next to the Qortal name in GO's top bar: green with a number means GO is online and sees that many accounts. Tap it: Hubs should be 1 or more (2 is typical) and Chat engine should say ready. If something looks wrong, Copy diagnostics gives you a report to send.

entries.q: What does Hubs 2/6 mean in Hub's Reticulum status?
entries.a: It means 2 of the 6 Qortal hubs in Hub's list are connected right now. One connected hub is enough for Hub to count as hub-connected; more give it spare routes.

entries.q: Does Reticulum start before I sign in?
entries.a: In GO, no: Reticulum and the chat engine start only after you sign in, so they don't slow down unlocking. In Hub, the Reticulum daemon starts when the app opens, and chat and online status begin once you are signed in.

entries.q: Can I use the same account on two computers with Hub?
aliases: hub laptop and desktop same account
entries.a: Yes. Each Hub installation has its own Reticulum identity and message stream, and chat for your account reaches both. Reading a chat on one marks it read on the other, and either can edit or delete your messages. Don't copy one computer's Hub data folder to the other; install Hub there and sign in instead.

entries.q: Can Reticulum be shut down by a company or government?
entries.a: Reticulum itself has no central switch: there is no registry, no required server and no owner, and anyone can run nodes and build networks. A particular network can still lose its links, though. Qortal chat today reaches devices through a short list of community hubs on the internet, so it depends on those hubs staying reachable.

entries.q: Is Reticulum anonymous?
entries.a: Reticulum packets don't say who sent them, and a link stays anonymous unless an app identifies itself inside it. Qortal chat is not anonymous, though: every message and status update is signed with your Qortal account, so others see which account sent it, and your online status is visible on the network.

entries.q: Can Sideband and Columba users message each other?
entries.a: Yes. Both are LXMF apps, and Sideband works with all other LXMF clients, so Sideband, Columba, Nomad Network and MeshChatX users can message each other whenever their devices can reach each other over Reticulum.

entries.q: What is LXMFy?
entries.a: LXMFy is a framework for building bots and automations that run over LXMF and Reticulum. Bots built with it exist for things like Home Assistant control and LLM integrations.

entries.q: What is RetiBBS?
entries.a: RetiBBS is an old-school bulletin board system for Reticulum networks, where users communicate securely through message boards.

entries.q: What are rnsd and presence_bridge running on my computer?
entries.a: They are the two parts of Hub's Reticulum. rnsd is the Reticulum daemon that holds the network connections, shared by all open Hub windows. presence_bridge is Hub's helper that carries online status, chat, calls and file transfers over Reticulum for the app. Both ship inside Hub and are stopped when Hub quits.

entries.q: What does "Reticulum chat is disabled" mean?
aliases: reticulum disabled settings stay on device
entries.a: Reticulum chat is switched off on this Hub (Enable Reticulum, or the Reticulum group chat switch), so Reticulum chat features don't run there; notification settings, for example, then stay on that device instead of syncing. Turn the switch back on in Hub's Settings to use them.

entries.q: Does Qortino use Reticulum?
entries.a: No. Qortino's model is fetched once from QDN and assembled on your phone; after that it answers fully offline. Nothing you ask it goes over Reticulum or anywhere else.

entries.q: Does Torq use Reticulum?
entries.a: No. Torq posts, replies, likes and follows are published on QDN under your registered name, the same data Quitter uses. In Hub and GO, Reticulum carries chat, online status and calls, not Torq.

entries.q: Does Q-Mail go over Reticulum?
entries.a: No. Q-Mail keeps mail on QDN as encrypted mail resources under registered names, and your node fetches them like other QDN data. Reticulum carries Q-Chat, not Q-Mail.

entries.q: Why might a Reticulum hub refuse my connection for a while?
entries.a: Reticulum's Backbone listeners automatically block an IP address that keeps connecting for a few seconds and dropping. By default that is 5 quick connections lasting under 20 seconds each, and the block lasts 12 hours. Avoid restarting Reticulum or switching networks over and over in a short time; other hubs in the list can still carry your traffic.

entries.q: How does Reticulum protect public entry points from spam?
entries.a: With several limits. Announces may use only a small share of bandwidth; when a burst of announces for brand-new destinations arrives on a public interface, Reticulum holds them so traffic for known destinations keeps flowing, and releases them once things calm down. Path requests have similar burst control, and announced interfaces need a valid cryptographic stamp.

entries.q: How often should a Reticulum app announce?
entries.a: Rarely. The Reticulum manual says most apps can announce when they start and then about once every 6 hours, and that needing to announce more than once an hour usually means the design is wrong. Interfaces can also enforce a minimum time between announces from one destination (announce_rate_target).

entries.q: What do the coloured status dots mean in Qortal chat?
entries.a: Green means online, red means busy, yellow means idle (signed in but not in use), and grey means offline or not seen on the Reticulum network. The status comes from the presence messages each device sends over Reticulum.

entries.q: Does Reticulum chat work on networks that only allow web traffic?
entries.a: It may not. Hub and GO need to reach Qortal's Reticulum hubs over TCP on ports such as 4400 and 4444, so a network that only lets web browsing through can block them, and chat then can't connect even though websites load. Try another network, such as mobile data.

entries.q: What can Nomad Network do?
entries.a: Nomad Network is a terminal-based program with a complete encrypted communications suite: LXMF messaging (direct, or delayed delivery for people who are offline), file sharing, a built-in text browser and a page server with dynamic pages and user logins, plus an RRC chat client and network tools.

entries.q: What is Micron in Nomad Network?
entries.a: Micron is the markup language Nomad Network pages are written in. Web-based Nomad Network browsers display it with the Micron Parser JS library, and apps such as Columba include their own page browser.

entries.q: What is a Reticulum instance?
entries.a: Any system running Reticulum is an instance: it can create destinations, send and receive, set up links and host services others can reach. A transport node is an instance that has also been set to route traffic for others. Phones, laptops and sensors are normally plain instances.

entries.q: Can I host a service from home on Reticulum?
entries.a: Yes. Any Reticulum instance can host destinations that anyone on the network can connect to, so you can offer a globally reachable service from your home or office, as long as there is some physical path for the packets.

entries.q: What is the difference between a Reticulum identity and a destination?
entries.a: An identity is a set of keys that stands for a person, device, program or service. A destination is an endpoint built from an identity plus an app name, and one identity can create any number of destinations. Whoever holds the identity's private keys controls all of its destinations, so those keys must be kept private.

entries.q: Why does Reticulum use 16-byte addresses?
entries.a: It is a trade-off between address space and packet size. 16 bytes (128 bits, from a truncated SHA-256 hash) is enough for many billions of devices on one network while keeping packets small, which matters on slow links. The manual notes that a one-line change could raise it to 256 bits if ever needed.

entries.q: What happens on Reticulum when I switch accounts in Hub or GO?
entries.a: The device keeps its own Reticulum identity and stays connected. The new account signs its own short-lived link to that device, and the old account's link expires or is removed, so messages for each account only route through the device while that account is signed in there.

entries.q: How does Reticulum chat cope with very large groups?
entries.a: Its syncing is built around the messages that are missing, not the size of the group: devices swap compact summaries and pages of events and never need full member lists. Large lists, such as all the groups an account follows, are split into pages that fit Reticulum's packets.

entries.q: Are my Reticulum chats backed up anywhere?
aliases: are my chats saved in the cloud
entries.a: Not in any central place. Your chats live in the chat database on each of your devices, and other members' devices, plus your own other devices, hold copies of group and DM history. A new or reinstalled device fetches recent history back from them (about the last month on Hub), so older history only survives on devices that already had it. GO's chat data is not copied to Google's backups.

entries.q: Why can't I read a group's chat right after joining?
aliases: cant see group messages after join
entries.a: Devices only hand out a group's messages to accounts the Qortal node confirms as members, so your join has to be confirmed on the chain first. Once it is, members' devices start sharing the group's history with you, and it fills in as you open the chat.

entries.q: What is Reticulum used for?
entries.a: Many things: messaging apps (Sideband, Columba, MeshChatX, Nomad Network), voice calls and group voice, browsing and serving pages, file transfer and file sync, remote shells, Git hosting, bulletin boards, bots, and sensor or telemetry data, often over radio as well as the internet. In Qortal, Hub and GO use it for chat, online status and calls.

entries.q: Does Reticulum run on Windows and macOS?
entries.a: Yes. Install Python (on Windows, tick the option to add it to PATH), then run pip install rns from the command line; on macOS use pip3. The fast Backbone interface works only on Linux and Android, so on Windows and macOS you use the TCP interfaces instead, as Qortal Hub does.

entries.q: Can Reticulum run on an OpenWRT router?
entries.a: Yes, on routers with enough storage and memory. Install python3, python3-pip, python3-cryptography and python3-pyserial with opkg, then pip install rns. The manual tested this on OpenWRT 21.02; you may need firewall rules and your own startup script, and pre-built OpenWRT packages are being worked on.

entries.q: Can I run Reticulum on Android without an app like Sideband?
entries.a: Yes, with Termux, a Linux terminal environment for Android. In Termux run pkg update and pkg upgrade, install python and python-cryptography with pkg, update pip, then pip install rns. For everyday messaging an app like Sideband is easier, and Qortal GO already has Reticulum built in.

entries.q: Does Reticulum collect telemetry or analytics?
entries.a: No. The Reticulum project states that absolutely no automated analytics, telemetry, error reporting or statistics are collected and reported by Reticulum under any circumstances; it relies on people sending feedback by hand.

entries.q: How can I support Reticulum development?
entries.a: The project accepts donations (Monero, Bitcoin, Ethereum, Liberapay and Ko-Fi are listed on its support page), plus well-informed feedback, code and learning resources. Running a well-placed transport node or sharing useful interfaces also helps the wider network.

entries.q: Why does pip refuse to install Reticulum on my Linux system?
entries.a: Newer Debian and Ubuntu releases block pip installs by default. Use pipx install rns, or run pip install rns --break-system-packages, which despite its name doesn't break system packages, or allow it permanently with break-system-packages = true in the [global] section of ~/.config/pip/pip.conf. If a dependency won't build, install your system's build-essential package first.

entries.q: Which Raspberry Pi OS should I use for Reticulum?
entries.a: A 64-bit Raspberry Pi OS. The manual recommends it because 32-bit versions don't always have packages for some dependencies. Install python3, python3-pip, python3-cryptography and python3-pyserial with apt, then pip install rns --break-system-packages.

entries.q: What is a hop in Reticulum?
entries.a: A hop is one step from one node to the next. A packet that goes from your device to a hub and on to another device has travelled two hops. Reticulum counts hops in every packet, prefers announces from fewer hops away, and allows up to 128.

entries.q: How does Reticulum find someone's public key?
entries.a: Usually from their announce, which carries the destination's public key and is signed by it. If your device knows only the destination hash, it can ask the network for the key: transport nodes act as a distributed store of public keys. Keys can also be shared other ways, such as a QR code.

entries.q: How do I know I'm talking to the right Reticulum destination?
entries.a: A Reticulum address is tied to a key, and only the holder of that private key can read traffic to it or prove a link to it, so no one else can answer as that address. What you must check is that you have the right address: compare the destination hash with the person through another channel, such as in person or by QR code.

entries.q: Why does Hub's Reticulum config say Managed by Qortal Hub?
entries.a: That first line marks a config Hub wrote itself. While Managed Reticulum config is on, Hub may rewrite a file with that marker at startup; a config without it is treated as your own and left alone. To keep your edits safe, turn off Managed Reticulum config, or remove the marker line.

entries.q: Why does Hub restart Reticulum by itself?
entries.a: When Hub's mesh settings change, for example it learns your public address through UPnP or its gateway or transport settings change, it rewrites its managed Reticulum config and restarts Reticulum so the change takes effect. Chat and calls reconnect a moment later.

entries.q: What is the Reticulum badge in GO's top bar?
aliases: badge next to qortal name go
entries.a: It is the small pill next to the Qortal name that shows GO's Reticulum status and how many Qortal accounts are online. Tap it for details (Online, Network, IFAC, Hubs, Known paths, Received, Sent and Chat engine, each with a short explanation) and for Copy diagnostics or Save as .md file.

entries.q: Is Columba open source?
entries.a: Yes. Columba is published under the Mozilla Public License 2.0, and its source code and releases are on the Columba project's repository. reticulum-kt, the Kotlin Reticulum by the same developers, uses the same license.

entries.q: What do the WebRTC and Reticulum labels mean in a Hub group call?
aliases: audio is using the reticulum fallback
entries.a: They show how your call audio is travelling. WebRTC means the audio goes over direct WebRTC links between participants; Reticulum means it is using the Reticulum fallback, for example because a direct link couldn't be made. The audio is encrypted with the call's room key either way.

entries.q: What audio codec do Qortal calls use?
entries.a: Opus. Group call audio is cut into 20 ms frames, encoded once as 48 kHz mono Opus (with in-band error correction where supported), and encrypted with the room key before it is sent. Receivers decrypt it, smooth out timing in a jitter buffer, decode it and play it.

entries.q: How do I let devices on my Wi-Fi reach a LoRa Reticulum network?
entries.a: Make one machine a gateway: give it the outside interface (for example an RNode), turn on transport, and keep it on your Wi-Fi. Other devices on the same Wi-Fi then reach the wider network through it with just Reticulum's default AutoInterface configuration.

entries.q: Does Reticulum work over IPv6?
entries.a: Yes. AutoInterface uses link-local IPv6 to find peers on a local network, and the Backbone interface carries TCP over IPv4 and IPv6; on a device with both, prefer_ipv6 makes it use the IPv6 address.

entries.q: Can Reticulum run over Yggdrasil?
entries.a: Yes. A Backbone interface can listen on the Yggdrasil tun device (for example device = tun0 with a port), or connect to a remote's Yggdrasil IPv6 address and port, so Reticulum runs on top of Yggdrasil like any other IP network.

entries.q: Can I turn off Community call support and still make calls?
entries.a: Yes. Turn it off on the System tab of Hub's Settings if you don't want your Hub to offer a STUN service, which shares your public IP anonymously with other Hub users. Your Hub still uses the STUN servers other Hubs announce, and calls fall back to Reticulum whenever a direct link can't be made.

entries.q: Can I turn off Reticulum in GO?
entries.a: There is no switch for it: GO's chat, calls and online status all run over Reticulum, so it is on while you are signed in. With Background sync set to Off, GO's chat pauses about a minute after you leave the app, and swiping GO away or logging out pauses its Reticulum connection.

entries.q: Is a Reticulum hub the same as Qortal Hub?
aliases: difference hub app and reticulum hub
is qortal hub a reticulum hub
entries.a: No. Qortal Hub is the desktop app. Reticulum hubs are community-run servers on the internet that Hub and GO connect to so they can reach each other. The Hubs line in GO's Reticulum details counts links to those servers, not Qortal Hub apps.

entries.q: Can I add my own Reticulum hubs to GO?
entries.a: No. GO writes its own Reticulum config with a built-in list of Qortal hubs each time it starts, and it has no Reticulum settings or config editor. Changing hubs and interfaces is only possible in the desktop Hub's Reticulum settings.

entries.q: How does proximity voice in Qortal Land work?
entries.a: It is voice between people whose avatars are near each other in Qortal Land, carried over Reticulum links between their devices. Each Land session signs, with its account key, a short-lived capability tied to its exact Reticulum address, and both sides check it before the voice link starts. Blocking an account blocks it across all of its sessions.

entries.q: How do Qortal Land games connect the players?
entries.a: Directly between the two players' devices over Reticulum. A challenge sends a signed invitation that names both players' Land sessions and Reticulum addresses; the other side checks it, and the game then runs over an authenticated Reticulum link that stays pinned to those two devices.

entries.q: What does GO's Copy diagnostics report include?
entries.a: It covers the Reticulum radio and hub links, the chat engine's state and start-up times, the WebView's capabilities and speed, whether your Qortal node answers, recent send failures, sync health, battery and background state, and the end of the engine's log. It never includes a URL or your API key (only whether one is set), and Qortal addresses, group, peer, conversation and file IDs and your own node's host are replaced with stand-in names.

entries.q: Can Reticulum send one message to a whole group?
entries.a: Only in a limited way. A GROUP destination uses a shared key, so everyone holding it can read what is sent to it, but such packets don't yet travel over several hops (the manual mentions a planned upgrade). Qortal group chat works differently: it keeps events on each member's device and syncs them between devices over links.

entries.q: Reticulum chat isn't working in Hub. What should I check?
entries.a:
1. In Settings, Reticulum tab, check that Enable Reticulum is on and the Reticulum daemon says hub-connected, with at least one hub linked.
2. Open Core information: P2P Hub health should turn Good after a short while.
3. Make sure Hub is connected to a working Qortal node, since group membership is checked there.
4. Check that your computer's date and time are set automatically.
5. If you edited the Reticulum config, restart Reticulum or Hub, or use Reset to Hub default.
6. Still stuck? Look at reticulum.log in the logs folder of Hub's app data.

entries.q: What is a private key?
aliases: what is a qortal private key
what does a private key do
entries.a: A private key is the secret that controls your Qortal account. It is made from your seedphrase, and it signs (approves) everything your account does: payments, name registrations, publishes and messages. Anyone who has it can do all of that as you, so never share it with anyone. GO and Hub keep it encrypted on your device with your wallet password and sign on the device, so your Qortal private key is never sent to the node.

entries.q: What is the difference between a private key and a public key?
aliases: difference between public and private key
entries.a: They are a matched pair. The private key is secret: it signs for your account, and whoever holds it controls the account. The public key is made from it and is meant to be shared: the network uses it to check your signatures, and others use it to encrypt messages that only your private key can open. Your address is a shorter code made from the public key. Share the public key and address freely; never share the private key or the seedphrase.

entries.q: Why must I never share my private key?
aliases: should i share my private key
can i give someone my private key
is it safe to share my private key
entries.a: Whoever has your private key controls your account. They can send all your QORT, sell or change your names, publish and chat as you, and read messages that were encrypted for you. The network only checks the signature, so nobody can stop them, and a payment they send cannot be undone. No real helper, admin or Q-App ever needs your private key.

entries.q: Where do I find my private key in GO?
entries.a: On Home, tap the gear on the Account Overview card to open Settings, then the Security tab. Enter your wallet password and tap Decrypt: the key appears, and Copy key copies it. GO blocks screenshots on this screen and drops the key again when you close Settings or GO locks. Only open it when you really need it, with nobody watching and no screen sharing on.

entries.q: Where can I see my public key?
entries.a: Open Address book from your avatar menu; it opens User search. Search your own name or address and it shows the account's address and public key. You can look up anyone else's public key the same way. Both are public, so showing them is safe.

entries.q: Is my private key the same as my seedphrase?
aliases: seed phrase and private key difference
entries.a: No. Your seedphrase is a list of words, and GO turns it into your private key, a long string of letters and numbers. Both control the same account, so both must stay secret. To restore an account in GO or Hub you use the seedphrase or a backup file, not the private key.

entries.q: Can I restore my account from a private key in GO?
entries.a: No. GO and Hub add an existing account in three ways: Seedphrase, Backup file, or Authenticate now (a backup file used without saving it). There is no field for a private key. Keep your seedphrase, or your backup file and its password, safe: those are what bring the account back.

entries.q: Can I change my private key or seedphrase?
aliases: private key leaked can i change it
entries.a: No. Your address is made from your keys, and your keys come from your seed, so an account can never get a different private key or seedphrase. If either may have leaked, the fix is a new account: create one, back it up, and move your QORT to it. A new wallet password only changes the lock on the copy saved on your device, not the key itself.

entries.q: What should I do if someone saw my seedphrase or private key?
aliases: typed my seedphrase into a website
entered seed phrase on a fake site
entries.a:
Act as if they can take everything, and be quick:
1. Create a new account and save its backup file and seedphrase.
2. Send your QORT from the old account to the new address.
3. Move coins in the built-in LTC, BTC and other wallets too: they come from the same seed.
4. Stop using the old account.
Nobody can freeze or reverse a payment once a thief has sent it.

entries.q: Is it safe to use a node that someone else runs?
aliases: node given to me by a stranger
custom node run by someone else
entries.a: For QORT it is fairly safe: GO signs on your phone, so that node never gets your Qortal private key and cannot move your QORT. But it sees what your phone asks it for, and it decides what it blocks. Coins are different: sending or trading LTC, BTC, DOGE, DGB, RVN or ARRR hands that coin's private key to the node, and whoever runs it could keep it and spend those coins. GO asks you to tick that you run the node yourself, so only tick it for a node you really do run.

entries.q: Why won't GO send LTC or other coins on the public node?
aliases: cannot send ltc on public node
blocked is a public qortal node
entries.a: Sending a foreign coin means handing that coin's private key to the node, and a key must never go to a shared public node. So GO stops with "Blocked: ... is a public Qortal node" and nothing is sent. Connect GO to a node you run yourself to send LTC, BTC, DOGE, DGB, RVN or ARRR.

entries.q: What is the trade proxy warning when I buy QORT on the public node?
aliases: i understand the trade proxy receives my private key
buy qort public node private key
entries.a: On the public node, a buy order paid with a foreign coin is finished by the Qortal trade proxy account. GO encrypts that coin's private key and sends it to that account, and whoever controls the account could spend that coin. GO tells you this and waits for you to tick that you understand. To keep the key to yourself, trade on your own node.

entries.q: Why does GO warn me when my node is on 127.0.0.1 or Tailscale?
aliases: private key sent to an address on this phone
entries.a: On a phone, 127.0.0.1 is whatever app is listening on that port, such as an SSH tunnel, and GO cannot tell whose it is. So before a coin's private key goes there, GO asks you to confirm your own node or tunnel is running right now. With a Tailscale address the key travels unencrypted and stays private only while Tailscale is connected. Go on only when you are sure.

entries.q: Why does GO block my private key on a connection that is not encrypted?
aliases: connection is not encrypted private key
plain http node private key blocked
use https vpn tailscale or a node on this device
private key would cross the network in plain text
entries.a: If your node's address uses plain HTTP instead of HTTPS, and the node is not on this phone or on Tailscale, anything sent to it can be read on the way. GO will not let a coin's private key travel like that, so it stops and nothing is sent. Give your node an HTTPS address, use a VPN such as Tailscale, or use a node on this device.

entries.q: Do my LTC, BTC and other coin wallets in GO need their own backup?
entries.a: No. GO makes the built-in BTC, LTC, DOGE, DGB, RVN and ARRR wallets from your Qortal seed, so your seedphrase or backup file restores them too. It also means that anyone with your seedphrase, or your backup file and its password, can take those coins as well, so guard them just as carefully.

entries.q: Can a Q-App read my seedphrase or private key?
aliases: do q-apps get my private key
can a qortal app take my wallet
entries.a: No. Q-Apps cannot read your seedphrase, private key or wallet password. They can only ask GO or Hub to do something for you, such as send coins or publish, and the approval window shows you the request first. The real risk is approving the wrong thing, so read each request before you accept. One thing to know: an app that uses your ARRR wallet makes GO send the ARRR seed to the node, and GO warns you before it does.

entries.q: What does signing a transaction mean?
aliases: what is a signature on qortal
entries.a: Signing is how your account says yes. GO uses your private key to make a signature for one exact action, such as a payment, and the network checks it with your public key. The signature fits only that action and does not reveal your private key, so it cannot be turned into a different payment.

entries.q: What is a seedphrase?
entries.a: A seedphrase is the list of 14 random words GO shows while it creates your account. GO turns those words into your private key, so the words alone can restore the account, with its QORT, names and built-in coin wallets, on any device. That makes them worth as much as the account: write them on paper, keep them offline, and never share them. Some guides call them the recovery phrase or Secret Key phrases.

entries.q: How many words is a Qortal seedphrase?
aliases: how long is a qortal seedphrase
entries.a: An account made in GO or Hub gets 14 words. Write all 14 in order, exactly as shown. When you restore, GO uses the phrase exactly as typed, so a missing, extra or misspelt word opens a different account.

entries.q: Can I see my seedphrase again later in GO?
aliases: where is my seedphrase in go
entries.a: No. GO shows the seedphrase only while it creates the account, and it never stores the words. The account saved on your phone and your backup file hold an encrypted key, not the phrase. If you did not write the words down, your backup file with its password is your way back. GO can still show your private key (Settings, Security), but it cannot show the words.

entries.q: I did not save my seedphrase. What should I do?
aliases: lost seedphrase but have backup file
entries.a: You are fine as long as you have your backup file and its password: together they restore the account. Keep at least two copies of the file, apart from the password. If you also have no backup file, or are not sure of the password, make a new account now, back it up properly, and move your QORT to it while you can still unlock the old one.

entries.q: Is saving my seedphrase optional?
entries.a: GO calls it optional and recommends the encrypted backup file as the main way back. Each one restores your account: the seedphrase on its own, or the backup file together with its password. Keeping both is safest, because if one is lost the other still works.

entries.q: What is the difference between my seedphrase, backup file and password?
aliases: seed phrase backup file password difference
entries.a:
Seedphrase: 14 words that restore your account on their own.
Backup file: an encrypted copy of your account key (a .json file) that restores it together with its password.
Wallet password: locks the account saved on your device and the backup file; on its own it restores nothing.
So you need the seedphrase, or the backup file and its password. Lose both and nobody can bring the account back.

entries.q: What does the Export button on the seedphrase screen do?
entries.a: It saves your seedphrase as a plain text file, qortal_seedphrase.txt, in the Qortal Go folder in your phone's Documents. That file is not encrypted: anyone or any app that can read your files can read your seedphrase. If you use it, copy the words to paper, then delete the file from the phone.

entries.q: Why is my seedphrase hidden on the create account screen?
aliases: cant see seed phrase when creating account
entries.a: GO keeps the words hidden until you tap Reveal, so nobody glancing at your screen sees them, and it blocks screenshots and screen recording there. After Reveal, the same button copies the words. Anything you copy can be pasted into other apps, so writing the words on paper is the safer way to keep them.

entries.q: What happens if I type my seedphrase wrong when restoring?
entries.a: GO cannot tell a wrong seedphrase from a right one: every phrase opens some account. One wrong word, letter or space gives you a different, empty account, with no warning. So after restoring, check that the address matches your old one. If it does not, remove that account and type the phrase again, carefully.

entries.q: How do I check that I restored the right account?
entries.a: Compare the address: it starts with Q and never changes for an account. Check it against a note you kept, a payment you made, or the name of your backup file, which ends with your address (qortal_backup_<address>.json). Your registered name and balance showing up again is a good sign too.

entries.q: Do capital letters and spaces matter in my seedphrase?
entries.a: Yes. GO uses the phrase exactly as you type it, so every letter, capital and space inside it counts. Spaces before the first word or after the last are ignored. Type the words in order with one space between them, exactly as you wrote them down.

entries.q: Can I make up my own seedphrase?
entries.a: Don't. GO picks the words at random with the phone's secure random generator. Any phrase typed at Import opens some account, so a phrase a person makes up, like a favourite quote, is far easier for someone else to guess. Use the one GO gives you.

entries.q: Can I keep my seedphrase in email or cloud notes?
entries.a: No. Email, cloud notes and synced files can be read by anyone who gets into that account or service, and your seedphrase is all a thief needs. Write it by hand on paper, keep it offline in a safe place, and think about a second copy somewhere else.

entries.q: Is there a printable sheet for writing my seedphrase?
entries.a: Yes. The Welcome to Qortal Q-App has a "My Secret Keys" sheet with 14 numbered lines on its Getting Started page. Save or print it, write your words by hand, and keep the paper offline in a safe place.

entries.q: When does GO ask for my seedphrase?
aliases: where do i enter my seedphrase
entries.a: Only when you choose Import account, then Seedphrase, to add an account yourself. GO never needs it to unlock, to approve a Q-App request or to fix a problem. If a Q-App, website, message or person asks you to type your seedphrase, it is an attempt to steal your account: close it.

entries.q: Should I give Qortino my seedphrase or private key?
entries.a: No. Never type your seedphrase, private key or wallet password into any chat, Qortino included. Qortino does not need them and cannot unlock or recover accounts. To restore an account, use Import account on the Enter Qortal screen.

entries.q: Does my seedphrase work in both GO and Hub?
aliases: use seed phrase on desktop hub
backup file works in hub and go
entries.a: Yes. A Qortal seedphrase opens the same account in GO, in Hub and on any other device. The account lives on the Qortal network, not in one app; each app only saves its own locked copy. A backup file works the same way: it opens in GO or Hub.

entries.q: What is a Qortal backup file?
entries.a: It is a small .json file, named qortal_backup_ followed by your address, that holds your account key encrypted with a password. With the file and that password you can restore the account on any device, in GO or Hub. GO saves it in your phone's Documents folder, under Qortal Go. The file never changes as you use the account, so one good copy keeps working; keep it private, and keep the password somewhere else.

entries.q: Why won't GO let me in until I save the backup?
aliases: must back up before entering go
back up your encrypted wallet before entering go
enter go disabled after creating account
entries.a: When you create an account, GO keeps Enter GO greyed out until you tap Backup wallet and the file is saved. It makes sure you leave with a way back in, because nobody can restore the account for you later. Once it is saved, Enter GO turns on, and Download another copy saves a second one.

entries.q: Is my backup file safe if someone gets it?
aliases: can someone open my backup file
entries.a: It is encrypted with your wallet password, so the file alone does not open the account. But whoever has it can keep trying passwords on their own computer for as long as they like, so a long password you use nowhere else is what really protects it. Never send the file to anyone. If it leaked and your password is weak, move your QORT to a new account.

entries.q: Can I open my backup file without its password?
entries.a: No. A backup file opens only with the exact password it was saved with, and nobody can reset or get around it. If you lost that password, your seedphrase is the other way back: Import account, Seedphrase, and choose a new password. With neither, the account cannot be recovered.

entries.q: Where should I keep my backup file?
aliases: best place for my backup file
how to store my backup file
entries.a: In more than one place, and not only on the device that holds the account. USB sticks kept offline are a good choice, and since the file is encrypted, a trusted family member can keep a copy for you. Store the password separately from the file, never in the same place.

entries.q: Can I keep my backup file in email or cloud storage?
aliases: store wallet backup in the cloud
entries.a: You can, because it is encrypted, and the Qortal wiki even mentions emailing it to yourself. The catch: anyone who gets into that email or cloud account can then try to guess your password at leisure. If you do it, use a long, unique password and never store the password there too. Offline copies on USB sticks are safer.

entries.q: What can someone learn from my backup file?
aliases: what is inside my backup file
is my address in the backup file
entries.a: Which account it is. The file name ends with your address, and the address is inside it in plain text, so anyone who sees the file knows it is yours and can look that account up. Your key is in there too, but encrypted with your password. Don't edit the file: GO checks it, and a changed file may no longer open.

entries.q: What does "already stored on this device" mean when I import an account?
aliases: account already stored on this device
entries.a: The account you tried to import is already in your account list on this phone, so GO did not add it again. Go back to the list and open it there. If you wanted to replace it, for example to give it a new password, remove it first and then import.

entries.q: Do I need a new backup after I receive QORT or register a name?
aliases: backup again after registering a name
entries.a: No. Your balance, names and history live on the blockchain, not in the file. The backup holds only your encrypted account key, which never changes, so an old backup still restores everything. You only need a new one if you want it locked with a different password.

entries.q: Does my backup file include my chats, settings or Tabs?
aliases: what is not in the backup file
entries.a: No. The file holds only your account key. Everything on the blockchain, such as your QORT and names, comes back with it. Things GO keeps only on the phone, such as Tabs folders and most settings, are not in the file.

entries.q: Can I import several backup files at once?
aliases: import more than one wallet file
entries.a: Yes. In Import account, Backup file, you can pick more than one file. GO adds every account it finds, says how many it imported and skips any already on the phone. Each account then unlocks with the password its own file was saved with.

entries.q: Can I rename my backup file?
aliases: does the backup file name matter
entries.a: Yes. GO reads the account from inside the file, so the name does not matter to it. Keeping the address in the name, as GO does (qortal_backup_<address>.json), helps you tell files apart. Keep the .json ending so GO lets you pick the file.

entries.q: What does Save account in GO mean when I create an account?
aliases: dont save the account on this phone
entries.a: It is the tick box on the create password screen, on by default. With it on, GO keeps the new account on this phone, locked with your password, so it is in your list next time. Turn it off on a phone that is not yours: then nothing is kept, and the backup file or seedphrase is your only way back in, so save them.

entries.q: How do I change my wallet password in GO?
entries.a:
There is no change-password button, but you can do it like this:
1. On Home, open Quick tools, Backup Wallet. Enter the current password, untick keeping the current password, set the new one and save the file.
2. Check the new file is in Documents, Qortal Go.
3. Remove the account (pencil on its unlock screen, Account details, Remove).
4. Import account, Backup file: pick the new file and unlock with the new password.
Turn fingerprint unlock on again after. Older backup files keep the old password.

entries.q: Is my wallet password the same on every device?
aliases: different password in hub and go
entries.a: Not necessarily. The password locks each saved copy, not the account itself. When you restore from your seedphrase you choose a new one; when you import a backup file, the account keeps that file's password. So your phone and your computer can use different passwords for the same account, while its keys are the same on both.

entries.q: How strong should my wallet password be?
aliases: how long should my wallet password be
entries.a: GO sets no minimum length, so it is up to you. The password is what protects your backup file if someone ever copies it, so make it long (a few unrelated words works well) and don't use it for anything else. Write it down and keep it apart from the backup file.

entries.q: Can I send QORT with my fingerprint instead of my password?
aliases: send qort asks for my password
entries.a: No. Send QORT asks for your wallet password every time, even with fingerprint unlock on. GO then shows the amount, the recipient's name with the full address, and the fee, and sends only after you confirm. Payments a Q-App asks for are confirmed in its approval window instead, which is one more reason to lock GO when you put the phone down.

entries.q: Is fingerprint unlock a backup of my account?
aliases: do i still need my password with fingerprint
entries.a: No. It only saves you typing the password on this phone. If the phone is lost or reset, or GO is uninstalled, it is gone, and you need your seedphrase or backup file again. If you forget the password, fingerprint unlock may still open GO on that phone, but Send QORT, Backup Wallet and showing your private key all ask for the typed password.

entries.q: Can someone else's fingerprint unlock my GO?
entries.a: Yes, if it is saved on the phone. GO uses Android's own fingerprint check, which accepts any fingerprint (or other biometric) enrolled in the phone's settings. So turn on fingerprint unlock only if every fingerprint saved on the phone is yours; otherwise use your wallet password.

entries.q: Can someone get past GO's lock by restarting the app?
entries.a: No. GO's lock survives a reload, a crash recovery and an app restart: until a real unlock with your password or fingerprint, GO shows the lock screen again. After a fresh start it always goes through the normal fingerprint or password login.

entries.q: What should I do if I lose my phone or it is stolen?
aliases: lost phone with go on it
phone lost what about my qort
entries.a:
Your account is not on the phone alone; it lives on the Qortal network.
1. Restore it on another device with your seedphrase, or your backup file and its password.
2. If someone could get into GO on the lost phone (a weak or known password, or their fingerprint saved on it), create a new account at once and move your QORT and coin balances to it.

entries.q: Can a thief get into GO on my phone?
aliases: is go safe if my phone is stolen
can they open my qortal account
entries.a: Not easily. The account saved on the phone is encrypted with your wallet password, and GO locks itself when idle (Settings, System, Auto-Lock When Idle) and then asks for your password or fingerprint. The weak points are a short password, someone else's fingerprint saved on the phone, and GO left unlocked. Use a strong password, keep auto-lock on, and tap Lock now when you put the phone down.

entries.q: Should I remove my account before I give away my old phone?
aliases: sell my phone with go on it
entries.a: Yes. First check the account opens on your new device. Then on the old phone: remove the account in GO (Account details, Remove), delete any backup or seedphrase files from Documents, Qortal Go, and uninstall GO or reset the phone. A phone that still holds your account gives its next owner something to try passwords on.

entries.q: Will my QORT and names come back when I restore my account?
aliases: do i get my names back
entries.a: Yes, if it is the same account. QORT, names and everything else on the blockchain belong to the account, not to the device, so they show up as soon as GO reaches a node. If the balance is zero or your name is missing, you most likely opened a different account, often from a mistyped seedphrase: check the address.

entries.q: Is my private key stored on the blockchain?
aliases: is my key public on chain
where is my private key kept
entries.a: No. The blockchain holds your address and, after your first transaction, your public key, never your private key. The private key exists only in your wallet: the encrypted copy saved in GO or Hub, your backup file, and what your seedphrase can rebuild.

entries.q: Can someone work out my private key from my address or public key?
aliases: get private key from public key
can my address reveal my private key
entries.a: No. Your public key and address are made from the private key in a way that only works one way, which is why they are safe to share. Your signatures prove you hold the private key without revealing it.

entries.q: What happens if I lose my private key?
entries.a: You can't really lose it on its own: it is rebuilt from your seedphrase, and it is inside your backup file. Restore the account with either and the same private key comes back. If you have lost both the seedphrase and the backup file (or its password), the key is gone with them, and nobody can recover the account.

entries.q: Should I write down my private key as a backup?
aliases: keep a copy of my private key
entries.a: There is little point: GO and Hub restore accounts from a seedphrase or a backup file, not from a private key. A written key is just one more thing a thief could find. Back up the seedphrase and the backup file instead, and reveal the key (Settings, Security) only when you really need it.

entries.q: How safe is my private key on my phone?
aliases: private key safe on my phone
is my key encrypted in go
where does go keep my private key
entries.a: GO saves your account on the phone encrypted with your wallet password. While you are signed in, GO can sign with the key, which is why the lock matters: keep Auto-Lock When Idle on and use Lock now. GO also blocks screenshots on the screen that shows the key, and keeps its data out of Android cloud backup.

entries.q: Is it safe to use Qortal on a shared or borrowed device?
aliases: use qortal on a shared computer
log in on someone else's device
entries.a: Only with care. Use Import account, Authenticate now with your backup file, so the account is not saved there. Log out when you are done, and don't leave your backup file on that device. Never type your seedphrase on a device you do not trust.

entries.q: How can I test my backup without risk?
entries.a: Log out, then on the Enter Qortal screen use Import account, Authenticate now, and pick your backup file: it opens the account for that session without saving another copy. If it opens and shows your address, the file and password work. To test the seedphrase, restore it on a spare device, check the address, then remove it again.

entries.q: Should I keep my seedphrase, backup file and password together?
aliases: backup file and password same place
where to keep password and backup
entries.a: No. Keep the backup file and its password apart, because together they open your account. The seedphrase opens it on its own, so keep it on paper, offline, somewhere safe. Spread out like this, a thief who finds only the file cannot use it, and a fire or loss in one place does not take everything.

entries.q: What should I check before I accept a Q-App request?
aliases: check before accepting a q-app request
q-app approval window what to check
should i accept this q-app request
entries.a:
1. Who is asking: Requested by shows the app's icon and name. It should be the app you are using right now.
2. What it wants: the question at the top, such as allow this app to send coins?
3. The details: recipient (name and full address), amount, coin, and every fee line, including any App fee.
4. Whether you started it: decline any request you did not ask for.
Declining is always safe; an accepted payment cannot be undone.

entries.q: What does "allow this app to authenticate?" mean?
aliases: what happens when i authenticate a q-app
can a q-app see my balance
entries.a: The app is asking who you are. If you accept, it learns your Qortal address and public key, and while that tab stays open it may also read your wallet addresses, balances and transactions without asking again. It does not get your private key or seedphrase. Sending coins and publishing still need their own approval.

entries.q: Should I tick "always authenticate automatically"?
aliases: should i let a q-app authenticate automatically
entries.a: Only for an app you use often and trust. The tick is remembered for that app's name, so from then on it gets your address and the read-only wallet access every time it opens, without asking. The other always allow boxes, such as chat messages from this app or your balance, work the same way. Payments and publishes have no such box and always ask.

entries.q: Should I accept session permissions from a Q-App?
aliases: i trust this app and understand these permissions will auto-execute
entries.a: Only if you trust the app. The window lists actions, such as publishing, joining groups or reading your wallet, that will then run without asking while that tab stays open, and you must tick "I trust this app and understand these permissions will auto-execute". Decline if it asks for more than it needs. Sending coins can never be granted this way, and closing the tab ends the permissions.

entries.q: What should I check when a Q-App asks to send coins?
aliases: allow this app to send coins
app wants to send my qort
allow this app to transfer the following asset
entries.a: Check the recipient line: GO shows the name and the full address it will pay, so compare it with who you mean to pay. Then check the amount, the coin and the fee. You must tick "I have read this request" before Accept works. A sent payment cannot be undone, so if anything looks off, decline.

entries.q: What does "allow this app to sign a transaction?" mean?
aliases: allow this app to sign a transaction
allow this app to sign and process a transaction
read the transaction carefully before accepting
entries.a: The app has built a transaction and wants your key to sign it. The window shows its type (Tx type), its details and "read the transaction carefully before accepting!". A signed transaction does whatever its type does, including moving QORT, so accept only if you understand every line and expected it from that app.

entries.q: What happens if I tap Decline on a Q-App request?
aliases: what does decline do on a q-app request
is it safe to decline an approval
entries.a: Nothing happens: nothing is signed, sent or published, and the app is just told you declined. Declining is always safe, so use it whenever you are unsure. If the request was genuine, you can do the action again in the app later.

entries.q: Why doesn't the approval window react to my taps?
aliases: cant tap accept because of an overlay
entries.a: While an approval is open, GO ignores taps that pass through another app's window drawn on top of it, such as a chat bubble or screen filter, so a hidden overlay cannot trick you into accepting. On Android 12 and later GO also hides those overlays. On older phones, close or pause the overlay app and tap again.

entries.q: Can a Q-App take my QORT without asking?
aliases: q-app spend my qort without asking
can an app send my qort automatically
does a q-app need permission to pay
can a q-app steal my qort
entries.a: No. Every payment a Q-App asks for opens an approval window that needs your Accept, after you tick "I have read this request". There is no always allow box for payments, and session permissions cannot include sending coins. So a payment only happens if someone accepted it, which is why GO should be locked when you are not using it.

entries.q: Can a fake Q-App pretend to be another app in the approval window?
aliases: q-app pretending to be another app
entries.a: Not by changing the name GO shows. Requested by comes from the tab the request came from, never from the app's own text, and GO strips hidden characters that could disguise a name. But anyone can publish an app under a name that looks similar, so read the name letter by letter. If GO cannot tell which app asked, it says Unknown Q-App.

entries.q: What does "allow this app to get your wallet information?" mean?
aliases: allow this app to get your wallet information
always allow wallet to be retrieved automatically
entries.a: The app wants one of your coin wallets, shown as coin: QORT, LTC or another. Accepting gives it that wallet's address and public key; for BTC, LTC, DOGE, DGB and RVN that public key lets it see all of that wallet's addresses and history. It cannot spend from it. The always allow box makes this automatic for that app and coin.

entries.q: What does "allow this app to make the following payments and publishes?" mean?
aliases: allow this app to make the following payments and publishes
entries.a: The app wants to send one or more payments and publish one or more things in a single step. The window lists each payment (who and how much), each publish and the total amount, and you must tick "I have read this request". Check every recipient and the total, because all of it goes through with one Accept.

entries.q: What should I check when a Q-App asks to update my group?
aliases: allow this app to update this group
entries.a: Look at the new owner line first. An update can change the group's settings and its owner, so a wrong name there hands your group to someone else. Accept only if you asked for exactly that change in an app you trust; the fee is shown too.

entries.q: What should I check when a Q-App asks to buy, sell or change a name?
aliases: allow this app to buy a name
allow this app to update this name
q-app wants to sell my name
allow this app to register this name
entries.a: Read the name and price lines. Buy shows the name and how many QORT it costs. Sell shows which of your names and the asking price; once someone buys it, the name and the data published under it are theirs. Update shows the previous and the new name. Each costs a fee, so decline anything you did not set up yourself.

entries.q: What does "allow this app to perform the admin action" mean?
aliases: allow this app to perform the admin action
q-app admin action on my node
app wants to restart my node
entries.a: The app wants to control your own node: stop, restart or bootstrap it, add or remove peers, force a sync, or add or remove a minting account. The window names the action and any value. Accept only in a node tool you opened yourself for that job. These actions are refused on a public node.

entries.q: What does "allow this app to delete hosted resources?" mean?
aliases: allow this app to delete hosted resources
allow this app to get a list of your hosted data
entries.a: Your node keeps copies of QDN data it hosts for the network. A Q-App can ask to list that hosted data, or to delete some of it from your node; the window says how many items. Accept only in a storage tool you trust. Neither works on a public node.

entries.q: Is it safe when a Q-App wants to save a file to my phone?
aliases: would you like to download from a q-app
app saves a file to my phone
entries.a: GO first asks "would you like to download:" with the file name, and saves the file in Documents, Qortal Go. Web pages such as .html and .svg are saved as text so they cannot run, and GO never opens or installs an app package (APK) it downloads. Still, open saved files only from apps and people you trust.

entries.q: What does "allow this app to send this chat message?" mean?
aliases: allow this app to send this chat message
q-app sends a chat message as me
always allow chat messages from this app
entries.a: The app wants to post a message as you, to the person or group shown, with the start of the text. Check who it goes to and what it says. Ticking always allow chat messages from this app lets it send messages as you from then on without asking, so keep that for apps you fully trust.

entries.q: What does "would you like to deploy this AT?" mean?
aliases: would you like to deploy this at
entries.a: An AT is a small program that runs on the Qortal chain, used for things like trades. Deploying one creates it and puts the amount shown into it, plus the fee, and you must tick "I have read this request". Accept only if you meant to start exactly that, in an app you trust.

entries.q: What should I do if I accepted a Q-App request by mistake?
entries.a: A payment, name sale or publish you accepted cannot be undone. Session permissions end when you close that app's tab, so close it. An always allow tick stays for that app, so stop using the app if you no longer trust it. Approving requests never gives an app your seedphrase or private key, so the account itself stays yours.

entries.q: Someone asked for my backup file or wallet password. Is that a scam?
entries.a: Yes. Nobody needs your backup file or password to help you, and nobody from Qortal will ever ask. With the file and the password they can take everything in the account. Real help is given with words; never send the file, the password, your seedphrase or your private key.

entries.q: Someone says they are a Qortal admin or developer and offers to help. What should I do?
aliases: someone pretending to be the qortal team
entries.a: Be careful, especially if they messaged you first. Look their name up in Address book (User search) and check the address against one you already know. Real admins and developers never need your seedphrase, backup file, password, private key or a payment to help you. Keep help in public groups, where others can see it.

entries.q: How can I check that a name belongs to the person I think?
aliases: is this the real person on qortal
entries.a: Open Address book (User search) and look the name up: it shows the address behind it. Compare that address with one you already trust, for example from an earlier payment or the person's own posts. A similar-looking name can belong to someone else entirely; the address is what counts.

entries.q: Can someone register a name that looks like mine or a well-known one?
aliases: fake name looks like an admin
entries.a: Yes. Any name nobody has taken yet can be registered by anyone, so impostors use names that differ by a letter, a number or a space. GO refuses payment recipients whose names hide invisible characters, but visible lookalikes still work. Check the address, not just the name, before you pay or trust someone.

entries.q: Someone sent me a link to verify or sync my wallet. Is it safe?
entries.a: No, it is a phishing trick. Your wallet never needs verifying or syncing through a website, and no real page needs your seedphrase, private key, backup file or password. Type them only into GO's own Import account screen, when you restore an account yourself. Free QORT or airdrop links that ask for them are the same trick.

entries.q: What happens when I tap a web link in a chat in GO?
aliases: tap a link in a message
is it safe to tap links in qortal chat
entries.a: A web link opens in your phone's browser, outside GO, and GO hands that site nothing from your wallet. Links that point back at GO itself or at this phone (localhost, 127.0.0.1) are refused. A qortal:// link opens a Q-App or site inside GO instead. Be wary of links from people you don't know, and never type your secrets into a page a link opened.

entries.q: Someone sent me an APK file in chat. Should I install it?
aliases: someone sent me an app file
